description: Bon Chic, Bon Genre (BCBG, "Parisian Chic") is the understated-elegance uniform of the traditional French high bourgeoisie, codified in the late 1970s–1980s in Paris and Versailles. Recognize it by a neutral wardrobe of navy, beige, camel, grey and cream — tailored blazers, trench coats, cashmere V-necks, cigarette pants — punctuated by discreet heritage accessories: a silk scarf knotted at the neck, a pearl strand, a structured leather handbag, loafers or ballet flats. Subjects are poised, well-groomed figures (solo, in couples, or small groups) on Haussmannian streets, stone steps, church parvises or seamless studio backdrops, lit softly and framed head-to-toe so the tailored silhouette reads cleanly.

name: Bondage
description: Bondage is a kink-derived aesthetic whose visual DNA is the restraint itself: leather straps and O-ring collars, silver chains and cuffs, shibari rope geometry on bare skin, and mirror-gloss latex/PVC, set in a black-dominated palette punctuated by saturated red and cold silver hardware. It reads through chiaroscuro contrast of skin against restraints, poses of vulnerability or dominance, and craft-forward ropework and leatherwork rather than explicit content. Subjects range from fragment close-ups of necks and wrists to runway catsuits, bound torsos of any gender, arrest-roleplay scenes, and even miniature rope-wrapped objects.

name: Bosozoku
description: Japanese outlaw biker-gang aesthetic (origin 1950s, peak Showa–Heisei streets) built on over-customized motorcycles and long black tokkofuku coats densely embroidered with gold-thread kanji, crests and phoenixes. Signature elements: towering sandan three-tier seats, candy magenta/purple/pearl paint with rising-sun ray graphics, gang flags and banners, hachimaki headbands, air horns and straight-pipe exhausts. Typical subjects: posed gang lineups, rows of parked custom bikes, night runs, convenience-store forecourts, rendered in saturated film-snapshot color.

name: Boujee
description: Boujee (aka Bougie, Material Girl, Night Luxe) is the social-media-native glamour of overt new-money display — champagne rituals, sequins, satin, fur and crystal jewels lit by harsh phone flash against night interiors, marble foyers and penthouse views. Its palette runs champagne gold, platinum silver, pearl ivory, blush and black-tie black, with sparkle treated as a surface texture over everything; subjects range from mirror-selfie party figures and black-tie men to macro lips, logo heels, chandelier halls and toasting flutes. Recognize it by flash-burned specular highlights, glitter and lens-flare overlays, brand-forward abundance and a first-person "posted, not staged" stance.

name: Brat_Summer
description: Brat Summer is the mid-2024 party microtrend born from Charli XCX's album Brat: an acidic "brat green" lime (core ~#8ACE00) used as flat graphic field, club-light wash or hero object, paired with lowercase condensed Arial-Narrow-style type, disposable-flash party snapshots, halftone collage graphics, and deliberately trashy Y2K/Indie-Sleaze styling (smudged eyeliner, strappy white tanks, leather miniskirts, lime PVC bags and nails). Recognize it by lime dominance plus messy, ironic hedonism; plan images that are loud, grainy, flash-hard and confidently imperfect.

name: Bravú
description: Bravú (Rock Bravú) is the visual language of the mid-1990s Galician rock movement: xerox-grade DIY collage of grainy black-and-white photography, hand-scrawled marker and stenciled lettering in Galician, and a high-contrast print palette of black, flag red, high-contrast yellow and green. Signature content collides rural and coastal Galician life — cows, tractors, mussels, crabs, bagpipes (gaita), village stone, Galician flags — with punk signifiers (mohawks, band tees, red stars), delivered with deadpan humor and child-friendly cartoon mascots like the Xabarín boar. Expect square album covers, flyer and magazine collages, overcast Atlantic daylight or harsh on-camera flash, and deliberate photocopy misregistration.

name: Brazilcore
description: Brazilcore is an early-2020s, TikTok-born streetwear aesthetic that filters Y2K fashion and football fervor through the Brazilian flag's green, yellow, blue and white. Its signature look pairs the yellow-and-green national jersey (or flag-color-blocked crop tops, tracksuits and shorts) with low-rise baggy jeans, cargo pants or miniskirts, captured as candid flash snapshots of street parties, bars and market corners. Load this skill when an image combines patriotic Brazilian sportswear, Y2K silhouettes and celebratory, color-blocked snapshot energy.

name: Brazilian_Bombshell
description: Retrospective label for the glossy supermodel glamour of Brazilian models in the 2000s–2010s Victoria's Secret era — sun-kissed bronzed skin, long glossy wavy hair, toned athletic-curvy bodies shown off in low-rise denim, slogan baby tees, lingerie and runway wings. Palette couples warm bronze, honey-to-espresso hair and denim/white/black bases with saturated pops of hot pink, turquoise, citrus yellow and lime, lit by direct camera flash, even studio gloss or golden sunlight. Mood is confident, healthy, carefree sensuality; compositions run from laughing group candids and backstage moments to glossy magazine covers and wind-blown beauty portraits.

name: Brazilian_Carnival
description: Brazilian Carnival (Carnaval Brasileiro) is the maximalist festival aesthetic of Brazil's pre-Lent revelry since the 1800s: saturated jewel-tone polychrome anchored by metallic gold, radial feather headdresses, glittered skin, sequin-and-bead costume bodies, masquerade masks, falling confetti and streamers, small multicolored frevo umbrellas, and dense parade rows in sambadromes or sunlit streets. Subjects range from close portraits of smiling costumed dancers to night-floodlit parade avenues, percussion blocos, papier-mâché giant dolls and ox effigies, and float tableaux; the mood is collective joy, abundance and charm. Load this skill when an image must read as Brazilian street or samba-school carnival rather than Venetian masquerade, retro pinup glamour, or generic party confetti.

name: Brazilian_Phonk
description: Brazilian Phonk is the cover-art aesthetic of the late-2010s funk carioca × phonk fusion: anime and manga anti-heroes rendered as near-silhouettes against a pure black void, wreathed in a single saturated neon aura (magenta, violet, acid green, electric blue) with blank glowing eyes, jagged lightning or flame energy, aggressive chrome typography and glitch artifacts. Recognize it by its black-void-plus-one-hue emissive discipline, confrontational centered figure, square streaming-cover framing, and a mood of aggression, hype and supernatural menace.

name: Bright_Tertiaries
description: Mid-2000s graphic, product and interior design aesthetic built on a tertiary palette (lime green, teal, purple, orange — or the lime/fuchsia/cyan variant), rounded edges, flat one-hue color blocks, bayadère irregular stripes and stylized vector florals with flourishes. Shows up on school and library interiors, girls' floral dresses, molded-plastic homewares, keypad-era phone shells, storage cubes and bubble-letter logotypes, all lit bright and even with a consumer-friendly "humanist" warmth. Recognize by saturated-but-soft tertiaries in matte flat blocks plus intricate floral or striped pattern surfaces; never neon primaries, never glossy skeuomorphic skies, never flat-figures corporate minimalism.

name: British_Countryside
description: British Countryside is the estate-sport aesthetic of the British nobility and their staff — hunting, shooting, equestrianism, golf — whose visual language crystallised between the Victorian era and the 1950s. Expect olive and moss tweed, brown leather, beige and honey-coloured stone with disciplined scarlet accents; plus fours, flat caps, brogues and Wellington boots; horses, gun dogs, double-barrelled shotguns; patchwork fields, dry stone walls, misted moors and lived-in country-house interiors with fireplaces, chintz and mudrooms. Recognise it by functional, weather-worn layering and picturesque overcast or firelight rather than polished luxury.

name: Britpop
description: Mid-1990s British guitar-pop movement look — Union Jack red, white and navy flashed against night black, khaki parkas, navy track jackets and Mod-fringe haircuts, captured in hard on-camera flash snaps or flat pop-art graphic layouts. Signature elements include flag-printed guitars and vest tops, terrace sportswear (track tops, football shirts, low-profile Adidas), slim retro dandy suits with skinny ties, pints of beer, red phone boxes, and bold slab typography with sticker-badge overlays. Typical subjects are clusters of lads and lasses in everyday British streets, pubs, supermarkets and music-press covers, projecting cheeky working-class pride.

name: Bro_Culture
description: Bro Culture is the North American hypermasculine subculture aesthetic of fraternities, sports teams, gyms, tailgates and festival fields — packed group shots of young men in jerseys, muscle tees, cargo shorts and frayed baseball caps with beer cans and Monster Energy in hand. Its color palette is deliberately unrestricted across the spectrum; coherence comes from saturated daylight or club-neon lighting, snapshot/stock-photo realism, cluttered status interiors (beer pong tables, trophy cases, Greek letters, neon signs, piled empties) and rowdy homosocial body language. Load this skill for images of male pack celebration, lift/gym pride, man-cave clutter, tailgate and rave crowds, or meme edits that rewrite familiar scenes as all-male parties.

name: Bro_Hoe
description: Mid-2000s Southern California party-girl offshoot of McBling: black skate/motocross graphic tees (Ed Hardy, Metal Mulisha, Affliction-type skulls, wings, stars and gothic lettering) cut with hot pink, white and red, trucker hats, studded belts, two-toned blonde-over-black hair, thick eyeliner and tanned skin. MySpace snapshot energy — direct camera flash, fisheye lenses, photobooth strips, Monster Energy cans, lifted trucks, DGAF poses. Recognize by the fusion of masculine moto/skate brand graphics with high-maintenance glam femininity.

name: Bronze_Age_China
description: The ritual metal culture of China's Xia, Shang and Zhou dynasties (c. 2070–221 BCE) — bronze ding cauldrons, zun and jue wine vessels, gu beakers, zhong bells and ge dagger-axes carrying symmetrical taotie masks, yunlei swirl grounds and cast jinwen inscriptions. Its palette swings between excavated malachite-teal patina crusts and the original dazzling "auspicious metal" gold, with jade blades, turquoise inlay and inscribed bone as companion materials. Composition is axial, banded and gravely ceremonial, lit by a single reverent source or museum spotlight.

name: Brostep
description: Brostep (American dubstep) is the maximalist EDM aesthetic of roughly 2009–2015, built on black-void compositions lit by a single toxic neon accent — Monster-Energy green, electric cyan, or ultraviolet purple — striking shattered glass, chrome machinery and hazard signage. Signature elements are gas masks and respirators, biohazard and radioactive symbols, skulls, neon laser slashes, particle-shatter bursts and beveled 3D chrome logotypes timed to the bass drop, with the high-contrast "Dubstep Joker" grin as its mascot trope. Typical subjects are masked or hooded figures, dystopian robots and monsters, emblem-like album logos and gamer HUD fragments, rendered in aggressive Cinema-4D-style digital art for album covers, YouTube intros and Call of Duty montages.

name: Brutagrafix
description: Brutagrafix (aka Nu-Brutalism, Graphic Brutalism, Brutalist Utilitarian) is a late-2010s/early-2020s poster, zine and UI aesthetic that fuses 1950s béton-brut concrete mass with playful digital graphics: oversized raw sans-serif type, hard offset shadows, thick black outlines, boxy grids, halftone photo cutouts and translucent flat panels in clashing green/red/blue/neon on stark white or near-black. Recognize it by loud, type-driven layouts that stay deliberately usable, spiced with 90s-internet artifacts (pixel checkers, dither, barcodes, repeated word-labels) and, in satellite registers, naive doodles, zine scrapbook tactility, folk woodcut motifs or anti-design collage chaos.

name: Brutalism
description: Brutalism is the architectural aesthetic of the 1950s–1970s built on raw, unfinished concrete (béton brut): monumental blocky masses, repetitive prefabricated modules, exposed structure, and a grey-to-buff monochrome palette punctuated at most by sparse primary-color accents. Typical subjects are civic and collective buildings — housing slabs, city halls, universities, libraries, theatres, churches, bus terminals — shot under flat overcast or hard daylight with tiny or absent human figures. Recognize it by board-marked concrete, deep coffered recesses, cantilevered megastructural forms, and an ornament-free, stoic civic mood.

name: Bubble_Bujo
description: Bubble Bujo is a 2020s K-pop stan decoration aesthetic built around 6-ring binders, idol photocards, stickers, beads and resin shaker keychains, dressed in bright candy pastels, gingham and holographic glitter. Its signature look is a collage-dense binder spread or flatlay in which a printed portrait photocard is haloed by letter stickers, cartoon bears, hearts, stars and smiley faces under bright, even, high-key light. Recognize it by tactile stationery craft — translucent PVC binders, pearl and plastic beads, glitter glue, glossy photocard paper — plus bubbly thick retro type; it is distinct from Kidcore's toybox primaries and Kawaii's character-first design.

name: Bubbleglam
description: Bubbleglam (also called Bubblegrunge) is a mid-to-late-1990s pop-fashion aesthetic of candy-saturated kitsch — hot pink and orange color fields, satin and vivid faux fur, excessive drag-inflected makeup, and blown-out flash lighting — fusing bubblegum pop, 1970s glam-rock revival and Club Kids excess with a wink of 90s cynicism. It surfaces as magazine editorials, CD single covers, perfume-ad campaigns and music-video stills: color-blocked group tableaux, baby doll dresses and miniskirts, lace and plush textures, bubble-letter and sunburst typography. Load this skill when an image or brief combines synthetic candy color, plush/satin materials, over-made-up faces and ironic playfulness.

name: Bubblegum_Bitch
description: A 200s-descended hyperfeminine "brat" aesthetic (aka Brat Aesthetic, Barbie Bitch, McBling Baddie, Sexy Barbiecore) built on a light-pink-to-hot-magenta monochrome field, glitter, rhinestones, satin and faux fur, fused with childlike cartoon icons (Hello Kitty, Bratz, Powerpuff Girls) and bold stylized profanity or bratty slogans. Typical images are flash-lit phone snapshots, pink flat-lay collages, detail crops of nails/chokers/dyed hair, or airbrushed Y2K graphic edits pairing cute characters with swear words, chains, stilettos and candy motifs. Recognize by the sweet-versus-jaded collision: bubblegum-soft surfaces carrying adult attitude, wealth flexing and ironic political text.

name: Bubblegum_Bling
description: Bubblegum Bling is the late-2010s hyperpop-era revival of 2000s McBling: sleek, hyper-feminine, digitally glossy imagery in hot pink, baby pink, silver and iridescent pastels. Its signature elements are glossy and translucent materials (jelly plastic, glass hearts, faceted gems), chrome and airbrush lettering, rhinestones, tiaras, fur and velour, sleek flip-phone-era technology, and starburst sparkle flares over render-smooth surfaces. Typical subjects are pop-star glamour portraits, product-style still lifes, rendered boudoir interiors, and album-cover type pieces native to TikTok and Instagram.

name: Bubblegum_Coquette
description: Bubblegum Coquette is a mid-2010s Tumblr-born coquette substyle that fuses a hyper-feminine bubblegum-pink pastel palette with 2000s girlhood nostalgia — swirly lollipops, roller skates, hair bows, pigtails, braces, stuffed animals, princess and Sanrio cartoons — set against deliberately suggestive adult-coded signals like too-small baby tees, lingerie silhouettes, thigh-highs and platform heels. Recognize it by pink-dominant high-key imagery, glitter and sticker overlays, teen-magazine collage layouts, glossy candy props, and its core juxtaposition of childish innocence with flirtatious eroticism.

name: Bubblegum_Dance
description: Late-1990s Scandinavian and Italian Eurodance aesthetic of the "living cartoon": hyper-saturated neon pink, electric blue, lime green and tangerine over glossy plastic playsets, blue CGI cyber backdrops and candy props, with performers styled as color-blocked human toys or replaced entirely by CGI mascots. Signature elements include bubble-letter logos, radial candy swirls and starbursts, dollhouse and space playsets, latex and metallic lamé costumes, spiked dyed hair, and flat high-key studio lighting. Reads as deliberately artificial, ironic, mass-market playful pop — toy-shop gloss, not club grit.

name: Buchón
description: Buchón is a 2000s Sinaloa, Mexico narco-culture aesthetic of conspicuous consumption — baroque gold-on-black Versace/Gucci silk shirts, thick gold chains, designer denim, beaded baseball caps or cowboy hats, posed with modified pickup trucks, exotic animals, gold-plated firearms and designer bags. Its visual DNA is horror vacui (every surface of body, garment and vehicle covered in logo, gold or ornament) captured in warm, faded amateur smartphone snapshots with chest-puffed, chin-up posturing. Recognize it by logomania, gold jewelry, the ranchero-luxury hybrid wardrobe and ostentatious props; the feminine counterpart, buchona, adds hyper-glam surgically enhanced styling, heavy makeup and quilted designer handbags.

name: Buckle_Bunny
description: Buckle Bunny is the pink-washed groupie fringe of rodeo culture — 1970s western dress filtered through hyper-feminine southern-belle kitsch, revived in 2024 via Chappell Roan and Pinterest coquette circles. Its visual DNA pairs hard western hardware (engraved trophy belt buckles, cowgirl boots, felt hats, horseshoes, denim cutoffs) with a governing bubblegum-pink wash, red-or-pink plaid, cherry pie and campy revolver motifs over denim blue, leather brown and cream. Expect lo-fi flash snapshots, faded film pastels, neon cursive diner signage, paint horses and lipstick-kiss prints rather than polished editorial western.

name: Buffalo_Style
description: Buffalo Style is the mid-1980s London styling aesthetic of Ray Petri's Buffalo collective (1984–89), built on colliding oversized, pinned-and-clamped tailoring with MA-1 flight jackets, kilts on men, boxer shorts and cowboy hardware, worn by street-cast, multicultural models with a deadpan "hard" stare. Recognize it in high-contrast black-and-white or sepia 35mm frames against matte studio backdrops, porkpie/bowler/cowboy hats personalized with pinned words or badges, and a palette of black, white, olive drab, indigo and sepia. It reads as authored editorial collage — style over fashion — never as glossy designer catalog or club costume.

name: Burlesque
description: Burlesque is the theatrical variety-show aesthetic descended from Victorian travesty revues and early-20th-century American striptease: corsets and bullet bras, V-fringe, ostrich feather fans, opera gloves, lace stockings with garters, top hats and harlequin diamonds, lit in warm spotlight reds against jet black, ivory and brass gold. Its images read as stage tableau, lithograph playbill, candlelit dressing room or faded troupe photograph — always carrying a wink of parody, tease and flamboyant exaggeration. Recognizable across three surface modes: saturated stage photography, sepia/monochrome archival print, and Art Nouveau poster lithography with lettering bands.

name: Burtonesque
description: Burtonesque is the gothic-whimsical illustration style descended from Tim Burton's 1980s–1990s films and sketchbooks: spindly, pale characters with oversized heavy-lidded eyes and dark eyebags, scratchy chaotic ink linework, Victorian-gothic ornament, and a gloomy palette of black, gray, bone white, dusty blue and olive green punctured by one stark color pop. Recognize it by grotesque exaggerated anatomy (wire-thin limbs, sunken cheeks, wispy hair), stripes and checkerboard staging, wrought-iron filigree, bare twisted trees, and a mood of melancholy playfulness rather than outright horror.

name: Busukawaii
description: Busukawaii (busukawa, "ugly-cute") is a 2000s Japanese meme-born aesthetic that dresses deliberately homely, grumpy or off-kilter subjects in earnest kawaii trimmings: pastel haze filters, glitter and sparkle overlays, heart and star stickers, satin bows, flower crowns and plush costumes. Recognize it by the tension between an ugly-but-lovable face (scowling pets, lumpy mascots, bootleg plush with crooked lips, off-model cartoon edits, anguished ordinary people) and a sincere candy coating of baby pink, lavender and primary-color pops, delivered in low-fi JPEG snapshot or amateur-edit quality.

name: Cabincore
description: Cabincore is an early-2020s internet aesthetic that romanticizes dwelling in a remote woodland cabin — raw timber, stone and wool interiors lit by wood stoves, string lights and campfire glow, set against conifer forest, fog and mountain dusk. Its palette runs brown, pine green, fog white and ember orange, with buffalo-check flannel, chunky knits, enamel mugs, cast-iron stoves and paper books as signature props. Recognizable subjects range from a tiny cabin dwarfed by tall trees, to first-person cozy interiors with feet up by the fire, to kraft-paper craft flat-lays and misty forest mornings.

name: Cacareco_Girl
description: Cacareco Girl is a Brazilian TikTok microtrend (2024) of portable maximalism: handbags, cameras, phones and pouches overloaded with sentimentally curated trinkets — plush collectibles (Labubu, Sylvanian Families), handmade bead chains, keychains, photo charms — in a vibrant eclectic palette of hot pink, cherry red, grass green and denim blue. Snapshot-lit close crops of cluttered carried objects, gingham and stripe accents, pearl-strung charms, and an anti-minimalist "inner child" warmth define the look. Use this skill to recognize or generate images of trinket-laden personal objects and the eclectic Brazilian fashion that surrounds them.

name: Cagole
description: Cagole is the hyperfeminine working-class aesthetic of Marseille and Provence (slang crystallized in the 1980s, visual code peaking in the 2000s): tanned skin under cakey, mismatched foundation, blue or white eyeshadow with kohl liner and overlined nude lips, long flat-ironed blonde or dark hair, leopard and zebra prints, tight low-cut dresses in mallow pink and deep red, ear hoops, rhinestone word-necklaces and platform stilettos. It appears in loud candid flash snapshots of laughing friend groups, pageant stages, club nights and sun-bleached Mediterranean streets, valuing excess, assertiveness and Provençal pride over any notion of restraint.

name: Campcore
description: Campcore is a 2010s outdoor-life aesthetic built around the occupied campsite: campfires, tent doors opening onto pine forest, enamel mugs, cast-iron kettles, wool socks and folded paper maps. Its palette is dark green, bark brown, greyish taupe and burnt orange, lit by firelight, blue-hour dusk, fog or lantern glow, with the human present as trace (socked feet, hands around a mug, a backed-turned hiker) rather than portrait. Recognize it when warmth, temporary shelter and well-used practical gear dominate the frame — as opposed to summit-hero adventure, domestic cabin interiors, or untouched nature.

name: Canadiana
description: Canadiana is Canada's national vernacular aesthetic, solidified in the 1960s: red-and-white maple-leaf iconography laid over snow, warm wood tones and sepia parchment, spanning hand-tinted trade-era snowscapes, folk ephemera collages, stone-hearth lodge interiors and mid-century advertising boards. Signature elements are exposed timber and fieldstone fireplaces, plaid wool and hides, maple leaves, ice skates, curling crests, vintage pennants and stamps, and snow-laden birch and spruce, all carrying a mood of cozy survival against harsh winter. Use when recognizing or generating Canadian national nostalgia, cottage and lodge interiors, winter trade labor, or vintage Canadian advertising graphics.

name: Candycore
description: Candycore is an internet aesthetic (visual lineage in late-2000s pop, term coined c. 2020) built on the maximalist, surreal depiction of candy, confectionery and dessert texture — lollipops, gumdrops, sprinkles, piped frosting, cotton candy, wrapped sweets — rendered in fruit-candy rainbow neons or sorbet pastels anchored by pastel pink. Signature cues are fill-the-frame abundance, glossy hard-candy shine and iridescent sugar glaze, candy used as decoration (makeup, hair, rooms, prints) rather than realistic food, and a playful, kitschy, nostalgic mood. Load this skill for candy piles, candy buffets and apothecary jars, freakshakes and loaded cones, sprinkle makeup and cotton-candy hair, sugar installations, or pastel-neon confectionery patterns.

name: Candyland
description: Candyland is a whimsical children's-media setting in which the entire world — terrain, flora, architecture, sometimes inhabitants — is constructed from sweets: cotton-candy clouds, gingerbread and biscuit buildings, lollipop and candy-cane trees, gumdrop hills, syrup water, rainbow candy-tile paths. Its palette runs in two registers, a hazy pastel-pink dreamscape and a fully saturated rainbow primary scheme, both unified by glossy hard-candy swirls set against fluffy sugar fluff under high-key diffuse light. Recognize it by edible geography at landscape scale: if the trees, roofs and clouds are confectionery, this is Candyland rather than candy-themed decoration.

name: Cani
description: Cani is the visual culture of working-class Andalusian (Spanish) youth from the 1990s–2000s: bootleg tracksuits and football jerseys, heavy gold chains and rings, sideways or backward baseball caps, tribal tattoos, hoop earrings and customized scooters, captured in harsh compact-camera flash. Its palette anchors on black, white and metallic gold punctured by vibrant football-team reds, greens and blues against beige Mediterranean walls and night-black flash falloff. Recognize it by the amateur snapshot register, gelled frosted-tip hair, group bravado poses and street, plaza or disco settings.

name: Cannibalcore
description: Cannibalcore is a Tumblr-born (c. 2020, via the Hannibal revival) aesthetic that frames consumption — blood, flesh, anatomical hearts, bared teeth, red wine, knives laid for a table of two — as a metaphor for devouring love and obsession. Its palette sits on a single red axis from bone-white and blush pink through cherry to oxblood and black, rendered in impasto oil paint, grainy cinematic stills, candlelit vanitas still life, pastel butcher diagrams and confessional quote cards. Recognize it by gore that is soft, optional and yoked to tenderness: blood soaked into white lace, a cherry pie spelling "eat your heart out," two foreheads touching through smeared crimson.

name: Caricaturism
description: Caricaturism is the likeness-distortion tradition running from 16th-century grotesque heads through 18th–19th-century print satire (Gillray, Nast) to MAD-magazine airbrush gloss, bobblehead toys, editorial ink-and-wash cartoons and crude MS Paint meme faces: a recognizable subject rebuilt with amplified identifying traits — monumental noses, jutting jaws, gap teeth, bulging eyes, colossal heads on shrunken bodies. Palette is mode-dependent but always face-first: saturated sunburst yellows and signal reds, newsprint cream and graphite, flat sage or blue-grey cartoon grounds, or sickly ochre and grey-green flesh in the grotesque register. Mood is humoristic and satirical, mockery as commentary, willingly verging on the grotesque and absurd.

name: Carson-Dellosa_Art_Style
description: North American classroom clip-art aesthetic (established 1976, dominant on 1980s–2000s bulletin boards) defined by one rigid face canon — oblong eyes with pupils seated low and turned outward, tiny high surprise eyebrows, a shiny pink oval nose, and a thin rounded smile flanked by cheek half-circles — stamped identically onto children, animals, and anthropomorphized objects alike. Saturated primaries with soft airbrush gradients, thick uniform black outlines, die-cut bulletin-board silhouettes, open waving poses, and chart-or-poster layouts with playful tilted lettering. Recognize it by emotional uniformity: every snowman, pencil, quilt, and question mark wears the same eager, simpering smile.

name: Casino
description: Casino is a gambling-floor aesthetic organized around playing cards, poker chips, dice and roulette wheels under designed light — neon tube washes, marquee bulbs, or chandelier gold. Its palette anchors in black, white, red and gold over baize green, splitting into an opulent High Roller branch (velvet, brass, formalwear) and a playful Tourist branch (slot-machine aisles, magenta-violet neon, casual dress). Every frame implies a bet in progress: decadence, luck and trickery staged inside an adult playground.

name: Cassette_Futurism
description: Retrofuturism of the early 1970s to mid-1990s built around chunky beige, cream and grey machine casings, boxy CRT monitors with curved phosphor glass, and data that lives on physical media — compact cassettes, cartridges, floppy disks, reel-to-reel tape. Palette is casing neutrals punctured by small red, green or blue LED points, olive LCDs and green phosphor; interfaces are fields of buttons, rotary dials, toggle switches and cryptic labels, often bolted onto legacy hardware. Typical subjects are microcomputers, control rooms, labs, handheld consoles, hi-fi stacks and spaceship bridges rendered with utilitarian, institutional calm rather than neon noir gloss.

name: Casuals
description: British football-terrace subculture of the late 1970s–1980s in which young working-class men wear expensive European designer sportswear — Fred Perry and Peter Werth polos, Sergio Tacchini, Fila, Ellesse and Kappa track tops, cricket and tennis knits, corduroy flares or stonewash jeans, white leather Adidas trainers — captured in faded consumer-film snapshots on terraces, trains and street corners. Palette of brand-coded blocks (tennis cream, oxblood, bottle green, navy, petrol teal, ice blue, optical white with contrast tipping) set against olive parkas, grey concrete, red brick and bleached overcast sky; wedge haircuts, tiny embroidered chest logos, group congregation and cool competitive pride.

name: Catholic_Horror
description: Catholic Horror is a religious-horror aesthetic codified in 1970s cinema (The Exorcist, Rosemary's Baby, The Omen) that stages Roman Catholic ritual — crucifixes, holy water, exorcism, priests and nuns, candlelit Gothic cathedrals — under low-key chiaroscuro and analog grain. Its palette is black, bone ivory, candle gold, wound red and cold stone blue; its motifs include weeping or cracked statues, votive candle rows, communion veils, ossuaries and gargoyles, all carrying solemn dread of possession, sin and death. Recognize it by sacred iconography treated simultaneously as weapon and wound: solemn, shadow-swallowed tableaux where the sacred is corrupted but never absent.

name: Catholic_Kitsch
description: Mass-produced, sentimental Roman Catholic devotional imagery and objects — glossy plaster and plastic statues, glittery rosaries, light-up shelf shrines, gold-foil holy cards and airbrushed Madonnas in candy pastel or saturated rose-teal-gold palettes. A 20th-century "lived religion" aesthetic of domestic altars, flaming Sacred Hearts, pope novelties and sweet-faced holy prints, sincere rather than ironic. Recognize it by frontal icon poses, radiant heart-glow, floral wreath borders, cherub rings, and cheap tactile materials (plaster, plastic, glitter, electric bulbs) rendered with unembarrassed sweetness.

name: Catholic_Mexican_Girl
description: A 2020s TikTok-born fashion microtrend (also "Latina Fairy" or "Mexican Fairy") that fuses coquette hyper-femininity with romanticized Spanish-colonial Mexican Catholicism: white cotton, linen or organza dresses with lace, ruffles and petticoats, cut off-the-shoulder or midriff-baring in a "virginal but not modest" register; gold crucifixes and rosaries worn as fashion necklaces; red ribbons, shawls and rose accents; double braids or lace mantillas; settings of candlelit home altars, veladoras, Marian statues, terracotta plazas and cantera-stone doorways. Palette of stark white, warm black, crimson/terracotta red and gold, photographed moody and blue-tinted or in faded film warmth, with solemn, statue-like poses. Recognize it by the modesty-versus-allure tension plus devotional objects used purely as accessories.

name: Cayetana
description: Cayetana (also Cayestyle, Pija) is a late-2010s Spanish TikTok aesthetic of upper-class daughterly understatement: loose neutral wardrobes in beige, white, black and navy, wide-leg trousers, oversized knits, Converse/Veja/Golden Goose sneakers, delicate gold chains, a designer handbag and black Ray-Bans, photographed as sunlit street snapshots or phone-in-front mirror selfies. Recognition hinges on studied casualness — natural makeup, unforced hair, heritage Spanish stone backdrops, vertical smartphone framing — rather than on any single garment. It separates from Old Money and Pijo by its Gen-Z camera-roll vernacular, and from Milipili and Torero by its muted, costume-free palette.

name: Changelingcore
description: Changelingcore is a late-2010s Tumblr-born aesthetic of neurodivergent otherness reclaimed through fairy folklore: mossy forests, fog-filmed ponds, pebble streams and fairy rings rendered in desaturated moss-green, humus-brown and bone-white under dappled shade or moonlight. Its signature is uncanny tenderness — body fragments fusing with plants, arms arching out of dark water, cute objects made slightly wrong — alongside hoarded collections of pebbles and shinies, layered eccentric clothing, and an aged-oil or muted-film surface. Typical subjects are barefoot figures half-swallowed by foliage, still lifes of strange collections, and fogged liminal waterscapes.

name: Chaotic_Academia
description: Chaotic Academia is the late-2010s Tumblr-born offshoot of the Academia family that pictures learning as lived-in disorder: scattered papers, illegible margin annotations, dusty paperbacks, sticky-note walls and incorrectly worn uniforms inside fluorescent classrooms, dim libraries and overcast city streets. Its palette is paper-white, beige, concrete gray and woody brown rendered in grainy, lo-fi light, and its signature move is deadpan humor — highbrow diction undercut by profanity or absurdity — in service of an anti-elitist love of study. Recognize it by cluttered desks and floors, torn and stained pages, candid snapshot framing, and institutional architecture used irreverently, never by candlelit reverence or curated tidiness.

name: Chernobyl_Stalkers
description: Documentary aesthetic of the illegal explorers of the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone — grainy, handheld photographs of anonymous figures in military-surplus gear and gas masks moving through abandoned Pripyat interiors, rusted Brutalist concrete and overgrown pine forest. Palette of black, oxidized hazard yellow and military green over concrete grey, with Soviet relics (cathode-ray TVs, wall mosaics, paper-strewn classrooms, Cyrillic slogans) as still-life anchors. Mood is furtive, melancholic and anti-authoritarian; lighting runs from overcast window light to blue-hour silhouettes.

name: Cherry_Emoji_Twitter
description: Cherry Emoji Twitter (CET, formerly Hoe Twitter) is a 2010s Twitter-born fashion and moodboard aesthetic of sexual liberation, built on a cherry-red / hot-pink / white palette loaded with cherry prints, glitter hearts, lollipops and glossy red lips. Its images are lo-fi phone selfies, pink moodboard collages, fruit-and-cake still lifes and succubus-tinged zine art that pair cutesy sweetness with erotic, mischievous menace — blood-red syrup, candle flames, devil horns. Recognize it by cherry iconography plus shameless "very bad while looking very good" styling; separate it from Baddie neutrals, Bubblegum Bitch candy-pastel, Femme Fatale noir, Nymphet vintage softness and Bimbocore plastic pink.

name: Chic_Modernist
description: Chic Modernist ("smart casual") is a contemporary chic aesthetic that re-issues timeless wardrobe classics — long tailored coats, trench coats, turtlenecks, blazers, fitted denim and chinos — in clean, modern-fitting silhouettes. Its palette is neutral-dominant (ink black, chalk white, stone gray, camel, olive, denim blue) with at most one saturated accent such as oxblood or rust, and pattern used only sparingly (windowpane check, pinstripe). Images read as effortless street-style or lookbook photography: vertical full-body framing, soft diffused daylight or even studio light, plain plaster walls or muted stone-and-concrete urban backdrops, polished leather shoes or clean sneakers, and a logo-quiet, understated elegance.

name: Chicago_Drill
description: Early-2010s South Side Chicago rap aesthetic — lo-fi camera-phone documentary frames of crews in baggy True Religion denim, white tees and designer belt buckles, shot on daylight street corners, porches and flash-lit hallways. Core palette of white, denim blue, red and black over brick-and-concrete neutrals, with deadpan stares, pointing hand gestures and unfiltered snapshot candor. Recognized by incidental digital degradation (flash blowout, compression grain, faded warm filter casts) rather than designed grunge, and by visible faces and colorful streetwear as opposed to masked, all-black anonymity.

name: Chicha
description: Chicha is the Peruvian kitsch poster aesthetic born in 1980s Lima from Andean migrant cumbia culture: fluorescent magenta, acid green, sun yellow and tangerine lettering blazing on black or saturated grounds, with sinuous hand-painted script, extruded 3D wordmarks, and horror-vacui fills of roses, stars, vines and Andean-tropical motifs. Recognize it by gradient-filled brush lettering as the hero element, screenprint flatness with grain, flyer furniture (date blocks, checker bands, slang slogans), and festive, defiant migrant pride. It is distinct from Lowbrow, Pop Art, 60s Psychedelia, Tropical and Cholo styles by its neon-on-black folk-kitch density and its poster-lettering protagonist.

name: Chinese_Dreamcore
description: Chinese Dreamcore (中式梦核) is a 2020s nostalgia aesthetic of millennium-era urban China (c. 1998–2010): empty school corridors with green oil-paint wainscots, white-tiled residential slabs with Bauhaus-style blue windows, shuttered shopping malls, magazine booths and fast-food counters, rendered in hazy digicam softness or smooth painterly game-scene renders. Its palette is beige ceramic tile, institutional mint green, faded banner red and saturated cobalt sky; its mood is the paradox of eerie-yet-warm, an emptied childhood space remembered like a half-dream. Recognize it by Chinese-language vinyl signage, CRT-era interiors, deadpan one-point liminal perspectives, and the near-total absence of people.

name: Chinese_Folk_Horror
description: Chinese Folk Horror (中式民俗恐怖, "Minsu Horror") is the folk-horror aesthetic built on Chinese funeral and marriage customs — red bridal hoods and coffin silk, paper effigies (zhi ren), joss paper, incense, and cinnabar-scripted talismans set in dim rural interiors of adobe, dark timber and ancestral halls. Its palette is the red–black–white triad with ritual gold-yellow paper accents, lit by a single candle, oil lamp or lantern under crushed shadows, fog and heavy vignettes. Typical subjects are gagged or closed-eyed brides, paper figurines with painted cheeks, altars and family trees, ancient wells, opera stages, graveyards and bagua mechanism puzzles, rendered as painterly semi-real game key art or grainy low-light renders.

name: Chinese_New_Year
description: The festival aesthetic of the Chinese Spring Festival (Chunjie): saturated vermilion-and-gold maximalism built from spring couplets, the '福' doufang, big red lanterns, Chinese knots with tassels, red packets and gold ingots, steaming New Year's Eve feasts, lion and dragon dances, and firework-lit winter nights. Rooted in pre-Qin ritual red but visually a modern commercial folk style of foil-stamped gold on red paper. Recognize it by red acting as the overwhelming ground color rather than an accent, auspicious hanzi brush calligraphy, dense hanging decorations, round-table family abundance, and snow-or-night festivity — distinct from Guochao's streetwear graphics and Neo-Chinese minimalism.

name: Chinoiserie
description: Chinoiserie is the 17th–18th-century European fantasy of China — pagodas, parasol-bearing mandarins, weeping willows, exotic birds and dragons scattered across soft pastel grounds, cobalt-on-white porcelain, or glossy lacquer reds and blacks, all punctuated with gold. Recognize it by Rococo asymmetry and gilded ornament carrying invented East Asian motifs on wallpaper panels, lacquer cabinets, brocades and blue-and-white porcelain. The mood is playful, luxurious, deliberately inauthentic exoticism.

name: Choco_Girl
description: Choco Girl (also Neapolitan Girl or Chocolatecore) is a kawaii theme layer from 2000s Harajuku street fashion, named on 2020s Tumblr/Pinterest, locked to a Neapolitan palette of cocoa brown, pastel pink and cream. Recognize it by chocolate-bar and biscuit prints, dripping-chocolate glaze patterns, chocolate-covered strawberries, hyperrealistic dessert accessories (cookie berets, biscuit purses, chocolate-bar necklaces), decoden cases crusted with plastic sweets, and Sweet Lolita or Himekaji silhouettes photographed in soft, hazy snapshot light.

name: Cholo
description: Cholo is the Chicano street aesthetic of 1960s East Los Angeles barrios, descended from 1930s Pachuco culture and recorded in grainy black-and-white or sun-bleached color against stucco, concrete steps and hand-tagged plaster. Its visual DNA is the oversized-over-baggy silhouette — flannel shirts, white tanks and striped polos above creased baggy khakis or denim stacked on Nike Cortez, Chuck Taylors or shell-toe Adidas, with white knee socks, bandanas, beanies, dark sunglasses and a single gold or silver chain — held to a neutral palette of black, white, concrete grey, khaki brown and denim blue. Stoic solo and crew portraits carry its core values of Hispanic pride and anti-assimilation.

name: Cholombiano
description: Cholombiano (also Kolombia, "Punks Tropicalizados") is the late-1990s cumbia youth subculture of Monterrey, Mexico — sculptural gel-stiff patilludo hair under an intentionally too-small perched cap, extreme oversized plaid and Hawaiian button-ups, hand-woven escapulario name panels, airbrushed Virgin of Guadalupe / San Judas Tadeo iconography, and Colombian-flag yellow-blue-red over a white base. Recognize it in vernacular flash snapshots of sonidero dance floors and street corners: baggy tumbadilla silhouettes, candy-saturated tropical color, DIY maximalism, and a mellow, community-proud pose.

name: Chonga
description: Chonga is the loud, working-class Latina subculture aesthetic of Miami (1980s–2000s origins, 2007 viral peak): hot pink and bright saturated tones, oversized tees or crop tops over low-rise jeans, bracelet-sized gold nameplate hoops, stacked bangles, gel-slicked buns and braids, thick eyeliner and extra-long acrylic nails. It is recognizable by sassy direct-to-camera poses, Spanglish graffiti and marker text with deliberate misspellings, lucite platform heels and chancletas, and MySpace-era flash-snapshot or saturated studio-gradient lighting. Load this skill to identify or generate Miami Latina excess aesthetics and to keep them distinct from Cholo, Choni, Baddie, Bimbocore and Cagole.

name: Choni
description: Spanish working-class youth aesthetic of the 1990s–2000s, the flamboyant "de barrio" feminine look: oversized gold hoops and layered chains, leopard and snake print, hot pink and fluorescent yellow over black or white satin, tracksuits and mini skirts, heavy makeup, teased hair and oversized sunglasses worn everywhere. Snapshot-flash or saturated TV-studio photography, confrontational pouts, group pride and deliberate cheap-glam maximalism. Recognize by clashing patterns, metallic shine and jewelry scaled to read from across the street.

name: Christian_Girl_Autumn
description: Christian Girl Autumn (CGA) is a late-2010s Instagram/Pinterest lifestyle aesthetic of hyper-curated cozy fall — chunky knit sweaters, oversized plaid blanket scarves, UGG or suede boots and skinny jeans in warm neutrals (cream, beige, tan, brown) accented by burnt orange and maroon, staged in pumpkin patches, leaf-strewn sidewalks and golden forests with a pumpkin spice latte held prominently in hand. Recognize it by faded warm film grading, soft daylight, long loose-waved hair or knit pom-pom beanies, and polished OOTD, faceless torso-crop or back-view framing that radiates wholesome "effortless happiness." Separate it from generic Autumn Aesthetic by the feminine fashion uniform plus coffee-cup prop, and from VSCO Girl by season, knitwear and warm-neutral palette.

name: Christmas
description: A seasonal festive aesthetic built on the red–green–white–gold tetrad, evergreen conifers strung with fairy lights, glass ball ornaments, wrapped presents, stockings, holly and Santa Claus, spanning candlelit cozy interiors, snowy light-covered neighborhoods and maximalist decorated rooms. Its range runs from Victorian nostalgic illustration and mid-century kitsch (tinsel trees, vintage figurines, flash-lit family snapshots) to pastel, golden, blue, coastal and Southern-Hemisphere summer variants, but every image carries at least one holiday signifier — tree, lights, ornament, gift, stocking or Santa. Use for December celebration imagery: decorating, baking, gift-giving, family gatherings and decorated exteriors.

name: Chromecore
description: Chromecore (Y2K Chromecore) is the silver-and-chrome product-design aesthetic of roughly 1999–2006: mirror, bead-blasted and stainless finishes (often silver plastic mimicking chrome), molded pill-and-lozenge curves, and cool blue gradient accents on flip/swivel phones, clamshell handhelds, PDAs, camcorders, curved-bezel monitors and Flash-era web graphics. Recognize it by lustrous silver surfaces carrying bright specular streaks, chrome-sphere ornaments, small glowing screens sunk in thick silver bezels, and seamless white studio lighting that radiates turn-of-the-millennium technological optimism. It is the metal-first, hardware-first wing of Y2K Futurism — no nature, no grime, no matte minimalism.

name: Chunyu
description: Chunyu (纯欲, "pure-desire") is an early-2020s Chinese aesthetic that fuses doll-like innocence — pale clear skin, red blush swept around the eyes and onto the nose tip, spiky lashes, glossy warm lips, soft black hair — with measured sensuality: bodycon knitted mini dresses, bared collarbones and shoulders, a milky pink-and-cream palette, whisper-thin chain jewelry and rhinestone nail art. Recognize it by soft diffused indoor light, vertical selfie-grade framing, and an "effortless, not trying" styling grammar that balances cute against sexy in every frame. It sits between Asian Baby Girl's bold glam, Coquette's vintage ribbons, and Nymphet's sun-faded romanticism.

name: Chuugoku_Musume
description: Chuugoku Musume (中國娘 / Zhonghua niang, "Japanese-Sino Feng") is the Japanese anime-born trope of the Chinese girl: a qipao-derived chaina-fuku with mandarin collar and frog buttons, twin dango-atama buns wrapped in cloth and ribbons, pandas, bamboo dim-sum steamers and kung-fu poses, rendered in saturated lacquer red, brocade gold, jade green and ink black. Originating in 1990s Japan (Chun-Li, Shampoo) and revived as a self-styled niche fashion on Rednote, it reads as kawaii playfulness fused with Chinese festive signifiers — including lolita and maid-apron hybrids, idol stage costumes, anime character sheets and studio lookbooks. Recognize it by the collar–frog-buttons–double-buns triad plus the red/gold palette; it is distinct from Chinoiserie (European porcelain fantasy), Guochao (Chinese heritage-pride streetwear) and plain Moe (cuteness without Chinese coding).

name: Cinnamon_Girl
description: Cinnamon Girl is a TikTok-born autumn lifestyle aesthetic (early 2020s) built on a warm brown-and-cream palette — cinnamon, caramel, beige, espresso — applied to cozy domestic and urban-luxury scenes: lattes dusted with cinnamon, cinnamon rolls, knitwear, shearling coats, wicker baskets, tortoiseshell clips, gold pendants and hair bows. It fuses autumn baking domesticity with Coquette and Downtown Girl polish and a melancholic-romantic undertow borrowed from Lana Del Rey's song of the same name, functioning as the fall counterpart to Clean Girl / Vanilla Girl. Recognize it by warm-brown color dominance, spice-coded food and drink, soft tactile materials, faceless intimate framing, and low-contrast golden or lamp-warm light.

name: City_Pop
description: City Pop is the visual register of Japan's bubble-era pop, mid-1970s through the 1980s: neon-soaked city streets and skylines, tropical resorts with palms and pools, modernist leisure architecture, and vintage cars parked on empty streets, all graded toward pops of magenta, cyan, red, yellow, blue and purple. Signature elements include random English words on signage and album-style titling, yuppie/resort fashion with voluminous wavy hair, and a flat airbrushed '80s record-sleeve illustration mode. Load this skill for images of sophisticated, upbeat 1980s Japanese prosperity — nightlife, beaches, poolside — as distinct from cyberpunk grit, vaporwave irony or After Hours loneliness.

name: Classic_Lolita
description: Classic Lolita is the mature, elegant pillar of Japanese Lolita fashion, cut after Victorian and Rococo dress with petticoat-supported A-line or tea-length skirts, pintucked bodices, tiered lace ruffles and heirloom sewn details. Its palette sits deliberately between Sweet Lolita's candy pastels and Gothic Lolita's black — off-white, brown, sage, dusty rose, muted blue, wine, navy and jewel tones — carrying antique-realistic florals, toile, heraldry and classical-painting prints, straw bonnets, canotiers, cameos, pearl strands and lace gloves. Typical images are lookbook-style portraits or dress-form displays of a full coordinated outfit in paneled antique interiors or quiet pastoral outdoors, under soft diffuse light with a faded, film-like grade.

name: Classicism
description: Classicism is the recurring Western tradition that holds the art of ancient Greece and Rome as the standard of excellence: idealized nude and draped figures, marble sculpture, the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders, and mythological or historical subject matter rendered with symmetry, balance and emotional restraint. Its palette is stone-led — marble white, warm limestone beige and sepia, softened by rose, salmon, ochre, olive and slate blue under even, diffuse daylight. Recognize it by anatomical idealization, frieze-like or axially balanced composition, logically falling drapery, smooth invisible finish, and a mood of calm grandeur; it spans antiquity itself, the Italian Renaissance and Neoclassical revivals, down to civic domes and porticoes used as statements of political authority.

name: Claymorphism
description: Claymorphism is a 2020s post-flat UI and illustration aesthetic of inflated, Play-Doh-soft 3D forms — chunky rounded shapes that float as discrete solid objects over pastel gradient fields, defined by deep outer shadows plus subtle inner shadows that read as puffiness. Its palette runs pastel blue, pink, lavender, mint and white with candy-saturated accent cues, and its subjects span app cards and buttons, 3D emoji and icon sets, clay mascots, and diverse chunky-proportioned people in everyday scenarios. Recognize it by matte-satin modeled volume, soft diffuse studio light, big rounded corners, clean bold minimal type, and an overall mood of friendliness, tactility and playfulness.

name: Clean_Girl
description: Clean Girl is a 2020s TikTok-born fashion, beauty and lifestyle aesthetic of hyper-curated effortlessness: dewy "glass" skin, slicked-back buns held by claw clips, gold hoop earrings, neutral athleisure capsule wardrobes, and wellness props like green juice, iced matcha and immaculate white interiors. Recognize it by a muted neutral palette (beige, cream, greige, brown, grey) punctuated only by sage/matcha green and polished gold, soft diffused lighting, orderly uncluttered compositions, and a groomed "model off-duty" calm that reads expensive while insisting it took no effort.

name: Cleancore
description: Cleancore (aka Safetycore, Hygienicore, Showercore) is a 2010s Tumblr-born aesthetic of hygiene and sterilized calm: cleaning sprays, soaps, detergent jugs, bubbles, bath toys and freshly wiped tile rendered in high-key white, pale blue, mint and teal with soft shadowless bloom. It splits into a sterile commercial "High" register (sanitizers, PPE, cynical brand imagery) and a kawaii "Low" register (rubber ducks, baby bath products, pastel star stickers). Recognize it by product-shot lighting, foam and water caustics, tile grids, and surreal flawless cleanliness.

name: Clockpunk
description: Clockpunk is a retrofuturist aesthetic that imagines Renaissance-era (14th–17th century) technology built purely from clockwork — exposed gear trains, springs, levers, winding keys, automatons and flapping-wing ornithopters — rendered in brass, bronze, gold, carved wood and polished glass. Its machines are treated as Baroque art objects: engraved, gilded, set with lenses and framed by Roman-numeral dials, concentric carved arches and Renaissance architecture, lit by candle flame or hazy daylight in a palette of gold, bronze, wood brown, parchment cream and silver. Recognize it by ornate mechanism-as-artwork, clockwork creatures, and pre-industrial craftsmanship; distinguish it from Steampunk (no steam, no Victorian iron), pure Italian Renaissance (no anachronistic machines), Baroque (no devotional theatre), and Dungeonpunk (no crude subterranean iron).

name: Cloudcore
description: Cloudcore is the 2019–2022 TikTok/Pinterest sky aesthetic: sunrise and sunset cumulus skies graded into dusty lavender, rose pink, baby blue, teal and golden orange, finished with glitter-sparkle overlays, kawaii line doodles traced onto cloud forms, and tiny lowercase motivational text. Its subject is almost exclusively open sky — towering cumulus, cirrus streaks, cloud reflections in water — shot low-angle with soft grain, light leaks and a pastel glow, in phone-wallpaper proportions. Recognize it by pastel cloud palette plus gentle wonder; it carries no religious iconography (Angelcore), no uncanny dread (Weirdcore), and no interior scenes (Lo-fi Art).

name: Clovercore
description: Clovercore is the late-1990s to early-2000s Japanese "fancy goods" stationery aesthetic — a subgenre of Heisei Retro — built on four-leaf clovers in lime and grass green over white or cream, nameless round animal mascots (bears, pandas, hamsters, cats), bubbly naive English about luck and dreams, musical notes, sparkle graphics, and gingham- or polka-dot-filled clover leaves. Recognize it by flat, bright, scan-like or flash-lit presentations of stickers, memo pads, pencil cases, resin phone charms and sticker binders, and by an innocent, lucky, childlike mood distinct from pink-led Puppycore or earthy Whimsy Twee.

name: Clowncore
description: Clowncore (also Circuscore or Clownpunk) is a 2010s–2020s Tumblr/TikTok aesthetic of clown, jester and circus play: white-face makeup with colored noses and diamond tears, rainbow stripe sequences, primary red-yellow-blue, oversized shoes, jester hats, harlequin diamonds and stacks of childlike plastic charms and slogan badges. Its mood is joyous, nostalgic and deliberately childish, with a pastel-kawaii branch and a goth/E-girl dark branch. Typical subjects are makeup selfies, extremity close-ups (feet, wrists, nails), charm flat-lays, handmade dolls and jewelry, and flat cartoon illustration.

name: Club_Kids
description: Late-1980s to mid-1990s New York nightlife subculture aesthetic built on DIY assemblage costumes, clown-and-cabaret theatrical face paint, and candy-saturated circus color shot on grainy direct-flash 35mm snapshots against black club voids. Androgynous self-invented personas stacked with found objects — synthetic wigs, fur stoles, veils, plastic beads, harlequin checks, dolls and hats — posing with media-savvy eagerness for the camera. Recognize by handmade grotesque camp plus analog flash grit; distinct from glossy pop candy, styled fashion editorial, and neon-on-black rave looks.

name: Cluttercore
description: Cluttercore is a 2020s TikTok-born interior aesthetic of "organized chaos": rooms in which every surface carries curated, sentimental collections — overflowing bookshelves, dense gallery walls, dolls and figurines, potted plants, layered textiles — rendered in highly saturated, varied color under warm lamplight, string lights or neon glow. Recognize it by floor-to-ceiling filled shelving, mismatched thrifted furniture, color-coded book spines, and personal storytelling objects arranged with deliberate, visible curation; it is curated maximalism defined in opposition to minimalism, not messiness.

name: Coastal_Cowgirl
description: Coastal Cowgirl is a sun-bleached 2020s micro-aesthetic (spring–summer 2023, US coastal South) that fuses Western ranch codes with nautical beach codes: straw cowgirl hats banded with cowrie shells, light-wash denim shorts, tan cowgirl boots standing on sand, seashells and pearls, all held in a baby-blue, cream and tan palette. Expect whimsical snapshot-style fashion flatlays, beach and pool vignettes, pale horses, surfboards and pastel cutout moodboard collages with a 2000s country-pop nostalgia (Hannah Montana, early Taylor Swift). Load this skill when recognizing or generating images that pair cowboy signifiers with seaside ones in a faded, high-key pastel range.

name: Coastal_Grandmother
description: Coastal Grandmother is a 2022 TikTok-born lifestyle aesthetic that romanticizes the relaxed, affluent ease of a Nancy Meyers beach-house heroine: cream linen, chunky cashmere knits, straw totes and hydrangeas in light-filled rooms. Its visual DNA is a white-cream-sand base washed with sky blue, dusty blue and navy, crisp natural fabrics (linen, cotton gauze, eyelet) plus wicker, pottery and blue-and-white china, captured in candid, sun-bleached snapshots of reading, gardening, market mornings and beach walks. Recognize it by high-key diffused daylight, faceless or behind-the-shoulder framing, and understated "quiet luxury" props — white wine, fresh flowers, canvas market bags — with no logos, no neon and no nautical kitsch.

name: Coastal_Style
description: Coastal Style (Beach House, Marine Style, Style Bord de Mer) is a sun-bleached early-20th-century interior aesthetic built on a white-and-blue foundation with light neutrals, light weathered wood, and woven fibers such as rattan, wicker, jute and linen. Signature elements include flooded diffuse daylight through sheer curtains, white shiplap or beamed ceilings, natural-fiber rugs, striped or fish-embroidered textiles, and maritime accents (shells, driftwood, rope, sail or crustacean prints) dialed anywhere from a whisper to an explicit theme. Typical subjects are airy open-plan rooms, porch and entry vignettes, styled shelves and tablescapes, and textile or tableware close-ups.

name: Cocalar
description: Cocalar is the kitsch visual culture of late-1990s Romanian men — bare chests or open silk shirts loaded with gold chains, oversized rings and aviator sunglasses, posed beside BMW/Audi badges or fanned banknotes in drab post-communist courtyards, bathrooms, beaches and Manele clubs. Its palette pits metallic gold and hot pink against concrete grey, institutional beige and brown ceramic tile, recorded in harsh on-camera-flash digicam snapshots with unironic, boastful pride. Recognize it by over-accessorized wealth display staged sincerely in deliberately unstyled, modest surroundings.

name: Coconut_Girl
description: Coconut Girl is a 2020s TikTok-born coquette subtype that nostalgically restages early-2000s tween beach-vacation culture — sun-bleached turquoise water, hot pink and sunny yellow swimwear, plumeria and hibiscus flowers, glitter mermaids and dolphins, motel signs, roller skates and Polaroid snapshots — all wrapped in soft-focus dreamy haze with sparkle bokeh and flower-sticker corner embellishments. Recognize it by the combination of tropical beach subject matter, Y2K plastic-cute textures (glitter, holographic vinyl, plush, crochet), and an overexposed, airbrushed summer glow in a bright multi-color palette of pink, turquoise, yellow and cream.

name: Coffee_House
description: Café aesthetic of third-wave coffee culture (term codified 1999, rooted in 17th-century European coffeehouses, 1950s–60s US espresso bars and Japanese kissaten): dark wood, chalkboard black and cream porcelain grounded palette, accented by mustard, forest green, maroon, navy and grey. Signature elements are the coffee ritual itself — espresso machine, latte art, cups on saucers, pastry display cases — plus hanging pendant lights, books and cameras left on tables, plants, and storefronts with awnings and gold-leaf window lettering. Subjects range from dim, cozy interiors and sunlit tabletops to street terraces, vintage signage and home-cafe trays.

name: Colorful_Pop
description: Colorful Pop is a 2010s Japanese graphic-design and illustration style of maximum-saturation neon magenta, cyan and yellow (lime-green accent) set against high-contrast black or white grounds, fusing anime-style characters with Pop Art grammar: halftone dot screens, onomatopoeia, paint splatters, geometric shards, pixel/glitch accents and integrated logotypes. Born in Pixiv artist circles and the J-core hardcore-techno scene — album jackets, rhythm-game UIs like Muse Dash and WACCA, card art — it reads as loud, playful sensory overload, spanning clean flat vector posters to painterly splatter illustration. Recognize it by fluorescent triad color, maximalist layered density and comic-print texture; never muted, never serene.

name: Communist_Chic
description: Communist Chic (Che Chic, Chekist Chic) is the Western fashion-and-media appropriation of 20th-century communist state iconography — hammer and sickle, red and yellow five-pointed stars, solid red flags, the high-contrast Guerrillero Heroico portrait of Che Guevara, faux Cyrillic type, and badge-topped ushankas — worn for irony, camp, shock value or pure style rather than belief. Born in mid-1970s punk and glam rock stagewear, commodified after the USSR's collapse into silkscreened tees, poly-blend flags and manifesto paperbacks, and re-refined by 2010s post-Soviet designers. Recognize it by a black-red-yellow palette, cheap mass-produced or luxe-parody materials, and a deliberate gap between totalitarian symbol and frivolous context.

name: Constructivism
description: Soviet avant-garde of 1915–early 1930s whose visual DNA is agitational geometry — flat red, black and bone-white planes driven on dynamic diagonals, wedges piercing circles, masts and cantilevers — fused with bold sans-serif typography and halftone photomontage in posters, book covers, porcelain and exposed steel-and-glass structure. Recognize it by a limited flat palette, declared industrial materials (metal, glass, plywood, concrete), asymmetric thrusting compositions and type set as structural mass; the mood is utilitarian shout and engineering diagram at once.

name: Cool_Britannia
description: Mid-1990s British youth-culture aesthetic (c. 1993–97) in which the Union Jack is treated as a pop object — flag red, white and blue saturated across dresses, guitars, backdrops, collages and magazine covers. Glossy tabloid layouts with sticker-like magenta and yellow type blocks, flash-lit celebrity photography, TV-studio glitter, and a fashion hybrid of 1960s Mod tailoring with parkas, track jackets and denim. Mood is cheeky, optimistic, ironical-but-sincere national pride: Britpop band group portraits, pop stars mid-performance, cover-line plastered magazines, terrace and stage crowds.

name: Coquette
description: Coquette is a hyper-feminine, film-faded vintage aesthetic descending from mid-2010s Tumblr "nymphet" culture and the 2020s Dollette wave on Pinterest/TikTok — powder pink, cream and dusty rose washed through analog grain, dense with bows, lace, ruffles, pearls, ballet flats and 1950s–60s Americana props (convenience stores, motels, lace curtains, cigarette packs on floral sheets). Typical subjects are doll-styled young women, girlish object still-lifes and bedroom interiors that pair flirtatious sweetness with melancholic, tragic-edged nostalgia. Recognize it by the desaturated pastel palette, high frill density, and soft window light or direct-flash snapshot treatment.

name: Corpcore
description: Corpcore (corporatecore, corporate chic) is a late-2023 fashion aesthetic, coined by HUGO BOSS's Techtopia show, that fuses 90s-derived office tailoring — boxy blazers, exaggerated shoulders, wide-leg trousers, pinstripes, houndstooth, tweed — with casual streetwear such as sneakers, straight-leg jeans, basic tees and baseball caps. Its palette is subdued neutrals (black, charcoal, gray, white, brown, navy, light blue) rendered in wool, poplin, leather and cashmere, photographed in white-collar settings, city streets and Fall/Winter runways with flash-lit or overcast deadpan candor. Recognize it by its central tension: rigorous, menswear-derived tailoring deliberately relaxed, oversized or subverted.

name: Corporate_Cyberspace
description: Corporate Cyberspace (also Corporate Gen-X Cyber, Proto-Y2K, Early-Y2K Cyber-Utopianism) is the 1993–2000 corporate imagination of the internet as shiny, clean and professional: sterile digital blues, deep navy, chrome silver and violet grid tunnels in low-poly early 3D, wireframe globes and data maps, layered translucent UI windows, pixelated system text, and stock-photo executives in blazers pointing at transparent screens. Optimistic and maximalist — gradient-mesh sails, beige CRT desktops, floating polygonal primitives and glowing office renders selling the digital frontier from trade-show floors, magazine covers and software boxes. Load this skill to recognize or generate early-to-late-1990s enterprise-tech advertising, editorial covers, exhibition graphics and interface-collage imagery, and to separate it from Factory Pomo, Memphis Lite, Corporate Grunge, Gen-X Home and Med-Tech Visions.

name: Corporate_Goth
description: Corporate Goth (Corpgoth) is a 1990s Goth substyle rebuilt for the office: black or charcoal tailored suits, pencil skirts and waistcoats carrying discreet gothic signatures — ornate silk, lace or velvet blouses, small-scale Victorian or Celtic jewelry, and at most one jewel-tone accent in burgundy, plum or emerald. Subjects read as composed professionals (neat chignons or sleek waves, pale matte skin, a sharp thin winged liner, dark plum lips, chunky-but-smart Mary Janes or oxfords) photographed in diffuse lookbook light or overcast street light. Recognize it by tailored office silhouettes with a whisper of dark detail — never theatrical Goth hardware, never beige corpcore anonymity.

name: Corporate_Grunge
description: Corporate Grunge (aka Grunge™, Neugrunge) is the 1993–2005 commercial dilution of Seattle grunge into advertising, album covers, movie posters, magazine covers and mall catalogs — soot-black, paper-beige, sepia and rust "sludge" palettes, grainy photocopy and rust textures, distressed typewriter/stencil/label-maker type, cut-and-paste collage and duotone decay photography. Recognize it by manufactured rebellion: torn paper edges, ink splatters, VHS glitch, industrial grime and tiny technical captions set against oversized corrupted logotypes on scanned, grain-degraded print surfaces.

name: Corporate_Hippie
description: Corporate Hippie (also Corporate Psychedelia, Psychsploitation) is the c. 1967–1973 commercial appropriation of hippie counterculture: flat, maximalist offset-print advertising, record sleeves, magazine pages and textile prints in saturated magenta, tangerine, sunflower yellow, lime, turquoise and violet on cream paper or ink black. Signature elements are warped bubble lettering, kaleidoscopic floral mandalas and sunbursts, hearts, doves and LOVE words, and evenly lit studio photographs of bell-bottomed models cut into graphic fields. Recognize it by its advertising logic — legible copy blocks, brand lockups, product heroes — wrapped in sanitized, consumer-friendly psychedelia.

name: Corporate_Memphis
description: Corporate Memphis (a.k.a. Alegria, Big Tech Art Style, Blob Web, Humans of Flat) is the flat vector illustration idiom of late-2010s/early-2020s tech branding: disproportionate human figures with diminutive heads, massive torsos and long boneless "bendy" limbs, blank or near-blank faces, and non-representational skin in blue, purple or green (or mixed natural tones), built from strokeless solid-color shapes on flat solid backgrounds with abstract geometric confetti. Its palette spans soft pastels to high-contrast primaries (blue, purple, yellow, pink, teal), and its subjects are generic, joyful work-and-life placeholders — teams collaborating, dancing figures, people cradling oversized phones. Recognize it by matte flat fills with no gradients or shading, impossible anatomy, and frictionless corporate cheer; it is distinct from Memphis Design (pattern-maximal, outlined), Neubrutalism (heavy strokes, hard offset shadows), Claymorphism (puffy 3D volumes) and plain Minimalism (non-figurative).

name: Costumbrismo
description: Nineteenth-century Spanish and Hispanic American picture of everyday custom — tavern tertulias, street types, horsemen and muleteers, market bargains, fairs and Holy Week processions — staged as small legible anecdotes against documented regional architecture. Palette is sun-baked and natural: whitewash cream, ochre and umber walls, olive-vine greens, dusty blue skies, cloak-and-top-hat blacks, with small saturated accents of majo sash red, saffron skirt and banner cloth. Figures are typified rather than psychological, costume is rendered as ethnographic document, and the handling runs from broad satirical brushwork (Madrid school) to smooth romanticized finish (Seville school), with a parallel lineage of ink wood-engraving for the press. Recognize by minimal action, maximal social detail, and a nostalgic, observant, gently satirical or celebratory mood.

name: Cottagecore
description: Cottagecore is a 2010s internet aesthetic of romanticized western agricultural life — sun-faded wildflower meadows, thatched stone cottages, English-style gardens, baking and handcrafts, farm animals, and prairie dresses in linen and gingham. Its palette runs moss green, straw, cream, dusty rose and baby blue under natural golden-hour light, rendered with faded film grain or soft watercolor handling. Recognize it by the constant human hand in nature — clotheslines, fences, picnics, planter boxes — and by strawberries, mushrooms and flowers repeating as motifs across fabric, dishware and print.

name: Cottagegoth
description: Cottagegoth (also Cottagegore, Dark Cottagecore) is an early-2020s internet aesthetic that turns Cottagecore's pastoral ruralism toward the macabre — fog-soaked woods, overgrown graveyards, animal bones, poisonous fungi, decaying cottages and solitary witch-hermit figures, all in muted earth tones of moss green, faded brown, grey and black. Recognize it by desaturated analog-film atmosphere, overcast or twilight light, memento-mori still lifes, and a mood of melancholic reverence toward wild, dangerous nature rather than toward horror shock.

name: Country
description: Country (also Farmcore, Countrycore, Southern Boy/Girl) is the lived-in aesthetic of rural American South and Midwest farm life: weathered wood, galvanized metal, denim, burlap and gingham in a palette of barn red, leather brown, hay tan and denim navy. Signature elements are red barns, wheat and corn fields, hay, pickup trucks, mason jars, sunflowers, cowboy boots and hats, snap-front western shirts, and flag-themed wood décor, photographed in golden-hour or overcast natural light with a sun-faded, matte grade. The mood is settled, practical and proudly domestic — home, hard work, family, tradition — never frontier adventure or romanticized cottage escape.

name: Cozy_Gamer
description: A 2020s, pandemic-born interior and lifestyle aesthetic that rebuilds video gaming as a soft domestic sanctuary — sage green, cream, soft brown and blush pink bathed in warm fairy-light and sunset-lamp glow, around wood desks, creamy mechanical keyboards, draped pothos and monstera leaves, pegboards of small treasures, plushies and pixel-art game screens. Recognize it by warm ambient lighting with no overhead source, lived-in curated desk setups, handheld consoles nestled on knit blankets, and cozy indie game worlds (Stardew Valley, Animal Crossing) glowing on screens; subjects range from full room-corner setups to top-down flat lays and intimate hand-on-controller close-ups.

name: Cozycore
description: Cozycore (Comfycore) is a late-2010s internet aesthetic of domestic comfort — warm-neutral interiors lit by candles, fairy lights, table lamps and diffused window light, piled with chunky knit blankets, soft pillows, steaming mugs, open books and pets. Its images crop to intimate, arm's-reach scale (lap point-of-view, overhead beds, windowsill still lifes), favor rumpled lived-in textiles in beige, cream, grey, brown and soft earth tones, and extend into naive hand-lettered and picture-book illustration. Recognize it by softness, slowness and self-care; separate it from rustic Cabincore, pastoral Cottagecore, seasonal Autumn/Winter aesthetics and screen-centric Cozy Gamer.

name: Craftcore
description: Craftcore is the late-2010s/2020 aesthetic of visible handiwork — chunky knits, crochet trims, patchwork, quilting, embroidery, beading, macramé and artisanal tie-dye on garments, pottery and home objects. Its palette splits between an earthy heritage register (rust, ochre, oat, moss, oxblood on raw wood and woven straw) and a vivid eclectic DIY register (strawberry red, cobalt, lemon, hot pink on cream or denim), always matte, fibrous and hand-touched. Recognize it by legible stitch definition, seam and quilt lines, brushstrokes, maker's hands, yarn balls and tools in soft natural light.

name: Crowcore
description: Crowcore (Corvidcore) is a Tumblr-born collector-and-nature aesthetic derived from Goblincore and Cottagecore but distinctly darker: black wool and corvid plumage, bone-white pearls and paper, mossy greens, and overhead hoards of shiny found objects — old coins, vintage brooches, seaglass, agates, feathers, rusty bottle caps, small blades. Signature content includes live crows, collection flat-lays on cloth or wood, dark layered thrifted fashion, and deadpan corvid meme graphics, all in soft overcast or misty light. Recognize it by the black/white/green triad punctured by metallic glint, the joy of kept trash-treasure, and dry crow humor.

name: Crust_Punk
description: Crust punk (crust, stenchcore) is the DIY garb and visual culture of early-1980s English punk-metal crossover, defined by soot-black denim buried under sewn-on band patches, studded and spiked battle vests, patchwork trousers, dreadlocks, combat boots and deliberate grime. Its palette is black plus earth decay — olive drab, rust brown, camo khaki, bleached bone — photographed in amateur snapshot mode: direct flash in squat halls, flat overcast daylight on streets and field edges. Typical subjects are full-body outfit portraits, curb-seated groups, gig candid shots and flat-laid patched garments, all reading as handmade, worn-out and politically militant rather than fashionable.

name: Cryptidcore
description: Cryptidcore is a 2010s Tumblr-born aesthetic of amateur cryptozoology and roadside conspiracy culture, rendered in muted 1970s–90s analog film tones — bark brown, khaki, moss green, fog gray — punctured by small uncanny accents of glow-in-the-dark phosphor green, tabloid magenta and VHS chromatic glitch. Signature elements include kitschy souvenir cryptid iconography (screen-printed saucers, embroidered patches, roadside cutouts), Polaroid snapshots and film grain, hand-annotated maps and yellowed sighting clippings, dark forests and abandoned buildings, moth imagery, and eerie tourist-trap warning signs under vast dusk skies. Typical subjects are cryptid silhouettes with glowing eyes, field-gear flat lays, vintage outdoor fashion, desert diners and highway signs, and evidence-style collages.

name: Cubism
description: Cubism (Paris, 1900s–1910s, Picasso and Braque) fractures objects and figures into interlocking geometric planes shown from several viewpoints at once, rejecting single-point perspective. It speaks in two main color registers — Analytic near-monochrome browns, grays and ochres with dense shard-like faceting, and Synthetic flatter, brighter planes often fused with pasted newspaper, wallpaper and stenciled type — plus offshoot registers of tubular metallic figures, crystalline Czech facets and Orphic color discs. Recognize it by still lifes of guitars, bottles, fruit and newsprint, faceted portraits, shallow compressed space, and lighting that comes from everywhere and nowhere at once.

name: Cult_Party_Kei
description: Cult Party Kei is a 2010s Japanese thrifted vintage fashion built on sheer nylon peignoirs, nightgowns and petticoats layered like a Victorian child's bedtime ensemble, in washed-out creams and ivories with sparse dull-pastel or red gingham accents. Signature elements include translucent robe-over-skirt layering, high loosely-defined empire waists, poofy tiered lace skirts, quilted yo-yo patchwork accessories, and small religious motifs. Typical subjects are street-snapped or bedroom-portraited wearers in rumpled secondhand layers, photographed with grainy snapshot or magazine-scan softness.

name: Cumbiero
description: Argentine villa youth aesthetic of cumbia villera (late 1990s–2000s, Buenos Aires shantytowns): crews in shiny nylon tracksuits, basketball caps and branded jerseys in neon lime, orange and celeste against black and white; bleached long-top/short-side haircuts, women's tight buns over shaved napes, untied "llantas" sneakers, keytars and bailanta dance-hall stages. Shot in flat snapshot or harsh on-camera flash realism against corrugated-zinc walls, concrete and graffiti, with defiant hand signs and packed group poses. Read this skill when images combine working-class Argentine street pride, appropriated sportswear logos and low-fi consumer-camera texture.

name: Curly_Girly
description: Curly Girly (aka Libby Lu Kid, Tween Diva) is the tween-consumer aesthetic of roughly 1996–2005: flat, glossy advertising, packaging and set design built around curled serif type (Curlz), swirls and frills in a pink–purple–violet palette cooled by baby blue and sparked with lime.
