Use this skill to recognize or generate 2000s hardcore-fashion imagery and to keep it distinct from emo, scene, horror punk, mallgoth and metalhead looks.

name: Fauvism
description: Fauvism (Les Fauves, Paris and the French Mediterranean, c. 1905–1908) is oil painting in which pure, straight-from-the-tube color is divorced from descriptive reality — vermilion, cobalt, emerald and cadmium yellow set in deliberate dissonant contrasts — laid on in thick, vigorous dabs across a flattened, simplified space. Signature elements include arbitrary facial and shadow hues (a green stripe down a portrait's face, teal planes on skin), patterned interiors and textiles, Mediterranean landscapes and harbor scenes, schematic nudes and dancers, and an undulating arabesque contour line. Typical subjects are landscapes, portraits, seated figures and readers, interiors, still lifes of vessels and fruit, and bathers.

name: Female_Horror_Game_Protagonist_Fashion
description: A 2023 TikTok-born fashion microtrend that styles the wearer as the final girl of a Japanese horror game (Fatal Frame, Silent Hill, Haunting Ground): hyper-feminine white or cream babydoll blouses with Peter Pan, puritan or sailor collars, lace shrugs and fitted vests layered over pleated or tiered-ruffle black miniskirts, thigh-high socks, knee boots, black chokers and skeleton-key pendants. Palette of white, cream, black and gray with sparse oxblood-red accents; lighting runs from soft catalog daylight to dim single-source interiors with flashlight cones and PS2-era grain. Recognize by the layered coquette silhouette — untucked frilled top elongating the waist over a short skirt, legwear bridging the gap — staged for or placed inside quiet, haunted interiors.

name: Femboy
description: Internet-native aesthetic of the late 2010s–early 2020s in which a male-identified, masculine-or-youthful-featured person performs codified feminine dress — thigh-high socks (black, pink, purple, striped or fishnet-layered), pleated mini skirts, oversized hoodies, cat- or bunny-ear headbands, chokers — in a palette of pink, lilac, baby blue, white and pastels anchored by black contrast pieces. Imagery is vernacular smartphone self-portraiture: bedroom mirror selfies, LED-washed rooms, plush bedding, soft doll-like hair and light eye-focused makeup. Recognize it by the deliberate juxtaposition of feminine garment grammar on a male-coded body, played with coy, soft, playful innocence.

name: Femcel
description: Early-2020s "chronically online" aesthetic built around the cluttered otaku bedroom as sanctuary: stacks of manga, moe figures and posters, 2000s Japanese tech relics (CRT monitors, beige PCs, flip phones) and 90s/2000s anime canon imagery, all shot or edited in deliberately unpolished lo-fi. Its signature move is juxtaposition — baby-pink kawaii pastels, plushies and moe girls welded to nihilistic lowercase captions, sketchy high-contrast "loser girl" drawings with eyebags and spiral eyes, and oldweb forum/Windows-9x screenshot artifacts. Recognize it by flash-lit snapshot candidness, screen-within-screen compositions, hoarded clutter, and deadpan despair packaged as cute; also known as Lainpilled, Hikikomoricore or Hikicore.

name: Femme_Fatale
description: Femme Fatale is the "deadly woman" aesthetic born of 1940s film noir and carried forward by spy fiction and neo-noir: a poised, mysterious seductress framed in black, oxblood-and-scarlet red, dark jewel tones and metallic gold, lit by chiaroscuro, candlelight or venetian-blind shadow. Signature elements include silk and leather couture, long gloves and veiled hats, red lips and nails, cigarettes and cocktail glasses, concealed knives and thigh holsters, wealthy old-money interiors, and deliberately withheld faces. Typical subjects range from period chanteuses and modern spies to macro fragments (lips, nails, a blade against lace) and black typographic declaration cards.

name: Fetish_Goth
description: Fetish Goth is the 1990s goth-club substyle that folds BDSM-derived gear — corsets, strap harnesses, O-ring chokers, fishnets, buckled platform boots — into sleek black glamour. Its visual DNA is near-total black rendered in mirror-gloss latex, PVC and patent leather, punctuated by silver hardware and blood-red accents, worn over pale skin with heavy black liner and dark lips. Recognize it by hourglass corseted silhouettes, strapped harness geometry, specular streaks on glossy surfaces, and a poised, confrontational mood in club, stage, studio or street portraits.

name: Feísmo
description: Feísmo is the unintended built aesthetic of Galicia, Spain, from the 1960s onward — unfinished concrete frames with rebar stubs, bare brick and cement-block facades, granite farmhouses capped by cantilevered brick additions, and clashing building heights under flat Atlantic overcast. Its palette is raw concrete grey, oxidised rust brown, dull orange brick and moss-stained granite, set against the deep wet green of the Galician landscape; its register is the deadpan documentary snapshot of inhabited incompleteness, never abandonment. Recognise it by the collision of old stone vernacular with ad-hoc modern construction, mismatched materials, half-finished forms, and utility infrastructure tangled through heritage.

name: Figuration_Narrative
description: Figuration Narrative is the French movement of the 1960s–early 1970s of politically charged storytelling painting: flat matte planes of vermilion, cobalt, cadmium yellow and olive green, hard black contours, and mass-media syntax borrowed from comic strips, film stills, press photography and letterpress headlines. Its scenes — anonymous street crowds, soldiers, dictators, shop-window mannequins, consumer glyphs — are mounted in panel grids, polyptychs, superimposed planes and clashing framings so that a static image reads as duration and as critique. Load this skill when an image pairs Pop-like bold flat colour with narrative sequence, typographic fragments and overt social or political commentary rather than consumer celebration.

name: Film_Noir
description: Film Noir is the monochrome crime-film aesthetic of 1930s–1950s Hollywood — black-grey-white palette, low-key chiaroscuro with venetian-blind shadows, fog and rain-slicked streets, fedoras, trench coats, revolvers and femme fatales. Recognize it by hard light-dark contrast, period costume and props (rotary phones, cigarettes, liquor glasses, detective files), Art Deco city nightscapes, and a mood of pessimism, secrecy and corruption.

name: Fisherman_Aesthetic
description: Mid-2020s Pinterest-coined fashion aesthetic (Fishermancore, Sardinecore) that reinterprets working-waterfront dress through a modern, often feminine lens: Aran cable-knit sweaters, Breton stripes, waxed barn coats, wellington boots, net totes and kitschy marine-life accents (sardine tins, lobsters, fish-shaped bags) in navy, cream, charcoal and earthy beige-green with pops of rainwear red or yellow. Recognize it by overcast harbor light, matte utilitarian fabrics, layered practical styling and one whimsical marine object per frame — understated chic, never yacht-club crisp or costume-literal.

name: Fjortis
description: Swedish 2000s teen-girl aesthetic of deliberate artificiality: orange fake-tan skin ending in an unblended jawline stripe (the "fjortisrand"), chalk-white ointment lips, black kajal "spider leg" lashes and teased platinum-blonde hair, captured in harsh-flash, low-resolution mirror selfies and high-angle duckface poses. Neon pink tops, intentionally visible push-up bras, low-rise jeans, zip-up hoodies and Canada Goose parkas signal status across bedrooms, parties and club interiors. Recognize it by the inverted makeup contrast (dark face / white lips / white-blonde hair) plus the amateur early-digital camera grammar of LunarStorm, Playahead and Bilddagboken profile pictures.

name: Flamenco
description: Flamenco is the performing-art aesthetic of Andalusia (modern form from the late 18th century), visually built on the ruffled, polka-dotted traje de flamenca, fringed Manila shawls, roses pinned into a bun, and the classical guitar, isolated against black voids, smoky studio gradients or glossy runway floors. Its palette anchors on red, black and white with gold, yellow and green accents, and its mood is duende — percussive tension, grief and pride frozen mid-compás. Recognize it by tiered volantes ruffles, lunares dots, silk fringe, arched braceo arms with broken wrists, heeled zapateado shoes, and hard single-source light carving saturated color out of darkness.

name: Flapper
description: Flapper is the youth aesthetic of 1920s Western women: knee-length, drop-waist tubular shift dresses, shingle-bobbed hair under pulled-down cloche hats, ropes of pearls, beaded fringe and feather boas, rendered in soft silver-gelatin or sepia studio light, flat Deco-bright poster color, or warm cinematic revival. Palette of ink black, ivory, beige and tobacco brown spiked with Deco brights in violet, jade and metallic gold; signature props include cigarette holders, chandelier earrings, sheer rolled stockings and 2–3 inch Mary Jane heels. Recognize by the straight "up-and-down" silhouette, kicked chorus-line legs, cupid's-bow lips and an air of cheeky, consumerist defiance.

name: Flat_Design
description: Digital-native vector aesthetic of the 2013–2023 interface era (post–Frutiger Aero), also called Vector Minimalism: matte solid color fields with no gradients, gloss or texture, a limited palette anchored in white, light grey, light blue and light green with a few saturated accents, rounded geometric shapes, grid-organized layouts and instantly decipherable pictogram icons. Typical subjects are smartphone and OS interfaces, tile/card grids, app icon sets, clean device mockups on seamless white, and simplified vector illustration (Corporate Memphis figures, layered silhouette landscapes). Recognize it by shadowless uniform lighting, crisp vector edges, generous whitespace and "function over style" orderliness.

name: Fleischer_Style
description: Fleischer Style (Rubberhose / Inkblot Cartoon / Old Cartoon) is the 1920s–1930s American animation look of Fleischer Studios: jointless noodle-tube limbs, pie-cut eyes, white gloves and oversized shoes on round ink-black bodies, staged in grainy grayscale film space with flat theatrical perspective, sentient objects and jazz-age musical gags. Recognize it by elastic squash-and-stretch anatomy, solid black ink masses against soft gray washes, whimsical-dark surreal sight gags, and — when color appears at all — a flat limited set such as poster red, cream and black rather than full-spectrum rendering.

name: Flogger
description: Flogger is the Argentine Fotolog-era teen subculture (peak 2007–2009) whose visual DNA is the amateur flash snapshot: androgynous teens with sleek ironed side-swept fringes covering one eye, neon color-blocked skinny jeans, loose V-neck tees and Converse-style sneakers, throwing peace signs in crowded friend huddles at malls and plazas. Its palette clashes hot pink, turquoise, lime and lemon yellow against black hair and neutral denim, with secondary modes in chibi avatars and annotated "how-to" diagrams. Recognize it by eye-covering bangs plus simultaneous neons plus upload-posed body language.

name: Flower_Power
description: Flower Power is the mid-to-late-1960s American peace-movement aesthetic: daisies and wildflowers worn in the hair, held to the face, or offered to soldiers; floral-print mod fashion; and a floral variant of psychedelia expressed in hand-painted, paisley-filled poster lettering. Its palette runs from saturated poster magenta, marigold, lime and violet to sun-bleached film pastels, lit by blown-out golden sunlight or flat screen-print evenness. Recognize it by flower crowns, garlands, pastoral gardens, curvy ornamental type, earnest tenderness and faded film grain — not by earthy tie-dye hippie rusticity or slick commercial retro.

name: Folk_Horror
description: Folk Horror is the rural horror aesthetic of folklore, surviving paganism and communal ritual: fog-bound woods, moorland clearings and isolated farmsteads inhabited by robed cults, antler- and bird-skull-masked figures, straw effigies and ruined stone chapels. Its palette is muted earth — moss green, bark brown, straw ochre, peat black, bone white — delivered through film grain, haze, overcast scatter or a single torchlit source. Recognize it by ritual circles and processions, animal masks and skins, gnarled mossy trees, standing stones and wreath-crowned figures, and by the tension of old superstition pressing against an empty modern countryside.

name: Food_Mascot_Kitsch
description: Food Mascot Kitsch is the advertising aesthetic of the American cereal-and-snack aisle: anthropomorphic cartoon mascots — tigers, rabbits, leprechauns, pitchers, peanuts, elf boys — with oversized heads, huge excited eyes and open-mouthed grins, drawn in thick black outlines against flat saturated primaries and appetite orange. Originating with the 1877 Quaker trademark and codified in the 1950s–60s Leo Burnett golden age, it lives on cereal boxes, snack bags, fast-food signage and advergames, framed by explosion bursts, speed lines and catchphrases set in starburst type. Recognize it by high-key flat lighting, milk splashes and cereal-confetti scatter, brand logotype lockups, and a mood of enforced, doubt-free cheerfulness.

name: Forestpunk
description: Forestpunk is a 2010s internet aesthetic of wild, self-sufficient wilderness life: fog-shrouded dense forest, bare winter woods, deer and crows, bone-and-antler still lifes, bushcraft camps and rough cabins, rendered in desaturated earth tones (deep green, bark brown, charcoal, black) with muted red and bone-white accents. Its signature fusion is gloom-grade natural atmosphere plus an explicit DIY/punk layer — hand-lettered anti-capitalist posters, pin badges on denim, flannel, worn combat boots, lo-fi grainy photography. Recognize it by raw, harsh nature paired with handmade, anti-consumerist artifacts; never pastel, never manicured, never cozy-glossy.

name: Fotonight_Web
description: Fotonight Web is a 2023-born meme aesthetic that runs 2000s Frutiger Aero gloss through Chinese Shanzhai knockoff culture: low-resolution Photoshop montages of blue skies, airborne goldfish, water splashes and Aero glass bolted onto bootleg phones, misspelled "Binbows" OS boxes and CJK WordArt banners. Its palette is a garish tertiary spread — sky cyan, lawn green, sunshine yellow, tangerine orange, fuchsia — carried on JPEG artifacts, mismatched cutout scales and skeuomorphic UI shine. Recognize it by the collision of corporate Aero optimism with cheap counterfeit print and straight-faced dream nonsense.

name: Four_Colors
description: Four Colors is the mid-2000s consumer-tech marketing aesthetic built on four saturated anchors — electric lime, sky blue, hot pink, neon orange — deployed as flat vector fields, quadrant color panels, and color-variant product lineups (iPod "Silhouette" campaign, Nintendo console variants, iPhone 5c). Recognize it by shadowless flat color blocks, black dancing silhouettes trailed by white earphone cords, glossy plastic product renders on white or pale gradient grounds, concentric-circle and starburst vector ornament, and playful rounded multicolor logotypes; the palette may expand into a full rainbow but the four anchors always organize the frame. Prime 2004–2013, with a longer afterlife in Japanese retail and broadcast design.

name: Frasurbane
description: Frasurbane ("90's Urbane") is the subdued, affluent postmodern style of late-1980s to mid-1990s American retail, advertising and interior design: earth-neutral palettes of brown, beige, tan, grey and cream warmed by a sepia-amber cast, punctuated by single restrained accents of green, blue or yellow; classical serif and italic typography; neo-traditional paneled interiors with columns, coffered ceilings and symmetrical bays; and curated still-life assemblages of scholarly objects — globes, astrolabes, compasses, clocks, sheet music, string instruments. Recognize it by textured paper grain, sepia or duotone photography, gilt frames and printed border devices, and a quiet "adult contemporary" sophistication aimed at baby-boomer suburbanites.

name: Frazzled_English_Woman
description: A 2020s TikTok microtrend, named by RUSSH magazine in 2022, that recreates the dishevelled charm of early-2000s British rom-com heroines — chunky layered knitwear, oversized trench coats, midi skirts or flared jeans, knee-high boots, claw-clip messy updos, skinny scarves and overstuffed practical bags, in chocolate brown, oxblood, oat, heather grey and moss green under overcast daylight or warm lamplight. Recognize it by deliberate bulkiness, loose hair strands, tangled wired earphones, paperbacks and a harried-but-witty mood; it explicitly rejects Clean Girl polish and Coastal Grandmother crispness.

name: French_Girl
description: French Girl (Parisian Chic) is the effortlessly cool Parisian lifestyle aesthetic born in 1950s–60s New Wave and yé-yé culture and revived in 2010s–2020s snapshot form. Recognize it by a neutral wardrobe — black, cream, beige, navy, denim — punctuated by a single red note (red lipstick above all), Breton stripes, trench coats, ballet flats, straw basket bags and a messy wind-ruffled fringe, set in Parisian apartments, cobblestone streets and café terraces under candid natural light or film grain. The mood is studied nonchalance: natural beauty, intellectual romance, visible ease and never visible effort.

name: French_Girly
description: French Girly (フレンチガーリー) is a late-2010s Japanese aesthetic and Girly Kei substyle that stages antique French Haussmann material culture — moldings, gilded mirrors, marble staircases, damask wallpaper — in a blush-pink, cream, white and black palette accented with pearls, gold, tweed and oversized satin bows. Recognize it by coordinated girly fashion (neck-bow blouses, berets, houndstooth or tweed skirts, quilted handbags, Mary Jane pumps) photographed in warm hazy softness inside French-style interiors, plus roses, desserts, lace, and lookbook-style presentation tied to indie brands such as Epine.

name: French_New_Wave
description: French New Wave (Nouvelle Vague) is the look of late-1950s–1960s French cinema: grainy black-and-white 35mm frames lit by found light — blown-out windows, overcast streets, single practical lamps — with handheld off-centre framing, jump-cut cropping and direct addresses to the lens. Signature subjects are young people in period dress (roll-neck sweaters, bob and pixie cuts, thin ties, lace and velvet) caught mid-gesture in cafés, apartments, classrooms and real city streets, surrounded by bystanders and consumer-modern clutter. The mood is cool, ironic and existential: realism, rebellion and cinephilia in greyscale.

name: French_Provincial_Style
description: French Provincial (French Country) is a 17th–18th century interior and architectural aesthetic from rural France that balances rustic simplicity with manor-house refinement: warm neutral plaster walls, walnut and oak furniture on cabriole legs, toile and floral textiles, arched doorways, exposed ceiling beams, terracotta or parquet floors, and restrained gilt, mirror and crystal accents. Recognize it by symmetrical, sun-flooded rooms that feel inherited rather than staged — cream, greige, pale grey, sage and dusty blue schemes punctuated only by small gold highlights and textile-born color such as rug madder or toile blue.

name: Frozen_Ukrainian_Princess
description: Frozen Ukrainian Princess is a Slavic winter-bridal aesthetic born from John Galliano's Fall/Winter 2009 "Frozen Ukrainian Brides" runway and revived on 2020s TikTok and Pinterest: porcelain bald-cap doll faces with smudged, melting dark eye makeup beneath layered coin-and-pearl veils, kokoshnik-shaped headpieces, sheer white tulle, fur trim and pale-gold folk embroidery. Its palette is ivory, cream, pale gold and frosted silver set against snow, frost and onion-domed church backdrops, with smoky grey-black concentrated at the eyes; the mood is spectral, ceremonial and melancholy.

name: Fruittari
description: Fruittari is a mid-2000s Finnish teenage-boy street style built on a voluminous bleached or two-tone "bird's nest" pouf with a bold side-swept fringe, tight skinny jeans, branded hoodies and beanies, big-buckled belts and white low-top sneakers. Its palette pairs black, white, heather grey and indigo denim with candy accents of pink, mint and red, captured in flat Nordic daylight or compact-camera flash with an amateur IRC-Galleria snapshot vernacular. Recognize it by groomed male peacocking — scarves, chains, stud earrings, rectangular glasses — posed proudly against mundane Nordic suburb backdrops.

name: Frutevil_Aero
description: Frutevil Aero is the meme-born 2024 inversion of Frutiger Aero: the glossy early-2000s stock-art vocabulary (translucent candy-colored computers, glass bubbles, lens flares, bokeh, mirror reflections) restaged inside ecological collapse — red blood-water and lava, smoky contaminated skies, cracked dry earth, skeletons, nuclear signage, bats and crows. Its palette runs red, brown, grey and black with ironic patches of green, rendered in naive digital photomontage fidelity. Recognize it by Frutiger Aero's cheerful glossy grammar surviving intact while everything it touches is poisoned, burning, or dead.

name: Frutiger_Aero
description: Frutiger Aero (Web 2.0 Gloss, c. 2004–2013) is the optimistic corporate design language of early Web 2.0: skeuomorphic gel-and-glass icons, translucent Aero window borders, and glossy 3D renders set under saturated blue skies with cumulus clouds. Its palette is sky blue, leaf green and white with tertiary accents (electric lime, hot pink, neon orange), and its signature motifs are water droplets, bubbles, tropical fish in crystal-clear water, lens flares, aurora ribbons, bokeh dots and a glossy Earth globe. Typical subjects are consumer-tech product shots (Windows Vista/7, iOS 1–6, Wii, PS3, early Galaxy phones), eco-utopian green architecture, nature-macro stock imagery, and clean one-point-perspective corporate renders.

name: Frutiger_Eco
description: Frutiger Eco is the corporate green-utopia gloss of mid-2000s to mid-2010s advertising, stock photography and packaging — a subgenre of Frutiger Aero built on high-gloss vector spheres, green-edited Earth globes, sprouting seedlings, wind turbines and solar panels, water droplets and pristine grassy hills under high-key sky-blue light. Recognize it by its locked foliage-green/sky-blue/white palette with yellow only as sunlight, by lens flares, bokeh and skeuomorphic shine on every surface, and by ad-layout negative space reserved for logos and slogans.

name: Funfair_Kitsch
description: Funfair Kitsch (Carnival Ride Art) is the airbrushed, LED-strobed visual language of traveling amusement rides from the 1970s onward — a standardized global export of Italian manufacture: neon pink, electric blue and high-visibility yellow gradients sprayed across glossy fiberglass ride shells, off-model bootleg cartoon mascots and nightlife collages painted from memory, marquee bulbs and RGB LED matrices flashing over visible trailer seams, hinges and grease-stained hydraulics. Load this skill to recognize or generate itinerant fairground facades, mascot lead cars, ticket kiosks, duck-pond game stalls and deep-fried food signage, with their uncanny, safety-washed, horror-vacui maximalism.

name: Funk
description: Funk is the visual language of 1970s African-American groove culture: flared trousers and jumpsuits in clashing saturated oranges, magentas, purples, golds and turquoises, platform boots, Afros, sequins, satin and velvet, star emblems and psychedelic sunburst graphics. Typical subjects are full-body studio portraits, coordinated band ensembles, theatrical cosmic stage costumes, dancers mid-groove, and flat poster art with concentric rings. Recognize it by maximalist clashing color, shine-plus-plush materials, exaggerated silhouettes (flare, platform, huge collars and capes), and joyful, swaggering Black self-presentation; a late-1970s earth-tone register also belongs to the style.

name: Furry
description: Anthropomorphic animal characters ("fursonas") expressed through crafted fursuits and toony cartoon artwork, in bright happy pastels and neons that are often unnatural for the species. Signature elements include sculpted foam-and-faux-fur suit heads with plastic mesh or anime-printed eyes, oversized paw gloves with contrasting paw pads, star/heart/paint-drip markings, digitigrade padding, and convention lanyards and badge clutter. The mood is cheerful, frivolous and radically accepting, captured in casual snapshot lighting inside convention halls, bedrooms, backyards and parks.

name: Future_Funk
description: Future Funk (Vaporboogie) is the euphoric visual language of the early-2010s internet dance microgenre: 1980s–90s cel-shaded anime figures caught mid-dance, mid-wink or mid-transformation, graded in hyper-saturated neon magenta, cyan and violet with CRT bloom and clean VHS grain. Chrome script and kanji typography, cassettes, spinning vinyl, arcade cabinets, disco beams and Japanese bubble-economy nightlife evoke an idealized 1980s that never ends. Recognize it by neon duotone washes over retro anime line art, loop-friendly repetition and unironic party optimism — the opposite of vaporwave's glitchy decay.

name: Futurism
description: Italian avant-garde (1909–1944) that paints speed itself: Cubism-derived fractured planes set into motion by rhythmic repetition, blur and radiating "lines of force," in bright, jarring Divisionist color — cobalt and teal skies against ochre, vermilion and chrome. Signature subjects are airplanes and diving aerial views, cars, trains, factories, cities, war machines, and asymmetric geometric fashion; signature structures are diagonal thrusts, spirals, light cones and interpenetrating planes. Recognize by machine euphoria and felt velocity — never by static, symmetrical or ornamental arrangement.

name: Gabber
description: Gabber is the working-class hardcore techno subculture of early-1990s Rotterdam: shaved heads or undercut skulls with tight braids and ponytails, colour-blocked 90s tracksuits (Australian L'Alpina, Cavello), satin bomber jackets with embroidered back patches, and Nike Air Max sneakers, shot on direct flash in warehouses, clubs and decayed industrial yards or tiled into documentary headshot grids. Recognise it by loud geometric sportswear colour-blocking (teal, magenta, violet, cobalt, lime) against black satin and concrete grey, hakken dance blur, photocopied rave-flyer graphics, and a communal, aggressive, deliberately unpretentious mood.

name: Galaxy_Print
description: Galaxy Print is an early-2010s Tumblr/Instagram fashion-and-graphic aesthetic that wraps leggings, hoodies, sneakers, flat-lay collages and quote graphics in saturated nebula prints — deep violet, electric blue and magenta clouds shot through with neon accents and white star speckles. Signature elements include all-over cosmic print on stretch fabric, sparkle and stardust overlays, silhouettes filled with nebula, and companion motifs of hipster mustaches, unicorns, wolves, cats and anime girls. Recognize it by cool cosmic saturation plus starfield scatter applied to everyday objects and casual fashion, distinct from realistic astrophotography, pastel-only kawaii, and warm summer-nostalgia palettes.

name: Ganguro
description: Ganguro is the mid-1990s Shibuya-born gyaru substyle whose visual DNA is the extreme value clash of a deep artificial tan against bleached blonde or silver hair, thick black eyeliner, and white concealer worn as lipstick and eyeshadow for a panda-like face. Signature elements include neon miniskirts, chunky platform boots, hibiscus flowers and leis, candy-plastic jewelry, and the saturated, flash-lit look of egg-magazine street snaps. Recognize it in loud, playful portraits of tanned Japanese teens where skin, hair, plastic and print are all pushed to maximum contrast and chroma.

name: Gardencore
description: Gardencore is a mid-2000s, nature-based aesthetic and the practical subgenre of Cottagecore, centered on home and community gardens: tended vegetable beds, greenhouses, terrariums and container plots, bare soil and compost, rusty hand tools, and upcycled junk planters such as boots, tins and watering cans. Its palette is earthy and weathered — sage and moss greens, soil browns, straw beige, rust orange, marigold yellow, galvanized silver-gray — lit by dappled daylight or soft overcast. Recognize it by harvest baskets, seed packets and hand-lettered labels, handmade miniatures, bugs and small animals, and a mood of thrifty, hardworking eco-consciousness rather than pastoral romance.

name: Garçonne
description: Garçonne is the androgynous "New Woman" style of 1920s Paris — a boyish, linear silhouette with flattened chest, sleek bobbed hair (coupe à la garçonne), and menswear-derived tailoring (blazers, trousers, crisp white shirts, bow ties, cloche hats) set in a near-monochrome palette of black, white, gray and beige punctuated only by deep red lipstick. Recognize it by cool dandyish poise, severe unornamented styling, and the soft matte grain of monochrome studio photography or muted sepia-olive print advertising; it is deliberately austere where the Flapper is decorative.

name: Gay_Nineties_Revival
description: A late-1960s-to-1970s American nostalgia mode that resurrects 1890s music-hall kitsch — fern-draped conservatory dining rooms of exposed brick, medium-stained oak and heavy brass, Tiffany-style stained-glass lamps hung low over tables, and ornate Vaudeville Tuscan slab-serif lettering in brown, orange and old gold. Recognize it by hanging ferns under leaded-glass skylights, playbill posters and album jackets with drop-shadowed slab-serif type, penny farthings and novelty inventions, and gilded Gilded-Age theatricality, often spiked with a psychedelic-era pop-color burst.

name: Geek_Chic
description: Geek Chic is a mid-2000s fashion aesthetic that restyles stereotypical nerd signifiers — oversized black horn-rimmed glasses, argyle sweater vests, bow ties, suspenders, gingham and plaid button-downs — as ironic, desirable outfits. Its palette sits in schoolhouse neutrals (heather gray, charcoal, black, cream) punctuated by oxblood red, mustard, navy and occasional mint, with prints doing the color work; typical images are snapshot-flat domestic, street-crossing or lookbook scenes showing knee socks, cropped high-waisted trousers, pleated skirts and leather satchels. The mood is playful, brainy self-awareness: intelligence worn as costume, nostalgia for the school uniform worn with a wink.

name: Gen-X_Home
description: Gen-X Home is the soft, domestic interior-and-product aesthetic of the late 1990s through early 2000s: muted earthy shells (sage green, warm oak, soft blue, terracotta, cool gray) color-blocked with saturated plum, tangerine, poppy and cobalt accents; curvy furniture, irregular glazed vases with gerbera daisies, and CRT-era tech housed in deep warm-wood cabinetry. Catalog-bright, high-key daylight, plush structured seating against metal-and-glass tables, statement pendants and halogen uplighters, curated shelf collections — the home-marketing twin of Corporate Cyberspace. Recognize it by lived-in pragmatic coziness plus bounded blocks of bold color, never full minimalism and never 1980s gloss.

name: Gen_X_Soft_Club
description: Gen X Soft Club (GXSC) is the late-1990s/early-2000s "down-to-earth" branch of Y2K Futurism: muted analog film in sage greens, dusty teals, beiges, tans and greys, washed with lomo cross-processing, bleach bypass, blur, bloom and vignettes over metro stations, airports, night storefronts and cityscapes. Signature elements are small lowercase Helvetica type, sparse vector line graphics, frosted glass and fluorescent glow, and anonymous blurred figures in civic interiors. Typical subjects range from album-cover layouts and soft-focus portraits to transit platforms and dusk cityscapes, all carrying a calm, gently melancholic urban optimism.

name: Gen_Z_Maximalism
description: Gen Z Maximalism (a.k.a. Dopamine Decor) is the 2020s TikTok-bred aesthetic of joyful clutter — full-spectrum, highly saturated clashing colors, patchwork and crochet and macramé textures, collage poster walls, plant-crowded rooms, and thrifted color-clash outfits shot in bright snapshot light. Recognize it by horror-vacui density, deliberate pattern clash, handmade and secondhand accumulation, and an anti-minimalist playfulness; its home turf is interiors and graphic design more than fashion. Use this skill to identify, plan, or separate it from Avant Basic, Decora, Kidcore, Dopamine Dressing, and Grocery Girl Fall.

name: Gen_Z_Soft_Club
description: Gen Z Soft Club is the late-2010s/early-2020s revival of 1990s soft-focus tech-ad minimalism: desaturated sage, pale blue, grey and stark-white imagery with lomo blur, bloom halation and motion smear, overlaid with tiny monospace or thin extended futuristic type and dot/square pixel grids. Typical subjects are underground electronic flyers and visualizers, candid blurred youth portraits, night-city infrastructure and high-key white voids. Recognize it as muted, fogged, millennium-nostalgic club ephemera — quiet optimism, never loud chrome Y2K.

name: Genderless_Kei
description: Genderless Kei is the mid-2010s Harajuku street fashion of deliberately androgynous styling: doll-like makeup on male-presenting faces, colored contact lenses, dyed bowl-cut or shag hair, slim silhouettes of skinny jeans or slim trousers under oversized tops, and delicate jewelry. Its color language swings between pastel, candy-saturated, and strict monochrome black-or-white, photographed in flat-lit Harajuku street snaps, high-key studio portraits, or sticker-decorated selfies. Recognize it by the gender-blurred read combined with a polished beauty finish, platform footwear, and disciplined palette families rather than by any single garment.

name: Genericana
description: Genericana is a heritage-branding design aesthetic of the 1980s through early 2010s that recreates 1920s–1950s American trade signage: sign-painting and wood-type lettering, badge/crest/label lockups with ribbons, seals and stamps, carried on kraft paper, felt, tin and glass against reclaimed wood, exposed brick and Edison-lit shop interiors. Its palette is ink black, cream paper, brick red, heritage blue and light brown, and its mood is manufactured artisanal heritage — a faux-premium "Est. 19XX" solidity adopted by the hipster wave of the Great Recession. Recognize it by arched bold serifs, centered emblems, ornate trade-card borders and rustic-industrial substrates, never by glossy modern branding or flat mid-century illustration.

name: Geo-Boho
description: Geo-Boho is an early-2010s Tumblr-born graphic and interior aesthetic that fuses stroke-based triangle geometry and elongated hairline sans-serifs with soft boho exoticism — dreamcatchers, feathers, animal totems, pale wood, macramé — all under a desaturated lo-mo haze of bone white, greige, dusty pastels and occasional prism gradients. Recognize it by centered triangle or mandala emblems, line-over-fill vector work, sun-bleached or string-lit ambient minimalism, and earnest spiritual-lite optimism on album art, boutique interiors, packaging, posters and music-video stills.

name: Ghostcore
description: Ghostcore is a 2010s internet aesthetic of ghosts, cemeteries and haunted domestic space, rendered in black, bone-white, sepia and fog-gray with heavy grain, dim flash light and the worn look of found photographs. Its signature elements are draped white sheets, translucent figures with pupil-less white or black eyes, handprints on glass, empty fog-bound graveyards, mansions and forests, and a deadpan humour that lets costume ghosts and occult zine collages sit beside genuine dread. Read it as photographic evidence of a presence that should not be there.

name: Gibson_Girl
description: American magazine aesthetic of the 1890s–1910s built on Charles Dana Gibson's pen-and-ink ideal of the "New Woman": a tall S-bend corset silhouette in a high-necked shirtwaist and floor-length flared skirt, voluminous pompadour hair often crowned by a wide-brimmed hat, and a serene, faintly haughty expression. The palette is strictly monochrome — ink black on paper white, or sepia and silver-grey studio photography — with motifs of sport, college life, the seaside, and wry dominance over bemused male foils. Recognize it by the S-curve posture, bouffant hair, magazine-plate reproduction texture (cross-hatch or halftone), and poised confidence; distinguish it from Edwardian society softness, Art Nouveau ornament, and the later pin-up.

name: Girl_Crush
description: Girl Crush is the K-pop concept aesthetic formalized in the late 2000s by 2NE1 out of late-1990s techno-performance roots: black-dominant punk, biker and techwear styling cut with silver chain hardware, combat boots, fishnets and crop-top-against-baggy-pant silhouettes, sparked by red or neon accents. Recognize it by assertive stagings of women — staggered group formations, wide stances, chin-up glares — on industrial scaffolding, concrete pads or seamless white promo voids, lit by flat lookbook light or saturated color gels. Its mood is subversive, hoydenish, androgynous confidence addressed to female fans rather than ingénue objectification.

name: Girls'_Sleepover
description: Girls' Sleepover (slumber party, pajama party) is the domestic, group-centered aesthetic of girlhood friendship: bedrooms and living rooms over-stuffed with pillows, sleeping bags and blankets, a pink-and-white palette opened to any accent color, and nights organized around spa rituals, junk food, board games, movies and girl talk. Rooted in 1950s suburban coming-of-age culture and filtered through 2000s tween media, its imagery ranges from flash-lit film snapshots and warm string-light forts to mid-century commercial illustration and tween book-cover cartoons, always centered on multiple friends in pajamas inside a stereotypically girly room.

name: Girly_Kei
description: Girly Kei (Gaari Kei) is a Japanese frilly-feminine fashion aesthetic born from 1990s magazines (Olive, CUTiE) and brands like Liz Lisa and LARME, built on pastel-pink, white and black coordinates of ruffled Peter Pan-collar blouses, high-waisted lace-hem skirts, bows and platform Mary Janes. It is recognized by lace, ribbons, frills, flower and heart prints, Sanrio-style kawaii props, perfume bottles and café sweet-trays, shot in soft high-key light often with sparkle or heart overlays. The style spans sweet pastel, gingham-preppy and black-anchored "Dark Girly" variants while keeping a preppy, idol-cute core.

name: Giscardpunk
description: Giscardpunk is a France-centric retrofuturist aesthetic of the Giscard d'Estaing years (1974–81, stretching into the 1960s and late 1980s): blue-grey concrete megastructures, orange TGV noses and Renault hatchbacks, beige Minitel terminals with teal pixel screens, and airbrushed magazine renderings of planned cities. Its visual DNA is period print — halftone grain, poster type bands, diagrammatic transit maps — laid over a cool blue/grey/cream field punctured by state-orange accents. Recognize it by French signage, clean brutalist geometry, daylight technocratic optimism, and videotex-era analog tech, distinct from cyberpunk noir and nation-agnostic cassette futurism.

name: Glam_Rock
description: Glam rock is the flamboyant British rock aesthetic of 1970–1976: platform boots, glitter and face paint, satin and crumpled metallic lamé, and androgynous performers posed on stages among drum risers and amp stacks. Its palette is maximalist — any hue licensed, unified by metallic sheen, candy saturation and hard spotlight against black voids — with camp theatricality, mullets and fluffed hair, bell-bottom flares and bodysuits as recurring signals. Recognize it by the fusion of rock gear (electric guitars, amp stacks, drum kits) with cabaret-grade makeup and glitter; it separates from disco's dancefloor gloss, goth's monochrome mourning and hair metal's 1980s spandex.

name: Glassmorphism
description: Glassmorphism is the 2020s UI aesthetic of translucent frosted-glass panels floating over vivid gradient backgrounds, defined by lowered fill opacity, Gaussian background blur, and thin semi-transparent white border strokes. Typical subjects are operating-system interfaces, app cards and widgets, icon grids, 3D glass renders and AR/spatial head-up displays, in palettes of electric blue, violet and magenta gradients or their pastel and dark-neon variants. Recognize it by seeing distorted, blurred color bleeding through a matte panel edge-lit by a hairline white stroke — never opaque flat fills, never glossy skeuomorphic reflections.

name: Glitch_Art
description: Glitch Art is the aesthetic of deliberate machine failure — pixel-sorted streaks, displaced horizontal slices, macroblock shards, scanline static and acid channel tints (magenta, cyan, violet, signal green) corrupting an otherwise legible photograph, film still or render, or dissolving it entirely into noise on a black void. Rooted in 1960s video sabotage and crystallized as a 1990s–2000s databending/datamoshing movement, it treats error as the subject: faces sliced into tinted bands, CRT and plasma screen artifacts, static fields, compression melt. Recognize it by the machine-grid geometry of its corruption (hard-edged rectangles, uniform scanline pitch, full-width band offsets) and by flat, screen-emissive color that ignores the lighting of the underlying scene.

name: Glitchbreak
description: Glitchbreak (also Sewercore, Laincore, Dreambreak) is a late-2010s internet aesthetic born from Spotify-tagged atmospheric breakcore: melancholic anime figures, often Serial Experiments Lain-like, dissolved in pixel sorting, datamosh smears and scanlines over deep purple, black and dull-green fields punctured by neon pink and cyan. Signature elements include dated Y2K browser UI, pixelated bitmap typography, rudimentary wireframe 3D, lonely digital environments and square album-cover framing. Recognize it by its muted dark palette and mournful, dissociative mood — darker and slower than Glitchcore, more figure- and mood-driven than pure Glitch Art.

name: Glitchcore
description: Glitchcore (aka Eyestraincore) is a 2020s TikTok-born aesthetic of maximalist digital corruption: clipping-neon rainbows, pixel sorting and datamosh, checkerboard and dither pattern fields, sticker symbols (stars, hearts, smileys, peace signs), and anime, cartoon and video-game characters buried under layers of glitch. Signature cues include eyestrain saturation, RGB channel split, error-dialog and VHS "PLAY" text, and candy-cute icons paired with sick-sweet emo captions. Load this skill when recognizing or generating saturated glitch collage, corrupted-cartoon nostalgia, or hyperpop-era visual overload.

name: Global_Village_Coffeehouse
description: Global Village Coffeehouse (GVC) is the US commercial-design aesthetic of the late 1980s through early 2000s — the "world vibes" look of 1990s coffeehouses, world-music album art, and eco-friendly food packaging. Recognize it by earth-tone grounds (terracotta, olive, beige, umber) warmed by airbrushed sunset gradients, rough woodcut-style line art with sketchy gaps and deliberately misregistered color layers, horror-vacui folk panels of petroglyph figures, spirals, suns, globes, hands and coffee-steam swirls, and hand-lettered irregular typography. It reads as warm, genial, faux-handcrafted multiculturalism: Starbucks-era coziness rendered as gouache and woodblock on recycled paper.

name: Gloomcore
description: Gloomcore is an internet-born visual aesthetic of fog-shrouded, liminal natural landscapes — evergreen forests, empty beaches, moors, streams, overgrown paths — rendered in muted greens, browns and greys with flat overcast or subtly "off" lighting and a soft-focus, snapshot-like surface. Its signature elements are mist and rain veiling distance, moss, lichen and fungus, dilapidated or plant-encroached structures, and optional shadowy beings, cryptids or surreal manufactured intrusions, all held in a tranquil-yet-on-edge dreamlike mood. Load this skill to recognize or generate quiet, desaturated, fog-bound nature imagery that reads as a half-remembered photograph rather than a crisp landscape print.

name: Goblincore
description: Goblincore is a 2020s internet aesthetic that celebrates the "ugly-beautiful" underside of nature — moss, mud, fungi, snails, frogs, bones — and the hoarded "shinies" (tarnished rings, buttons, crystals, painted pebbles) of a carefree forest collector. Its visual DNA is earth-toned and shadowed: dark green, olive lime, bark brown, black loam and bone cream, punctuated by small saturated pops of mushroom-cap red, spore pink or candle amber; maximalist clutter, wet and worn textures, secondhand cloth, and intimate ground-level or hand-held scale under dappled woodland, overcast or candlelight. Load this skill to recognize or generate images of forest-floor macro specimens, cluttered trinket shelves and jars, mossy streams, worn adventurer clothing, or scavenged-object collages.

name: Golden_Age_of_Detective_Fiction
description: Interwar (1920s–1930s) country-house mystery aesthetic built on the clash of aristocratic elegance and sudden violence — oak-paneled manor rooms, pearl strands, white tie and metallic brocade set against a single trace of blood, poison or a displaced clue. Palette of walnut and mahogany browns, ivory and pearl creams, oxblood red and poster orange under low tungsten lamplight; signature props include magnifying glasses and fingerprint powder, taxidermy and antler trophies, leather-bound private libraries, crystal decanters, steam trains and storm-lashed manor exteriors. Use for suspect ensembles, great-detective portraits, evidence still-lifes and cluttered estate interiors that read as polished suspense rather than horror, noir, academia or spy thriller.

name: Googie
description: Googie is the populist Space Age commercial architecture of late-1940s-to-early-1970s Southern California — coffee shops, motels, gas stations, car washes and bowling alleys with upswept cantilevered roofs, parabolic arches, flying-saucer discs, starbursts and boomerang geometry in chrome, neon and pastel-plus-primary color blocks. Recognize it by roadside pole signs towering over open sky, rooflines that sweep upward as if in motion, and an unabashedly optimistic, car-culture futurism. Also known as Populuxe or Doo Wop.

name: Googie_Kitsch
description: Googie Kitsch (Googie Revival) is the late-1970s-through-1990s revival of 1950s American atomic-age commercial pop: upswept roofs, boomerang tables and pillars, starbursts, orbit-diagram atoms and shooting stars, flashy neon pylons and script signage in flamingo pink, turquoise, mint and bold primaries over checkerboard floors and chrome. Typical subjects are coffee-shop and diner interiors, roadside snack-bar signage at night, cocktail lounges in saturated colored light, and flat print-ad or album-cover graphics with cutout figures, martini glasses and hand-lettered type. The mood is a tongue-in-cheek Jetsons utopia — automated fun, plastic modular space, consumer optimism — never dystopian.

name: Gorecore
description: Gorecore (also Fleshcore, Slaughtercore, Murdercore) is a transgressive internet aesthetic of stylized bloodshed: saturated scarlet-to-oxblood reds staged against black and bone-white, carrying bloody knives, razor-blade and spike hardware, skeleton and organ motifs, SFX fake blood, and slasher-film grain. Typical subjects are body fragments (pale necks, bleeding hands), knife-themed goth-punk accessories and garments, creepy naive drawings, and high-contrast red-on-black posters or collage grids. Recognize it by hard red/black contrast, viscous paint-like drip silhouettes, and sweet-versus-deadly juxtapositions — never by photorealistic clinical gore or pastel softness.

name: Goreweb
description: Goreweb (also Chaoscore, AGC Style, LiveLeakcore) is a 2020s internet aesthetic, a subgenre of Opium streetwear branding, that recasts mid-2000s shock-site horror — LiveLeak watermarks, cursed JPEGs, fake gore, deep-fried compression — into high-fashion hype imagery. Recognize it by bitcrushed black fields, arterial-red watermark text and splatter, spiky symmetrical slam-metal logotypes, dental and medical horror, Oldboy and gimp-mask streetwear motifs, thermal/night-vision casts, and degraded merch mockups. Its mood is aggressive, desensitized and shitpost-ironic — never vulnerable.

name: Gorpcore
description: Gorpcore is the 2010s outdoor-utility streetwear aesthetic: technical shell jackets, fleeces, puffers and baggy cargo pants in muted earthy greens, browns, greys and blacks, punctuated by occasional high-visibility orange, yellow or electric-blue accents. Signature elements are visible layering, hoods and beanies, functional hardware (zippers, buckles, drawcords, taped seams), small outdoor-brand logos and chunky hiking sneakers or boots, photographed in flat overcast light on mountain trails, in conifer forest, or against mundane urban concrete. Faces are often half-hidden by hoods, neck gaiters or wraparound shield sunglasses; the mood is understated, prepared and deliberately unpretentious.

name: Goth
description: Goth is the music-born subculture aesthetic of late-1970s/1980s Britain (London, Leeds, the Batcave club), built on a black-dominant palette accented by deep purple, crimson, emerald and bone-white. Its signature elements are backcombed, teased deathhawk or shag hair; pale matte skin with heavy graphic eye makeup; fishnets, lace, velvet, studded leather and corsetry worn as outerwear; and heavy silver occult jewelry (ankhs, crucifixes, skull rings). Typical subjects are androgynous figures in pensive studio portraits, club and street snapshots, domestic group shots and romantic mourning tableaus, rendered in grainy monochrome or faded amateur color.

name: Goth_Punk
description: Goth Punk (J-Punk) is a Japanese street fashion of the late 1990s–2000s that fuses goth and punk into black-dominant coordinates cut with red tartan, black-and-red stripes and red contrast stitching, loaded with silver chains, studs, buckles, spikes and exposed zips, worn by androgynous figures in thick-soled platform boots. Typical images are Japanese brand catalog and advertisement scans, street snaps, and clean cel-shaded anime character art featuring skull, spider, bat and cross motifs, bondage pants, pleated tartan skirts, sailor collars and edgy "Engrish" print. Recognize it by the black/red/white triad, the density of tartan-plus-metal hardware, and casual androgynous styling — distinct from Victorian Goth, Visual Kei stage wear, and Western Emo.

name: Gothabilly
description: Gothabilly (also hellbilly, dark pin-up) is a 1990s subculture aesthetic that cuts 1950s American rockabilly silhouettes — wiggle dresses, pencil skirts, swing skirts over petticoats, cuffed trousers, waistcoats — in a goth palette of black ground punctured by red, cream and purple, with polka dots and leopard print as pattern breaks. Recognize it by horror-kitsch motifs (skulls, bats, spiderwebs, coffins), pin-up grooming (victory rolls, Bettie bangs, winged cat-eye liner, dark red lips), fishnets, lace gloves, satin or PVC sheen, platform and creeper shoes, and a campy macabre-glamour mood that favors mood over aggression.

name: Gothic
description: Gothic is the literary and visual aesthetic of late-18th-century British Romanticism's dark side — haunted castles, crumbling ruins, weathered graveyards, candlelit interiors and wild storm-lashed moors, rendered in a near-monochrome palette of soot black, fog grey and bone white with oxblood red and mourning purple as the only saturated accents. Signature elements include silhouetted spires and wrought-iron gates, ghosts in white, memento mori skulls, ravens and bats, red velvet, candelabras, antique books, and a rendering lineage split between pen-and-ink book illustration (Beardsley, Doré, Gorey, Kay Nielsen) and chiaroscuro Romantic oil painting (Fuseli, Goya). Mood is suspense, dread and the sublime: emotion over reason, antique decay over modern shine.

name: Gothic_Belly_Dance
description: Gothic Belly Dance (also Dark Fusion Belly Dance or Tribal Goth) is a 1990s US performance-costume aesthetic that fuses American Tribal Style belly dance with Goth subculture: bare-midriff choli tops, hip skirts and coin-and-chain belts rebuilt in black lace, leather and velvet, loaded with bone, wood and stone jewelry, dreadlocks, piercings and tribal tattoos. Its palette is black-dominant with deep reds, purples and dark earth tones, photographed in low-key studio gloom, saturated stage gels, overcast cool light or high-contrast monochrome. Recognize it by the dance posture plus coin-metal-and-bone ornament over gothic darkness — never by glittering cabaret gold or pure street-goth fashion.

name: Gothic_Lolita
description: Gothic Lolita (gosurori) is a Japanese street fashion of the late 1990s, pioneered by Mana of Malice Mizer, that fuses the doll-like, petticoat-supported Lolita silhouette with dark Western Goth elegance. Recognize it by knee-length black A-line or bell skirts over petticoats, lace-trimmed blouses with rectangle headdresses or side-worn headpieces, hime-cut jet-black hair, dark wine lipstick, and motifs of crosses, bats, coffins, chandeliers and deep red roses, accented with ivory lace or jewel tones (crimson, royal blue, purple). The mood is melancholy, mysterious, Victorian-doll elegance — neither punk aggression nor pastel cuteness.

name: Graffiti_Pop
description: Graffiti Pop is the 1980s–early-1990s commercial packaging of New York street graffiti and hip-hop into a mass-media shorthand for "urban cool": wildstyle and bubble-letter murals, tags on brick, chain-link fences, street lamps, trash cans and run-down cars, lit by neon spray accents (hot pink, neon green, purple, electric blue, red) against grey concrete and rust. Typical subjects are baggy-clothed street kids, breakdancers, DJs, cartoon mascots in big trainers, boomboxes and spray cans, framed as music-video sets, TV intros, album covers, arcade ads and faded 35mm snapshots. Recognize it by the collision of grungy urban-decay props with saturated, airbrushed, cartoon-confident colour and hand-styled lettering.

name: Grandmillennial
description: Grandmillennial (Granny Chic, New Traditionalist) is an early-2020s interior and lifestyle aesthetic that layers floral chintz, toile wallpaper, needlepoint pillows, ruffles, pleated lampshades, wicker and polished dark-wood furniture in pattern-on-pattern rooms grounded in soft pastels (sage, powder blue, blush) and punctuated by richer traditional notes (cobalt blue-and-white china, olive green, mahogany, burgundy). Recognize it by curated inherited clutter — china collections, gilt-framed heirloom paintings, gallery walls, brass vases of garden flowers, skirted tables — and by modest vintage-inspired fashion with pearls, brooches and monograms; the mood is sincere nostalgia and comfort, never ironic kitsch and never minimalist.

name: Granola
description: Granola (Granola Girl/Guy, "crunchy") is a 2010s Instagram-and-TikTok lifestyle aesthetic of earnest outdoor recreation, built on lived-in Patagonia fleece, flannel shirts, Birkenstock sandals, Kånken packs and reusable water bottles photographed on trails, campsites and lake edges. Its palette is sun-faded earth — bark brown, olive moss, oat beige, terracotta rust, deep lake blue — rendered in soft natural light with a film-faded snapshot grain. Signature reads: unposed laughing candids, mossy forest and mountain biosphere, granola bowls and enamel mugs, friendship bracelets and braids, and Pinterest-style moodboard collages with handwritten captions.

name: Grażynacore
description: Grażynacore is the earnest-but-ironized visual dialect of glittery greeting graphics circulated by Polish women around 60 on Facebook, descended from 1960s socialist-bloc sound postcards and 1990s Disco Polo cassette art. Recognize it by saturated pink/red/brown/gold palettes, blinking glitter stars and bokeh sparkle, clipart roses and steaming coffee cups with cream hearts, soft-focus animals, and Polish diminutive greetings ("kawusia", "serduszka", "Miłego dnia") set in glossy serif or script type over layered photo-and-clipart collage. The ironic variant keeps the warm container intact while inserting deadpan dissonant figures — communist-era politicians, Pope John Paul II, anime and video-game characters — into the same roses-and-coffee format.

name: Greaser
description: Greaser is the 1950s American working-class youth aesthetic of pomade-sculpted pompadours and ducktails, black leather or denim jackets over fitted white T-shirts, cuffed blue jeans and boots, posed with cigarettes, switchblades and flame-painted hot rods. Its palette is black, white and red held in check by denim indigo and asphalt gray, rendered in grainy 35mm snapshots or saturated revival-film color. Recognition anchors: gang group tableaus, defiant leisure, gleaming combed hair, and a machine cult of kustom cars and motorcycles.

name: Green_Academia
description: Green Academia (Botanic/Earthy Academia) is a 2020s internet aesthetic of field-science scholarship: pressed plants, nature journals with ink handwriting and Latin labels, bones, fossils, fungi, moss, and cloth-bound books studied in greenhouses, vine-choked libraries and damp forests. Its palette is desaturated moss-and-forest green with bark brown, parchment cream and stone grey, lit by overcast or window light with a faded analog film finish. Recognize it by the fusion of scholarly apparatus (specimens, journals, collections, old books) with living or preserved nature; distinguish it from Dark Academia (no gothic candlelight), Light Academia (no cream-and-marble classicism), Campcore (no recreational camping gear), Gardencore (no cozy cottage cultivation) and Goblincore (no muddy chaotic hoarding).

name: Grime_Art
description: Grime Art (aka the Zombie Effect) is a mid-2010s internet-born digital style in which portrait photographs are invaded by hand-drawn cartoon slime: melting, dripping flesh in pastel pink, acid green or bright purple, solid glowing white eyes, droopy eyebags, extra eyes and pizza- or vomit-textured skin. Recognize it by the tension between an untouched photographic substrate and flat, vibrantly sickly, gravity-obeying goo confined to faces and hands, plus optional dripping hand-lettered captions. Typical subjects are selfies, celebrity portraits, memes, party snapshots, classical paintings and cartoon characters zombified into grotesque-playful caricatures.

name: Grindhouse
description: Grindhouse is the 1970s American exploitation-cinema aesthetic — degraded analog film (heavy grain, scratches, blurry motion), decaying urban sprawl, and shouted one-sheet poster design in blood red, soot black, aged-paper cream and one saturated accent such as flame orange, hot magenta or acid yellow. Signature elements include practical splatter effects, halftone dots and fold-creased print textures, collage anti-hero compositions with taglines and credit blocks, theater marquees and drive-in ephemera, and marginal "problematic" characters — blaxploitation heroines, vigilantes, bikers, sex workers, zombies. Recognize it as pulp social commentary worn as analog damage, revived by the 2007 Tarantino/Rodriguez double feature and neo-grindhouse game and music-video styling.

name: Grocery_Girl_Fall
description: Grocery Girl Fall (Grocerycore) is a 2020s TikTok-born fashion and interior microtrend, crystallized in autumn 2023, that furnishes clothes and rooms with edible vocabulary: fruit-shaped ceramic vases and lamps, pasta- and radish-print textiles, hyperrealistic food candles, anthropomorphized snack plushies, papier-mâché produce. Its palette is produce-aisle saturation — tomato red, butter yellow, leafy green, strawberry pink — staged either in thrifted vintage domestic rooms or on flat candy-colored studio grounds, always with camp humor and handmade DIY texture. Recognize it by food-shaped functional objects, food prints, and playful maximalist grocery displays; separate it from Maillard's brown tonality, Whimsigothic's occult dark, and non-food maximalism.

name: Groovival
description: Groovival is the late-1980s-to-mid-2000s revival aesthetic that fuses 1960s mod, flower-power hippie and 1970s disco imagery with acid-rave smileys and cyberdelic liquid swirls, in a high-key candy palette of yellow, pink, baby blue, purple, green and white. Recognize it by flat oversized daisy prints, tie-dye spirals, peace signs, kaleidoscopic radial bursts, bubble-groovy lettering, colour-block mod minidresses and go-go boots, all rendered with period revival production tells — vector flats, halftone print, lava-lamp CGI gradients, glossy catalogue photography — and a knowingly satirical, nostalgic wink.

name: Grunge
description: Grunge is the visual language of the Seattle sound of the late 1980s to mid-1990s: thrifted oversized flannel, ripped faded denim, vintage band tees, combat boots and unkempt hair, shot on grainy analogue film or assembled as torn, photocopied zine collage. Its palette is earthy and muted — brown, army green, grey, burgundy, faded denim blue — under overcast daylight, harsh club flash, or high-contrast black and white, with distressed textures, eroded handwritten type and slouchy anti-fashion silhouettes throughout. The mood is apathy, angst and lived-in authenticity: everything looks worn, borrowed and deliberately unpolished.

name: Guido
description: Guido/Guidette is the loud, flash-lit aesthetic of working-class Italian-American crew culture from New York and New Jersey — 1970s disco roots, late-2000s Jersey Shore peak — built on bronze tanning-bed skin, gel-sculpted blowouts and crown poofs, gold crucifix chains and rosaries, Ed Hardy/Fila logo wear, leopard print and hot pink against Italian-tricolore accents. Recognize it by tight crew group poses under harsh on-camera flash at beaches, boardwalks and clubs, where vanity, machismo and conspicuous consumption are worn sincerely, not ironically.

name: Gulf_Futurism
description: Gulf Futurism is the hypermodern aesthetic of the Arabian Gulf petro-states (born 2008, named 2012), pairing desert haze and colossal infrastructure — striped water towers, lattice-skinned skyscrapers, rusted oil crawlers, mirrored linear megacities — with traditional Gulf geometric ornament and oil-slick iridescence. Recognize it by sun-bleached sand-and-bone palettes punctured by one bold stripe, lattice or coral accent; sterile empty megastructures under washed pale skies or amber dust; tiny or absent humans; and a mood of prosperous alienation and surreal exaggeration.

name: Guochao
description: Guochao (国潮, "National Trend" / China-chic) is the post-2018 Chinese commercial-pop aesthetic that collides late-Qing and Republican-era signifiers — qipao, Peking-opera Dan headdresses, calligraphied folding fans, xiangyun clouds — with modern streetwear, gadgets and brand-poster grammar. Its visual DNA is saturated vermilion red locked against turquoise/kingfisher blue, gold trim, ink-brush jianghu typography with red seal stamps, dense collage or solid-red product staging, and confident, rebellious posing. Recognize it by opera coronet plus sneakers, palace wall plus product render, and brush-calligraphy title blocks treating heritage as something worn, sold and remixed.

name: Gurokawa
description: Gurokawa ("grotesque cute" / "creepy cute") is a Harajuku-born Japanese aesthetic of the 2000s–2010s that fuses kawaii fashion grammar — candy pastels, hot pink, ruffles, bows, mascot charms, maximalist accessory stacking — with anatomical horror motifs: glossy eyeballs, fake blood drips, brains, bones, organs, teeth, and cute monsters caught mid-mischief. Recognize it by bright high-key lighting, gaudy all-over prints and charm clusters, and gore rendered as shiny toy-scale props rather than realistic wounds. Typical subjects are street-fashion coords, accessory flat lays, vinyl plush and dolls, nail art, and superflat-influenced chibi illustration.

name: Gustavian
description: Gustavian — Swedish Neoclassicism of Gustav III's reign (c. 1772–1809) — is the pale Nordic translation of Louis XVI France: straight fluted or tapered legs on painted, lightly distressed grey-white furniture, restrained carved ribbons, medallions and laurel wreaths, gilding used as punctuation, and blue-and-white checks or linen stripes beneath crystal chandeliers and gilded mirrors. Interiors are high-key and airy in creamy whites, powdery blues, pale greys, soft yellows and muted greens, composed symmetrically to bounce scarce winter light. Recognize it by painted wood instead of showy grain, classical grammar at domestic scale, and a mood of elegant restraint poised between palace formality and rustic simplicity.

name: Gutter_Punk
description: Gutter Punk is the street-documentary aesthetic of transient punk nomads (crusties, punk-à-chien, perroflauta): tattered, patch-and-stud-covered clothing in black and weathered earth tones, dreadlocks or mohawks, facial tattoos and stretched piercings, and near-constant animal companions — dogs draped over laps, cats perched on shoulders — amid sidewalks, curbs, doorways and squat circles. Snapshot-flash or flat-overcast lighting, oversized backpacks, busking instruments and panhandling cups separate it from stage-bound crust or folk punk. Load this skill when recognizing or generating images of street-squatting punk travelers, buskers with dogs, or DIY anti-fashion squalor.

name: Gyaru
description: Gyaru (gal) is the Japanese street-fashion subculture born in mid-1990s Shibuya, defined less by any single garment than by eye-enlarging makeup (droopy tareme liner, circle lenses, stacked false lashes, aegyo-sal eye-bag highlight), bleached or pink/silver-dyed voluminous curled hair, and maximalist over-accessorizing over animal print, denim, hot pink and black. Recognize it in flash-lit full-body street snaps and magazine-scan layouts: platform or thigh-high boots, fuzzy leg warmers, long deco nails, brand bags, oversized bows, peace-sign group poses, and a loud, confident, unapologetic mood that spans neon ganguro extremes, black-and-pink agejo glamour, and pastel hime sweetness.

name: Gyaruo
description: Gyaruo (ギャル男) is the masculine half of Japan's late-1990s-to-2000s Gyaru street fashion: young men with bleached, teased, high-volume "sujimori" hair, often artificially tanned, wearing tight brand-logo clothing layered with studded belts, wallet chains, stacked bracelets and sunglasses. The palette swings by substyle between black/white/gold and leopard print (Rock, Biker, Onii end), camo earth tones (Military), and sun-bright pastels or club neons (Surfer, American Casual, Sentaa Guy), delivered as Shibuya street snaps, harsh night-flash candids, or saturated Men's Egg magazine spreads with Japanese headline typography. Recognize it by volume-streaked bleached hair, peacocking hand gestures, accessory overload, and early-2000s Japanese snapshot/print media texture.

name: Hacker_Chic
description: Hacker Chic is the 1990s-crystallized aesthetic of computer intrusion and hacker subculture: near-black interiors lit only by phosphor-green or cold-blue terminal screens, monospace code and digital rain, CRT monitors, chunky keyboards, CDs and cables, gloved hands, hooded silhouettes and Guy Fawkes masks. Its signature moves are the screen as sole light source, text-as-texture (terminal logs, ASCII art, nfo headers), and anonymous or obscured figures, carrying an anti-corporate, information-wants-to-be-free mood. Load this skill for images of hacking culture, terminal interfaces, hacker dens, mask portraiture, or clandestine tech noir.

name: Hadeko
description: Hadeko is a mid-to-late 2000s Japanese street fashion from Amerikamura, Osaka, built on saturated primary and full-rainbow palettes: oversized tie-dye shirts, baggy harem pants, rainbow-striped knits, and enormous frizzy "bonzura" wigs crowned with star clips, pom-poms and tiny perched hats. Recognize it in casual street-snap photographs of playful maximalist outfits where rainbow bands, tie-dye swirls and clashing primaries run from the wig halo down to platform shoes, with plastic toys, bead strands and smiley charms as accents. It sits next to Decora and Kidcore but is garment- and wig-driven rather than accessory-count-driven or nostalgia-driven.

name: Hair_Metal
description: Hair metal (glam metal, sleaze rock) is the 1980s Sunset Strip hard-rock look: enormous backcombed, permed and teased hair, androgynous kohl-and-lipstick makeup on male performers, and layered studded leather, fishnet, animal print, denim and chain hardware. Its palette anchors black leather, platinum blond and chrome silver against saturated magenta, violet, scarlet and navy gel-lit backdrops, appearing in studio promo shots, album covers, stage photos and airbrushed illustration. Recognize it by volume-first silhouettes, crucifix-and-bangle jewelry, bandana-and-scarf layering, and a hedonistic "sex, drugs and rock 'n' roll" party-glamour mood.

name: Halbstarke
description: Mid-1950s West German youth-revolt aesthetic: black leather jackets, riveted denim jeans, checked shirts, studded belts, heavy boots and the Elvis-quiff ("Elvistolle"), captured in grainy monochrome press reportage on German street corners, tenement doorways and Vespa scooters. Subjects loiter in gangs, slouch against brick and rubble-era walls, or surge in cinema and concert crowds; the mood is defiant, bored and anti-"Spießigkeit". Recognize it by the greaser-derived uniform placed inside German-speaking urban scenery and a documentary silver-gelatin black-and-white treatment.

name: Halloween
description: Halloween (Spookycore, All-Hallows Eve) is the mass-market holiday aesthetic of the supernatural and the harvest: a black-and-orange core dyad lit by candle glow, string lights, neon tube or blacklight UV, populated by carved jack-o'-lanterns, black cats, bats, spiders, skeletons, sheet ghosts and B-movie monsters. It spans registers from 1920s–60s sepia pin-up greeting cards and candlelit gothic graveyards to UV-fluorescent party rooms, pastel kawaii sweets and novelty skeleton knitwear. Recognition hinges on theatrical spookiness — camp, cute or gothic, but always staged as holiday decor, costume, candy or mascot graphic — rather than genuine terror.

name: Hallyu
description: Hallyu (the Korean Wave) is the visual surface of South Korean pop culture — K-pop idol grooming and stylist-built stage concepts, K-drama romance, and K-fashion's milky pastel lifestyle. Expect ivory/cream bases washed with blush, peach, sakura and lilac; pearl and fine-gold jewelry; perfectly styled, dyed hair with light makeup and a single small earring; fan-culture artifacts like photocard grids, poster walls and idol collages; sheer-curtain daylight and high-key product light, with saturated violet-magenta stage gels as the concept-driven exception. Load this skill for images evoking Korean idol media culture, fandom rooms, Korean beauty coords, or soft romantic Korean lifestyle scenes.

name: Han-Western_Eclectic
description: Han-Western Eclectic (Han-Yang Zhezhong) is a 2010s–2020s Chinese fashion aesthetic that layers vintage Western finery — lace, tulle, poke bonnets, lace parasols, pearl necklaces, Mary Jane shoes — onto preserved Ming-style Hanfu silhouettes: stand-collar jackets with side frog closures, wide sleeves, and pleated horse-face skirts. It reads as high-key pastel (ivory, blush, porcelain blue, sage) in soft, blooming daylight, with a genteel, nostalgic leisure mood set in rose gardens, white colonial facades, and lace-curtained rooms. Recognize it by its double signature: a historically cut Hanfu garment left intact, plus antique European accessories and trim — never modern Western wear.

name: Hands_Up
description: Hands Up (Handz Up!, aka Commercial Trance / Dancecore) is the graphic aesthetic of mid-2000s to early-2010s German and Central European eurodance: near-black canvases lit only by electric blue, neon pink, vibrant green and electric orange light trails, particle bursts and rainbow equalizer bars orbiting silhouetted or desaturated stock-photo dancers and headphone-wearing DJs, crowned by glossy chrome-beveled 3D logotypes. Signature elements include neon swirls wrapping a mid-action figure, shattering-glass energy bursts, oversized headphones, and optional JDM tuner cars; the mood is euphoric, maximalist digital-club optimism of YouTube visualizers and compilation covers. Use when recognizing or generating 2005–2013 eurodance cover, flyer or wallpaper art.

name: Happy_Rock
description: Colorido / Happy Rock is the Brazilian teen pop-rock aesthetic of roughly 2009–2012: androgynous band-and-fan looks built on neon-candy color-blocked skinny jeans, customized graphic tees, glossy vests and puffer jackets, straight fringed hair with dyed streaks, and statement sunglasses or thick-rim glasses. Recognize it by high-key white or sun-saturated promo lighting, one dominant saturated hue per person in a group, vector-sticker and notebook-doodle graphic overlays, and an unmistakable mood of optimistic, friendship-driven fun — a deliberate anti-emo brightness.

name: Harajuku_Fashion
description: Umbrella street-fashion aesthetic of Tokyo's Harajuku district (1970s to present): maximalist, decorative, attention-grabbing coordinates spanning candy-pop magenta, mint, lemon and lavender through to goth and Visual Kei black, often clashed inside a single outfit. Signature elements include Sanrio-type character goods, polka-dot/star/skeleton prints, platform soles, layered socks and leg warmers, vividly dyed twintails, toy-like accessories and handmade headwear, typically captured in flat-daylight street snaps, crowded Takeshita Street scenes, cluttered boutique interiors, or bright solid-backdrop studio portraits.

name: Haunted_Mound
description: Haunted Mound (aka Butcher House Aesthetic, Rural Horrorcore, Sematarycore) is a late-2010s Northern California underground-rap aesthetic that photographs rural American mundanity — dirt roads, ranch houses, graveyards, cabin lofts, gas stations — through a deep-fried, flash-lit, over-sharpened lo-fi lens in burnt orange, blood red, black and forest green. Signature elements include the 2012-drill-derived uniform (baggy True Religion jeans, New Rock platform boots, Affliction-type graphic tees, Realtree camo), chainsaws and box cutters, taxidermy and sheet-ghost props, the "Harold" tree sigil, hooded Nazgul-style cloaks, and Pen & Pixel-style airbrush covers swapping luxury for hearses and skeletons. Load this skill when an image combines corrupted-snapshot degradation and rural occult myth with streetwear flex, rather than urban drill polish or cinematic folk horror.

name: Hauntology
description: Hauntology is the 2000s British "lost futures" aesthetic: decayed artifacts of 1960s–70s welfare-state media — Brutalist concrete, Public Information Film grain, subverted civic posters, VHS tracking lines, xeroxed halftones — in muted olive, institutional mustard and aged-paper cream. Recognize it by faceless or masked figures, empty institutional corridors, folk effigies in overcast fields, and obsolete tape hardware, all treated as memory-decayed archive material carrying melancholy and quiet dread. Where Analog Horror frightens and Vaporwave ironizes, Hauntology mourns a future that never arrived.

name: Health_Goth
description: Health Goth is an early-2010s, net-art-born fashion aesthetic that fuses high-performance technical sportswear (mesh jerseys, compression gear, PVC/latex, technical sneakers) with sterile, rendered futurism in a strict black-white-grey monochrome. Signature elements include brand logos used as pure graphic contrast, angular futuristic typography, transparent and vacuum-sealed packaging, chrome and frosted translucency, clinical white voids and 3D-rendered interiors, and transhumanist props such as prosthetics and body-enhancement tech. The mood is clinical, anti-nostalgic and minimally dystopian — an "exercise in aesthetics," not a lifestyle.

name: Heart_Emoji_Meme
description: Heart Emoji Meme (also called Soft Edits or Wholesome Edits) is a late-2010s Stan Twitter / K-pop fandom editing aesthetic in which candid photos, cartoons, pets and even "cursed" images are buried under maximalist swarms of glossy Apple/Android heart emoji, blush stickers, heart crowns and radial "shaking" motion blur. Its palette is hot pink, red, pastel purple and white with gold sparkle accents, capped by lowercase Arial or Snapchat-bar captions of exaggerated affection. Recognize it by platform emoji glyphs layered as crisp digital stickers over an ordinary snapshot base, vignette/zoom blur, and a soft hazy "precious" glow.

name: Hedi_Boy
description: Hedi Boy is the early-2000s rock-luxury menswear aesthetic built on Hedi Slimane's ultra-skinny silhouette — skin-tight black jeans or razor-narrow tailored trousers, cropped motorcycle leather or minimal tailored jackets, pointed Cuban-heel boots, voluminous mod-cut hair and black Wayfarer sunglasses worn indoors — rendered in a jet-black, charcoal, grey and white monochrome. Its native imagery is campaign and runway photography: seamless grey studio backdrops, high-contrast black-and-white or desaturated cool color, elongated vertical full-body framing, and poses of frontman nonchalance (head-down "underlook", slouched sprawl, mid-stride walk). Revived in the 2020s as "Haute Indie Sleaze", it carries androgyny, self-aware irony and rock 'n' roll romanticism as core values.

name: Heisei_Retro
description: Heisei Retro is a 2020s Japanese nostalgia aesthetic that stacks the consumer pop of 1989–2019 — Tamagotchi, decoden-decorated flip phones, Game Boys, QuickSnap disposable cameras, profile books, Sanrio-type plush, gyaru accessories — into candy-saturated maximalist collages, flat-lays and shop displays. Its palette anchors on hot pink with mint green, lemon yellow and cherry red accents; its signature language is blob katakana typography, sticker and speech-bubble overlays, sparkle bursts, glossy plastic and plush textures, and flash-bright or high-key lighting. Recognize it by dated early-digital tech plus clutter plus candy print language; it differs from Showa Retro (sepia, analog-only) and from generic Kawaii (no era markers).

name: Heistcore
description: Heistcore is the glamour-of-transgression aesthetic of the elaborate theft — vault doors and wall safes, gold-framed oil paintings swung open on hidden hinges, gloved hands cupping loose sapphires, scattered stacks of high-denomination banknotes, paper blueprints and forged IDs. Its palette is dark, deep and metallic (black, brushed steel, gold, cream paper) punctured by saturated jewel tones of ruby, sapphire and emerald, with motifs of catsuits, rubber masks, champagne, fur and museum wealth running from 1920s Egyptomania through mid-century caper cinema to contemporary heist media. Recognize it by the trio of security machinery, anonymous hands or masked faces, and Old Money objects framed as target or loot.

name: Hellenic
