description: Hellenic is the contemporary internet aesthetic of ancient Greece and its mythology — white marble statuary and colonnades, gold laurel wreaths and drachmas, red-figure pottery, pomegranates, grapes and wine, lyres, owls, thunderbolts and other god-attributes, staged with devotional reverence. Its palette spans marble white, beige and silver, ceremonial gold, ceramic black-and-terracotta, Aegean blue and, in its modern romantic register, blush-pink florals; light ranges from hard Mediterranean noon to museum diffuse to candlelit Greek-revival interiors. Recognise it by meander (Greek key) borders, peplos and chiton drapery, contrapposto figures, attribute-based god iconography and mythic still-life altars.

name: Herki
description: Herki (Херки) is the Russian late-1990s/early-2000s teen subculture that compressed goth fashion into a cheap, fandom-driven uniform: black mesh and tulle, pale powdered skin under panda-thick black eyeliner, ankh chokers and the Ville Valo knit beanie, photographed on early digital compacts against Soviet apartment interiors (wall-hung grandmother's carpet, olive-green painted stairwell walls) or overcast cemeteries. Recognize it by black-dominant frames with subdued red/plum accents, harsh direct-flash snapshot lighting, performed adolescent melancholy, and VK/LiveJournal-era photo grammar with handwritten Cyrillic overlays.

name: Heroic_Realism
description: Heroic Realism is the state and wartime propaganda-poster style of the 1910s–1940s (peak 1920s–1930s): idealized, larger-than-life heroes — soldiers, factory workers, farmers, national personifications — painted in realistic lithographic or painterly technique with noble exaggerated anatomy, commanding gestures (pointing index finger, raised fist, uplifted tool or flag), radiating light rays and silhouetted masses behind them. Its palette is limited spot printing on cream paper: flag red, institutional blue, ink black, signal yellow and national colours, paired with bold all-caps condensed typography carrying an imperative message. Recognize it by vertical poster format, matte print texture, moral urgency and monumental scale; subjects range from recruitment and war bonds to labour drives, space race and civic campaigns.

name: Heroin_Chic
description: Heroin Chic is the early-1990s fashion-photography aesthetic of emaciated, androgynous youth — pale clammy skin, sunken dark-ringed eyes, stringy hair, angular collarbones and loose black clothing, shot on grainy black-and-white film in bare studios or run-down interiors with a vacant, apathetic deadpan. Its palette is black, paper white and greyed flesh, with at most a single oxblood-red lip accent; its mood is nihilist detachment, a reaction against glossy 1980s health. Recognize it by monochrome film grain, thin bodies, hollow stares and editorial-or-snapshot framing in the Calvin Klein Obsession register.

name: HexD
description: HexD (also Surge, Hexxed, Hex) is the late-2010s SoundCloud microgenre aesthetic of deliberately degraded Old Web cover art — compressed, pixelated anime girls (succubi, vampires, winged figures) buried under Blingee-era glitter, occult stamps like hexagrams and demonic sigils, 2000s game sprites, and mismatched WordArt text. Its palette is white, pink, purple, black and holographic iridescence, all crushed by JPEG artifacts, GIF banding and dither. Recognize it by the cute-versus-occult clash: sparkle-strewn, low-resolution, melancholic "deep internet" collage that looks like a 2004 web graphic resaved a hundred times.

name: Hexatron
description: Hexatron is the dark, sleek sci-fi aesthetic of mid-2000s-to-early-2020s gaming hardware, game CGI and film interfaces: near-black grounds lit by self-emissive neon blue, hexagonal and faceted angular geometry, holographic terminal-style UIs, and glossy 3D-rendered technology covered in panel-line ornamentation. It inherits Frutiger Aero's gloss and 3D shine but strips out all nature, substituting sharp corners, white-and-gunmetal shells, and red-orange alert accents. Recognize it by hex motifs, particle-ring holograms, product-render robots and consoles, HUD glyph columns on black, and chamfered, greebled machine surfaces.

name: High_School_Dream
description: High School Dream is the nostalgic, media-shaped fantasy of the American high school as portrayed in 1980s-rooted, late-1990s/200s teen film and TV: bright school-spirit primaries (cherry red, royal blue, mustard yellow, hot pink) over cream institutional tile and mint locker enamel, with letterman jackets, pleated skirts, decorated lockers, cheer squads, pep rallies, yellow school buses and diner booths. Images stage teens as ensemble archetypes in idealized school spaces, rendered either as polished cinematic stills or grainy 35mm flash snapshots. Load this skill for stylized school-spirit imagery, teenage ensemble melodrama, or Y2K teen-media nostalgia.

name: Hime_Gyaru
description: Hime Gyaru ("Princess Gal") is a late-2000s Shibuya gyaru substyle of hyper-feminine princess glamour: pastel pink-and-white coordinates of lace, frills, pearls and rose prints, crowned by enormous curled honey-blonde hair (teased sujimori volume, blunt bangs) topped with oversized bows, fabric-rose clusters or tiaras, and a doll-face of circle lenses, heavy false lashes and high pink blush. Recognize it by high-key pastel photography, boutique interiors and Shibuya street-snap settings, decorated flip phones, and head-to-toe coordinated royalty motifs (bows, roses, pearls, rococo prints). Distinguish it from Lolita by its mature, glamorous silhouette and gyaru makeup, and from Agejo by its pastel court palette instead of black-red-gold hostess glamour.

name: Hime_Lolita
description: Hime Lolita is the princess branch of Japanese Lolita fashion: pastel Rococo-revival coordinates built on petticoat-supported bell or sack-back silhouettes, knee-length or longer, layered with copious lace flounces, ruffle tiers, satin bows and rose clusters, and crowned with miniature crowns, large bonnets or rose headdresses trailing lace veils. The palette runs pale pink, ivory, baby blue, mint and pale yellow with metallic gold as the only accent; hair is teased into high-volume curls and finished with pearls, lace gloves and heeled tea boots. Recognize it by opulence that exceeds Sweet Lolita plus regal headwear and 18th-century Robe à la Française gown lines.

name: Himekaji
description: Himekaji ("casual princess") is the 2008–2012 Japanese street style that dresses Hime Gyaru's rococo princess silhouette down into everyday wear: mini-length rose-floral and plaid skirts under cable-knit cardigans, fur-collared capes and ponchos, in dusty pink, ivory, beige and brown. Signature elements are lace trim, tiered ruffles, waist bows, Peter Pan collars, opaque tights with bow-trimmed Mary Janes or knee boots, and gyaru-descended dolly makeup (circle lenses, intense round pink blush, pink gloss) over long wavy hair. Typical images are head-to-toe coord snapshots, magazine catalog lineups and scans, mirror selfies, dress-form coord displays, and blush close-up portraits in soft high-key or muted film light.

name: Hip-Hop
description: Hip-Hop is the visual culture of the Bronx-born four-element movement (DJing, MCing, breaking, graffiti): concrete plazas and block-party streets, wildstyle murals in spray-can saturation, cut-out album-cover collages with chrome or gold gradient display type, flame motifs, iced-out chains and baggy brand-logo streetwear. Its palette swings deliberately between documentary concrete gray, spray-can magenta/cyan/lime, gold-on-black bling, and airbrushed pastel dreamscapes, unified by halftone print grain, on-camera flash or theatrical spotlight, and a boastful, communal energy. Recognize it by graffiti lettering on public walls, turntables and corded mics, freeze-pose dancers, crew group shots, cash-and-car props, and sticker-grade cover graphics like Parental Advisory blocks.

name: Hipness_Purgatory
description: Hipness Purgatory ("Twee Hipsterdom") is the hand-drawn visual language of 2000s–early-2010s hipster and twee culture: scratchy, thin pencil-and-ink linework on printer-white or notebook-cream paper, naive childlike figures, everyday objects, hand-lettered captions and scrapbook/collage materiality, splitting into a sparse deadpan register and a maximalist candy-psychedelic doodle register in black, white, blue, yellow, green, orange and hot magenta. Recognize it by wobbly amateur-confident line, visible paper grain and fold creases, flat marker color that misses its outlines, and an ironic handwritten voice; the whole thing reads as millennial optimism done DIY and deliberately anti-polish.

name: Hippie
description: Visual culture of the mid-1960s–early-1970s American counterculture (San Francisco Haight-Ashbury, Woodstock), recognizable by its twin palette of earthy brown, olive, mustard and rust alongside saturated psychedelic rainbow tie-dye and paisley. Signature elements include peace signs, flowers worn in the hair, bell-bottoms, fringed suede, headbands and bandanas, stacked handmade beads, and long unstyled hair on all genders. Typical subjects are festival crowds in meadows, outdoor meditation, flower-carrying protest marches, and communal groups in layered handmade clothing, captured in candid available light with film grain or golden-hour backlight.

name: Hippie_Goth
description: Hippie Goth (Boho Goth, Bohemian Goth, Gypsy Goth) is a 1980s fusion of Goth and Hippie dress: a black-or-brown spine layered under flowing bell sleeves, tiered maxi skirts, sheer chiffon shawls, lace, crochet and fringe in jewel and earth tones of plum, burgundy, forest green and rust. Signature signifiers are celestial and occult hardware (sunburst chain belts, cross and pentacle pendants, tarot, crystals), wide-brim or top hats with teashades, platform boots, and botanical, paisley or tie-dye prints, worn by mystic, free-spirited figures on stages, city stoops and forest paths in faded analog light. Recognize it by layered drape-in-motion, dark romanticism softened by folk craft, and grainy 70s–90s film warmth.

name: Hipster
description: Hipster is the analog-nostalgic, anti-corporate subculture aesthetic of gentrified city neighborhoods and Pacific Northwest woods, rooted in the 1940s and peaking 2009–2014. Its visual DNA is lo-fi film photography (grain, lifted blacks, washed filters), vinyl records and film cameras, fixie bikes, thrifted flannel, suspenders, round glasses and full beards, quirky storefront signage, and distressed stamp-style typography on paper. Palette swings between nature-based earth tones, deliberately dissonant "unstylish" clashes, and gothic/artist black-on-off-white minimalism.

name: Hollywood_Regency
description: Hollywood Regency (Regency Moderne) is the interior, architectural and landscape style of Southern California movie-star homes from the 1920s–1950s: jewel-tone lacquer, silk and velvet against black-and-white checkerboard floors, gilt or silver sunburst mirrors, palms, Greek keys, and zebra/leopard animal-print accents over chrome, mirrored glass and crystal chandeliers. Rooms are staged like film sets — symmetrical, glossy, saturated — with slim-profile furniture, lacquered walls, and glamorous figures in satin. Use when recognizing or generating opulent, theatrical interiors, star-house exteriors with mansard roofs and Doric columns, or cocktail-hour glamour vignettes.

name: Hopecore
description: Hopecore is a 2020s TikTok/Instagram editing aesthetic of radical optimism: low-resolution found-footage nature, animals and tender candid moments washed in lens flares, white bloom and sparkle filters, overlaid with short second-person affirmations in basic serif or sans-serif type. Recognize it by sunlit meadows and tree canopies, blown-out "divine" glow, grainy video-still softness, and gentle caption text addressing the viewer; it descends from Corecore as its anti-doomscrolling inversion.

name: Horror
description: A dread-first aesthetic running from folklore-derived Gothic to modern slasher, survival-game and mascot horror, unified by high-contrast darkness, blood red and drained sickly palettes, and the uncanny corruption of familiar forms. Signature elements include masked or monstrous figures half-swallowed by shadow, corrupted children's mascots and dolls, grime and decay, rationed single-source lighting, and faces fixed past normal into grin or grief. Subjects range from ghosts, slashers and cosmic entities to wrong-feeling domestic rooms, always played straight to trigger fight-or-flight rather than playful spookiness.

name: Horror_Punk
description: Horror punk ("fiendcore") is the visual language of the late-1970s/early-1980s US punk subculture that wears classic-monster iconography as identity: black leather and studs over corpse-paint white faces, devilock fringes and deathhawk mohawks, grinning Crimson Ghost-style skulls, tombstones, bats and campy comic-book gore. Its palette is black-grounded with blood red, deep purple, sickly pale white and creature green, deployed across band cluster portraits, emblem-dense poster art, painted jacket backs and gel-lit stage shots. Recognize it by the mix of punk hardware (studs, patches, bullet belts, band tees) with Universal Monsters and 1950s B-movie schlock treated with irony and affection rather than dread.

name: Hot_Cheeto_Girl
description: Late-2010s TikTok meme aesthetic caricaturing a hyper-feminine, working-class high-school girl: Flamin' Hot Cheetos or Takis packaging used as prop, wardrobe and backdrop, in a loud palette of brand red-orange, logo yellow, black and gold. Signature signals are huge gold hoop earrings, extra-long acrylic nails, dramatic false lashes, overlined glossy lips, butterfly clips, and flash-lit selfie or sticker-collage framing with a defiant, mid-chew attitude. Recognize it by snack-bag graphics plus deliberate "too much" loudness in mundane school, home or brand-saturated settings.

name: Hot_Rod
description: American automotive subculture aesthetic from 1930s Southern California dry lakes: stripped pre-1949 Fords with chopped roofs, exposed chrome V8 engines, deep gloss lacquer in red, black and yellow, hand-painted flames and pinstriping. Recognize by fenderless upright grilles, fat rear tires, dry-lake/drag-strip/garage settings, companion pin-up and greaser fashion, and black-cream-red screen-print garage posters. Mood: speed, wrench-turned craftsmanship, mid-century Americana anti-conformity.

name: Huang-mao
description: Huang-mao ("yellow hair") is the Chinese-speaking world's visual stereotype of the young street layabout: cheaply bleached brassy-blond hair in a mullet, buzz cut or bowl cut, loud floral or abstract-print shirts, skinny tees, muscle shirts, denim or leather jackets, thin gold chains, tattoos and a cigarette. Born in 1980s–90s Hong Kong triad films and copied by marginalized mainland Chinese youth of the 1990s–2000s, it pits warm brassy hair and gold against cool teal night-market gloom, fluorescent grey and concrete, framed like a realist crime-drama still or poster. Recognize it by loitering groups, confrontational gestures, night food stalls and an unpolished, mixed-color-temperature screen realism.

name: Hygge
description: Hygge is the Danish aesthetic of cozy contentment — candle and firelight glow, chunky knit wool, Fair Isle socks, ceramic mugs of tea, and intimate first-person views of laps, hearths and window nooks. Its palette runs from flame amber and oat cream to deep hearth brown, with only sparse cool accents (cobalt glaze, denim, grass green); its subjects are small pleasures staged in a hyggekrog corner or beside a fireplace, usually with partial human presence rather than faces. Recognize it by warm low light sources, lived-in textile texture and sheltered intimacy; though strongest in autumn and winter, it is a year-round mood that also admits gardens, grass and soft summer daylight.

name: Hypebeast
description: Youth streetwear status culture of the mid-2000s through late 2010s, built on limited-edition sneakers, box logos and oversized back prints from drop-culture brands (Supreme, Off-White, BAPE, Palace, Yeezy). Visually: black/white/grey base outfits punctured by scarlet, safety orange or volt accents and loud prints (camo, plaid, diagonal hazard stripes), documented in flat-light urban fit pics, sneaker still lifes and drop-day queues. Recognize it by logo legibility, grail footwear as the focal point, and the resale-tag scarcity narrative.

name: Hyperborean
description: Hyperborean is a 2020s TikTok/4chan edit aesthetic built from chaotic, deliberately degraded VHS-glitch collage: idealized "ancient European" source plates (Greco-Roman statue busts, snowy mythic fantasy painting, crusaders, Nordic warriors) stacked with esoteric sun-wheel emblems, conspiracy charts, anime figures and shitpost meme faces (Trollge, Wojak), capped by pixel-font slogan banners. Recognize it by conflicting source palettes unified under tape damage — chromatic-aberration fringes, scanlines, macroblocking, mirrored kaleidoscopic borders — and by its solemn-vs-absurd juxtaposition. Documented here for recognition and critical analysis; its hate-symbol and slogan layer is detection-only and must never be reproduced in generation.

name: Icepunk
description: Icepunk (Coldrave) is an early-2010s internet microgenre aesthetic of frozen monochrome — deep cobalt and pale ice blues, whiteout snow, frost crystals, light glowing inside ice, mist and desolate winter landscapes, all mediated through dithered early-CGI, Y2K chrome type and glitched Unicode snow-glyphs. Born in 2011 as a self-declared meme reaction against seapunk, it pairs numb blizzard isolation with ironic mixtape-cover grandeur: snow-laden towers and castle spires, low-poly frozen figures, literal "ice" gems, cyan glow on black voids. Recognize it by a cold-only palette, crystalline or crushed-digital texture, and a mood of desolate, numb, half-joking cold.

name: Imparsthetic
description: Imparsthetic (Scamarticlecore) is a 2020s TikTok-born subgenre of Weirdcore that recycles the look of 2000s–early-2010s web scam articles: surreal digital collages and manipulated "found" photos whose bodies, fruits and gadgets carry extra or wrong parts (supernumerary eyes, USB tongues, meat-filled denim), annotated with bold marketing text, arrows, circles and speech bubbles. Its palette swings between sterile stock-photo white pierced by saturated organic accents (raw-meat red, apple green, pill-mosaic multicolor) and harsh-flash amateur snapshot color, all at low-fi JPEG fidelity. The mood is disgusted curiosity with the fourth wall intact — the image is a discovered curiosity or false advertisement, never a message addressed to the viewer.

name: Impressionism
description: Impressionism is the Paris-born painting movement of the 1870s–1880s (Monet, Renoir, Degas, Pissarro, Morisot, Sisley, Cassatt) that records the fleeting effect of daylight on modern life. Recognize it by small, thin, visibly broken brushstrokes of unmixed color, open and cropped compositions, violet-blue shadows instead of black, and a matte, unvarnished surface that reads as a rapid "impression." Subjects range from rivers, harbors, gardens and tree-lined paths to cafés, boulevards, boating parties, dancers and domestic intimacy — always ordinary modern life caught in a single consistent light.

name: Incelcore
description: Incelcore (aka E-punk, bedroom punk, losercore) is a late-2010s post-Internet aesthetic born on 4chan's /r9k/ and /mu/, recognizable by dithered black-and-white or low-bitrate snapshot imagery, crude MS Paint wojak/soyjak drawings, cluttered NEET bedrooms with CRT monitors, energy-drink cans and cigarettes, and collage cover art mixing red blackletter type, chrome Y2K lettering and clipart. Its signature is deliberate amateurism — flash-lit webcam photos, JPEG artifacts, rough magic-wand cutouts — paired with retro gaming hardware, provocative slogan clothing and deadpan ironic provocation. Load this skill when imagery reads as terminally-online DIY album art or room documentation rather than any designed or photographic tradition.

name: Incroyables_and_Merveilleuses
description: Parisian Directoire-period (1795–1799) fashion-subculture aesthetic: women in sheer, high-waisted white muslin column gowns with ribbon-tied sandals, reticules and cashmere shawls; men in very short coats with oversized collars, chin-swallowing cravats, tight pale breeches and knotted club canes. Palette of ivory and powder pastels anchored by black hats and umber grounds, with slate blue, nankin buff and coral red as the only saturated notes; rendered in hand-coloured fashion plates, smooth neoclassical oils and flat naive panel portraits. Mood is theatrical, ironic extravagance — elegance pushed deliberately past good taste as an anti-Jacobin political joke.

name: Indie
description: Indie (vintage indie / indie grunge) is the muted, analog aesthetic of 1980s–90s British independent music culture: grainy monochrome or duotone-tinted film photographs, faded pale neutrals with desaturated blue, red and green, and record-sleeve or fanzine graphics set over ordinary working-class subjects in thrifted anoraks, cardigans, striped t-shirts and jeans. Its signature motifs are records and CDs, books and poetry, Polaroids and melancholy overlaid text, all carried in a moody, unassuming, nostalgic atmosphere that deliberately rejects mainstream gloss. Use when recognizing or generating images of analog, anti-glamour alternative music culture in the post-punk indiepop lineage.

name: Indie_Kid
description: Indie Kid (New Indie / TikTok Indie) is the 2020 TikTok aesthetic of grainy, oversaturated smartphone snapshots showing thrifted early-2000s fashion — crop tops with baggy jeans, sweater vests, tartan tennis skirts, bucket hats, polymer clay fruit earrings, butterfly claw clips — in skateparks, convenience stores, grassy parks and sticker-covered bedrooms. Its palette clashes neon lime, cobalt, tangerine, hot pink and lilac over natural denim, wood and grass backdrops, edited with heavy saturation, lifted or punched contrast, visible grain and optional fisheye distortion. Recognize it by candid friend groups, POV sneaker shots, smiley and rainbow motifs, blush-heavy makeup, and an ironic coming-of-age, main-character mood.

name: Indie_Sleaze
description: Indie Sleaze is the flash-blitzed party-documentary aesthetic of mid-2000s to early-2010s nightlife in New York, London and Los Angeles: grainy compact-camera snapshots with harsh on-camera flash, red-eye, hard wall shadows and blacked-out backgrounds. Signature elements are smudged eyeliner, messy bleached or greasy hair, ripped and striped tights, band tees, American Apparel basics, thrifted fur and metallic statement pieces, neon pink/green and silver pops against black, and a cigarette in hand. Typical subjects are candid crowds, couch pile-ups, It-girls and dance-punk performers mid-party — always people, never polished, never staged-clean.

name: Indiecraft
description: Indiecraft is the mid-2000s handmade-media aesthetic of maquettes, puppets, felt and construction-paper collage staged like tiny theatre sets and shot in soft warm light or faded vintage film casts. Signature elements include cardboard architecture, stitched felt creatures, cut-paper geometry, everyday objects given dot-and-smile faces, and scale play between human bodies and oversized craft props, all in a palette running from cardboard brown and cream to construction-paper mustard, tomato, teal and magenta. Recognize it by texture first: if the world in frame looks built by hand from paper, yarn, felt or clay — seams, tape and wobble included — it is Indiecraft.

name: Indigenous_Futurisms
description: Indigenous Futurisms is a plural, present-tense speculative aesthetic (term coined by Grace Dillon, practice rooted in 1990s–2000s Indigenous digital art and ongoing) that folds regalia, beadwork, ribbonwork, hide and feather material culture into science-fiction frames: starfields, ruined-and-regrown cities, desert horizons, low-poly machinima and photo-composite cosmos. Palette deliberately varies by culture but clusters around hide ochre and tan, turquoise and ribbon-satin reds, cosmic indigo-black with star white, and saturated pop accents; signature elements include processional rows of regalia figures, celestial bodies overhead, critical pop-culture remix (Star Wars iconography repainted in Indigenous material culture), and beadwork treated as technology. Mood is sovereign, resilient and often wry — presence in the future, never nostalgia for the past.

name: Industrial
description: Visual language of the industrial music subculture, from mid-1970s UK (Throbbing Gristle, Industrial Records) through 1980s EBM and rivethead culture: monochrome xerox-grain photography, brutalist and constructivist stencil graphics in black, concrete grey, bone white and stark signal red, raw metal, concrete, chain-link, military surplus and fetish gear, obsolete machinery and dystopian decay. Recognized by high-contrast duotone, distressed screenprint, authoritarian-propaganda layout grammar used subversively, deadpan uniformed group portraits, and harsh beam-and-haze stage light. Cold, confrontational, mechanized mood; shock deployed as social critique.

name: Industrial_Decay
description: Industrial Decay (also Urban Decay) is the photographic aesthetic of abandoned post-industrial structures — factory halls, metro stations, silos, gantry cranes, bridges, beached ships — rendered in muted grays, earth browns and rust reds. Its signature elements are flaking rust and corrosion, crumbling concrete, broken glazing, peeling paint, intruding moss and vines, and debris heaps, lit by diffuse daylight through failed roofs and windows. Born from late-20th-century urban exploration photography of deindustrialized cities, it locates beauty in material deterioration itself and carries a somber, contemplative, nostalgic mood.

name: Industrial_Gothic
description: Industrial Gothic is the machine-dread aesthetic of the late 1970s through late 1990s: monochrome, sepia and gunmetal imagery of exposed wires, pipes, bolts and gears, peeling paint and rust, lit by a single harsh spotlight or a cold cathode glow, with muted oxide red or deep blue as the only accents. Its subjects are strange, overwhelming machines, distressed monochrome human faces, flesh-machine fusions, and cavernous black-painted club and retail interiors, carried chiefly by metal and industrial album art, graphic design and video-game environments. Recognize it by the combination of decay texture, theatrical low-key lighting and nihilistic mood rather than by any one object.

name: Ink-wash_Feng
description: Ink-wash Feng (Shuimo Feng) is the modern Chinese design aesthetic descended from Tang-dynasty literati ink painting and the Shanghai Animation Film Studio's ink-wash animation: a monochrome black-white-gray spine built on five-tone ink gradation, dominant negative space (liubai), wet-bleeding xieyi brushwork, and small muted mineral accents of cinnabar, ochre or indigo. Typical subjects are misty mountains and rivers, bamboo and rocks, flowers and birds, floating clouds, tiny temples and boats, vertical calligraphy lines with red seals, and figures in sheer gradient hanfu or trailing ink-ribbon drapery. Recognize it by void-heavy asymmetric composition, diffuse mist-modulated light, and brushed, bleeding edges instead of hard outlines — whether on paper, packaging, fabric, or digital game key art.

name: International_Typographic_Style
description: Swiss / International Typographic Style graphic design of the 1930s–1960s: asymmetric poster and identity work built on invisible mathematical grids, neutral grotesque typefaces (Helvetica, Univers, Akzidenz-Grotesk) deployed at monumental and minute scales, flat limited-palette ink fields on paper white or black, objective black-and-white photography and geometric pictograms. Recognize it by flush-left ragged-right text blocks, tiny functional metadata (dates, places, credits), letterforms cropped by the trim, repeated modular geometry, and overprint transparency effects. The mood is clean, anonymous, objective clarity — design as public information, not decoration.

name: Internet_Awesomesauce
description: Late-2000s-to-mid-2010s Tumblr/YouTube/DeviantArt aesthetic of ironically "epic" random humor: galaxy starfields used as canvas, full-spectrum rainbow gradients, photo-collage cats, unicorns and dogs augmented with laser eyes, junk food raised to mock-heroic status, pixel sprites and chrome airbrush lettering. Recognition hinges on saturated maximalist collage, deliberate scale and lighting mismatches, and meme-era quotation (Nyan Cat, Shooting Stars, Doge, rage faces) treated with faux-grandeur.

name: Ishoku_Hada
description: Ishoku Hada (異色肌) is a Harajuku-born Japanese fashion and avant-garde makeup subculture of the mid-2010s in which the skin is painted an opaque, oversaturated fantasy hue — candy pink, cyan, violet, lime, tangerine — to build an anime- or alien-inspired persona. Signature elements include clashing maximalist prints (leopard, stripes, polka dots, checks), cartoon-fantasy headwear (antennae, horns, cross clips, heart-shaped sunglasses), weird-cute plushies, fuzzy leg warmers, fishnets and manba-derived sticker makeup, captured in flash-lit, cluttered snapshot portraits. Typical subjects are solo or small-group portraits of painted-face youth in clubwear posing playfully at the camera.

name: Ita
description: Ita (itasha, itabag) is a 2000s Japanese otaku aesthetic of skinning vehicles, bags and cases in full-surface anime, manga and videogame character art, maximalist Japanese text and attached merchandise. Its visual DNA is the decorated object itself — a vinyl-wrapped car, train, truck or helicopter, a badge-stuffed bag — rendered in saturated, franchise-keyed color and photographed proudly at meets, conventions or neon-lit streets. Recognize it by fandom decoration applied to a physical surface, never by generic anime imagery alone.

name: Italo_Disco
description: Italo Disco is the sleeve-and-stage aesthetic of late-1970s to 1980s Italian synthesizer dance music: soft hand-airbrushed illustration in pastel-to-neon gradients (magenta, teal, cobalt, lemon), glamorous melancholic figures in sharp 1980s fashion, and sincere sci-fi camp — laser grids, robots, chrome, palm trees, cosmic backdrops. Recognize it by airbrushed skin and skies with no hard edges, diagonal color-block or script typography, halftone and graph-paper patterns, and a mood of romantic escapism; it is distinct from American disco's gold-glitter photographic realism and from synthwave's hard digital neon.

name: Japandi
description: Japandi is a minimalist interior and object aesthetic of the late 2010s that fuses Japanese wabi-sabi with Scandinavian hygge: warm neutral palettes (off-white, greige, oat, mid-brown), pale oak and bamboo, linen and bouclé textiles, matte imperfect ceramics, washi paper lanterns, and sculptural branches arranged sparsely and asymmetrically. Recognize it by low unadorned wood furniture, lime-plaster walls, diffused daylight, generous negative space, and few but deliberate objects; typical subjects are serene rooms, tablescapes, and craft-object still lifes.

name: Japanese_Ivy_Style
description: Japanese Ivy Style (Ametora) is Japan's reverent, detail-obsessed reproduction of 1960s American collegiate dress — button-down oxford shirts with a precise collar roll, natural-shoulder navy blazers, creased khaki chinos, penny loafers over white socks, tipped cricket vests and cardigans, with madras plaid and seersucker stripes as controlled pattern bursts on a navy/khaki/white/grey ground. Recognize it in mid-century silhouettes shot as didactic magazine pages (halftone grain, Japanese text columns, English display type), grainy campus or street snapshots, or muted modern lookbooks with thick-rimmed glasses and studied-leisure props like books, records, flutes and tennis rackets.

name: Japonisme
description: Japonisme is the late-19th-century European and American assimilation of Japanese art — ukiyo-e flatness, asymmetry, contour and pattern — into Western painting, posters, printmaking and the decorative arts. Recognize it by flat planes of indigo, vermilion, olive and chrome yellow laid against cream paper or gold grounds; cropped, off-center compositions with high or absent horizons; women in kimonos with fans, parasols and folding screens; rain streaks, clawed waves, plum blossom, chrysanthemums and calligraphic cartouches. It sits between ukiyo-e (its Japanese source), Aestheticism (its tonal cousin), Impressionism (its borrower) and Art Nouveau (its descendant).

name: Jejemon
description: Jejemon is the Filipino youth internet aesthetic of the late 2000s–early 2010s: lo-fi webcam and phone-camera selfies of teens in flat-brim caps (often rainbow-striped), scene side-swept bangs, basketball jerseys, flannel and skinny jeans, wrapped in Blingee-era glitter borders, mirror-duplicate collages and rainbow WordArt captions written in leetspeak "Jejenese" (JeJeM0N pOh!!, iM1SsYuUh). Candy-bright magenta, purple, cyan and yellow sit over flash-blown bedroom interiors, stairwells and schoolyards, with crew group poses, peace signs, duckfaces and silicone wristbands. Recognize it by Taglish leetspeak text overlays, DIY sparkle/lens-flare editing, Nokia-era SMS screenshots and proudly cheap, exuberant DIY styling.

name: Jersey_Maid
description: Jersey Maid (ジャージメイド, "Tracksuit Maid") is a Japanese hybrid fashion aesthetic (2008–present) that fuses oversized athletic tracksuits with maid costume grammar — a frilly apron and lace headwear worn over a zip-up track jacket or jersey dress with sporty sleeve stripes, finished with slouchy leg warmers and chunky platform sneakers. Recognize it by its pastel blue / lavender / pink or strict black-and-white palette with occasional cyber-neon accents, its matte polyester-knit-versus-crisp-lace texture clash, and its mirror-selfie, studio-look and neon-lit street framing.

name: Jiangnan_Water_Town
description: Regional waterside aesthetic of China's Taihu Lake basin: canals functioning as streets, Suzhou-style houses with white plaster walls and black tile roofs, small stone arch bridges, and wupeng black-awning boats under misty drizzle. Palette of ink black, weathered plaster white and jade-teal water, lit by diffuse overcast or soft dusk light, with wet bluestone and mirror-calm reflections. Recognize by the water-network town fabric — upturned eaves, lattice flower windows, willows, oil-paper umbrellas, lantern-strung eaves — and a serene, poetic, slow-life mood.

name: Jiangshi_fiction
description: Jiangshi fiction is the horror-comedy folk-fantasy look of 1980s–90s Hong Kong cinema: hopping reanimated corpses in black Qing-dynasty mandarin official robes, pale green-tinged skin, arms locked outstretched, sealed by yellow cinnabar-script Taoist fulu talismans, opposed by Taoist priests with peachwood swords, glutinous rice and eight-trigram mirrors. Its palette is cold night teal, fog grey and corpse-pale green punctured by talisman yellow and cinnabar red, staged in dim ancestral halls, mortuary rooms and misty walled courtyards. Recognize it by the rigid hop posture, the Qing official hat and rank-badge robe, and the exorcism prop kit; separate it from wuxia by its undead stiffness and funerary folk-horror tone.

name: Jiggy_Era
description: Late-1990s hip-hop and R&B aesthetic (1997–99, aka the Shiny Suit Era) built on oversized metallic vinyl and patent-leather suits, fisheye-lens music-video cinematography, chrome-and-black "cheese grater" sets, saturated single-colour lighting, and "Ghetto Fabulous" luxury props — champagne, speedboats, casino neon, platinum chains. Palette anchors are neon green, royal blue, silver chrome and black, extended by candy-red, violet and steel-teal vinyls; mood is celebratory, escapist, millennial-optimist. Recognize by glossy reflective tailoring, ultra-wide lens distortion, illuminated industrial tunnels, small tinted shades and chrome script logos.

name: Jirai_Kei
description: Jirai Kei ("landmine type") is a 2020s Kabukichō, Tokyo subculture aesthetic that pairs ultra-feminine coordinates in a strictly limited black–white–muted-pink palette — ruffles, Peter Pan collars, satin ribbons, lace, heart-shaped hardware — with a dark undercurrent of color-matched energy drink cans, pills, syringes, box cutters, Kuromi/My Melody plushies and night neon street scenes. Images are heavily processed: hazy pale-pink high-key filters or harsh flash under red-magenta signage, anime-proportioned eye editing, twin tails with hime-cut bangs, tear-bag "pien" makeup, and emoji/sticker/speech-bubble overlays. Recognize it by the two-color outfit discipline, the cute-versus-menacing prop juxtaposition, and the eerie puppy-eyed sadness beneath the sweetness.

name: Jologs
description: Philippine working-class youth aesthetic of the late 1990s to late 2000s, split between a masculine pole of baggy streetwear — oversized basketball jerseys, checkered polos, bandanas, headcaps, sunglasses, wide-leg denim pooling over chunky sneakers — and a feminine pole of Jolina-pop maximalism: floral prints, platform wedge sandals, plastic beads, star clips and pastel teen-magazine collages. Anchored in dark masa colors (denim indigo, maroon, brown, gray, black) that collide with loud pink-lilac-lime pop overload, and delivered through period media: on-camera-flash digicam snapshots, faded film scans, halftone magazine pages and friendster/hi5-era glitter graphics. Reads as loud, tacky, proudly unrefined rebellion.

name: Juggalo
description: Fan-subculture aesthetic of the Insane Clown Posse fandom (Detroit, mid-1990s onward): hand-applied black-and-white evil-clown face paint over casual hip-hop and skater merch, Hatchetman logos, Faygo soda bottles, and Dark Carnival horror-circus iconography, captured in lo-fi snapshot flash, dim club light, or overcast festival daylight. Recognize it by matte white greasepaint faces with black hatchet brows and blacked-out grins, candid groups of painted "family" at festivals, tailgates and club shows, and a confrontational yet warm working-class mood.

name: Juminocore
description: Juminocore is a 2020s Western-coined internet aesthetic (TikTok/Pinterest, circa 2024) built on the curated clutter of Heisei-era Japanese kawaii trinkets — gachapon capsule toys, Sanrio and Rilakkuma character goods, sticker-plastered Nintendo DS clamshells and dangling acrylic phone charms. Its palette is muted sage green, cream white, silver and powder blue with small strawberry-red and peach accents, photographed in bright, soft, high-key daylight as flat lays, packed shelves, charm-laden bags and decorated handheld tech. Recognize it by maximalist but color-coordinated small-object density, glossy plastic and plush textures, and optional hand-drawn star doodles or scrapbook overlays on pastel surfaces.

name: Junkpunk
description: Junkpunk (Salvagepunk, Scavenged Punk, Scrappunk) is a 2010s salvage aesthetic in which weapons, clothing, machines and whole settlements are built from repurposed trash — rusted scrap, lashed cordage, bullet-casing necklaces, corrugated shantytown walls — each object legibly employed for something other than its original purpose. Its palette is bronze, brown, tan and black stretched toward ochre, oxide green and signal red; its motifs are broken machines, e-waste piles, barricades, layered scavenger fashion and Dada-descended collage, lit by bleached desert sun, single-bulb alley light or neutral studio documentation. Recognize it by visible joinery and rebuilding: welds, zip ties, twine lashings and lived-in clutter signal optimism-in-ruin rather than despair.

name: Kandi_Raver
description: Kandi Raver (Kandi Kid) is the handmade-bead jewelry subculture of the American rave scene, early 1990s to present: forearms stacked wrist-to-elbow in pony-bead bracelets, multi-strand cuffs and perler-bead pixel panels in clashing neon rainbow, exchanged through the PLUR handshake at clubs, blacklight parties and daytime festivals. Recognize it by glossy plastic bead maximalism worn on arms and hands, snapshot flash or UV lighting, dyed hair, fishnets and fuzzy leg warmers, and poses of trading, hugging and peace signs.

name: Karasu_Zoku
description: Karasu Zoku ("crow tribe," later called Mode fashion) is the 1980s Japanese all-black avant-garde style born from Yohji Yamamoto and Rei Kawakubo's 1982 Paris "black impact": head-to-toe matte black in heavy, asymmetrical, ankle-length layers of wrinkled cloth — deep V-necks, collared capes, saggy skirts, slashed sleeves, heavy pants — on androgynous figures with choppy black hair. Recognize it by monochrome black differentiated only by texture and value, flat diffuse light, and grey studio or Tokyo street settings, with zero accent colour, zero jewellery, zero occult iconography. Typical subjects are full-length standing or walking figures, runway models, and small flocks of black-clad pedestrians.

name: Kawaii
description: Kawaii is the Japanese aesthetic of childlike cuteness that crystallized in 1970s Japan around Sanrio/San-X character culture: pastel palettes anchored by white with pink as the default lead, rounded chibi forms with oversized eyes and blush cheeks, anthropomorphic animal mascots, strawberries, decorated sweets, plush toys, lace-and-ribbon trinkets, all under bright, shadowless light. Recognize it by flat candy color, sticker-and-sparkle decoration, rounded girlish typography or Japanese text, and a mood of innocent, fluttering delight; it spans illustration, product design, fashion, food and interiors while refusing shadow, sharpness and adult gravity.

name: Kawaii_Gamer
description: Kawaii Gamer is the late-2010s Western streamer-room aesthetic in which gaming hardware is rebuilt in cuteness: pastel pink, purple and blue PCs, keyboards, controllers and cat-ear headphones, bunny-eared gaming chairs and cat-paw pillows, buried under maximalist Sanrio, Pokémon and anime plush, figurines and Japanese snack clutter lit by neon signs and LED wash. Recognize it by pastel-dominant color on white structural bases, kawaii anime fan-art wallpapers glowing on monitors, and TikTok setup-tour framing; the subject is always the marriage of gaming technology with kawaii merchandise.

name: Key_West_Kitten
description: Key West Kitten is a late-2010s Tumblr/Pinterest aesthetic of romanticized, hyperfeminine Florida Keys beach life, rendered in a washed-out pastel triad of teal, pink and pale yellow with a hazy, dreamlike faded-filter surface. Signature elements are palm trees, roadside beachside motels and diners with script signage, heart-shaped sunglasses, ice cream and milkshakes, pink dolphins, flamingos, seashells, pools and floaties, and vintage swimwear, all drawn from Lizzy Grant-era Lana Del Rey nostalgia. Recognize it by its faded-2000s-snapshot texture, vernacular roadside Americana preferred over luxury, and coquette softness with a wistful, childhood-memory melt.

name: Kidcore
description: Kidcore (also "Kidult") is a late-2010s internet aesthetic of 1990s–early-2000s childhood nostalgia: saturated primary colors and rainbow stripes, glossy plastic toys, stickers, pony beads and cartoon graphics assembled with a more-is-more abundance. Typical subjects are toy and bead heaps, ball pits and play rugs, stickered faces and decorated sneakers, striped knitwear and overalls, sprinkle-laden sweets, and playful children's-store interiors, all rendered in bright high-key or casual flash light. Recognize it by primaries-on-white loudness, toylike plastic shine and franchise-era motifs — never muted, never moody, never minimalist.

name: Kinderwhore
description: Kinderwhore is an early-1990s US punk-grunge fashion aesthetic built on childlike babydoll and Peter Pan-collar dresses in nursery pink, ivory and baby blue, deliberately ruined with ripped fishnets, combat boots, smeared red lipstick and raccoon eyeliner. Its signature read is innocence-versus-ruin: thrift-torn satin and lace, messy bleached hair clipped with barrettes, caught in harsh flash snapshots or grainy black-and-white gig film with an ironic, confrontational deadpan. Load this skill when images pair doll-like feminine costume with punk distress, smeared glamour and amateur lo-fi photography.

name: Kingcore
description: Kingcore is the martial, mature branch of Royalcore — regal authority rendered in black-dominant chiaroscuro lit by antique gold, with deep crimson, royal blue and imperial purple as the only saturated hues allowed. Signature elements are pointed crowns, steel swords gripped or raised, chessboards, heraldry, fur-trimmed military coats with bullion embroidery, lions and black horses, oil-paint tableaus and flame-lit still lifes. Typical subjects are monarchs, commanders and the instruments of rule, composed with patience, confidence and menace held in check.

name: Kissaten
description: Kissaten is the aesthetic of the mid-20th-century Japanese coffeehouse: dim amber light through Tiffany stained glass, ornately carved dark wood, forest-green or scarlet velvet booths, shelves of mismatched porcelain cups, siphon brewers and copper kettles, and pudding, parfait or cream-soda floats crowned with a cherry. Recognition hinges on the Showa-era Japanese graphic layer — kanji and katakana signage, oval enamel signs with floral wreath borders, hand-lettered storefronts — set against a palette of brown, forest green, scarlet, amber and cream with small saturated soda-float accents. The mood is hushed, nostalgic and frozen in time, never bright or kitschy-loud.

name: Kitsch_Las_Vegas
description: Kitsch Las Vegas is the tacky, over-the-top spectacle culture of the Las Vegas Strip from the 1950s through the 1970s — figurative neon signage blazing against black night, wall-to-wall hot pink and cherry-red interiors, wedding chapels, slot machines, showgirls and rhinestone Elvis impersonators. Its visual DNA is saturated red-to-magenta chroma, bulb-studded and tube-bent signage, feather-and-sequin costuming, and crowded staged tableaux of conspicuous wealth, rendered in vintage color-film or postcard-chrome saturation. Load this skill when images of casino signs, shotgun weddings, gambling floors or showgirl spectacle must read as deliberately tacky spectacle rather than modern luxury.

name: Kmeng_Steav
description: Kmeng Steav (Bek Sloy) is the early-2010s Cambodian street-youth aesthetic: dyed side-swept fringes over one eye, checkered polos and counterfeit-logo tees tucked into skinny jeans, crew snapshots packed around scooters, village porches and club doorways. Its palette runs blue, yellow, black, purple and white under faded warm phone-camera filters or magenta club light, with peace signs, finger hearts and remix-DJ watermarks sealing the "cute but gangster" party mood. Recognize it by crowded low-res group frames, knockoff brand prints, and fringed hair as the crown of the look.

name: Knightcore
description: Knightcore is a Tumblr-born martial-medieval aesthetic centered on the figure of the knight: weathered steel plate and chainmail, riveted leather, wool cloaks, and swords gripped in gauntleted hands, set against misty forests, castle ramparts, fields and open skies. Its palette is silver steel, earth brown, dark green and fog grey, punctured only by heraldic red or royal blue, lit by overcast diffusion, dusk amber or candlelit sepia. Recognize it by armor-and-weapon close crops, chivalric and religious symbolic imagery, and a solemn, honorable mood — never courtly opulence, never high-magic spectacle, never horror.

name: Kogal
description: Kogal (kogyaru, Heisei gyaru) is the mid-1990s Japanese schoolgirl branch of Gyaru culture: high school uniforms deliberately broken into fashion — hitched-up plaid skirts, beige knit sweaters, slouched white loose socks over loafers or platforms — worn with bleached or honey-dyed hair, heavy make-up and, in the classic era, tanned skin. Signature cargo includes decoden (phone cases, mirrors and trinket boxes crusted with pearls, cabochons and whipped-cream glue), added neck bows, charm-laden shoulder bags, and glossy daytime street-snap group poses. Palette runs beige, white, black and pastels laid over grey, navy or lavender plaids.

name: Korean_Cozy_Beige
description: Korean Cozy Beige (also called Beige Milk Tea or Korean Neutral Beige) is a Korean Instagram-to-Pinterest aesthetic of tidy domesticity in an ivory–oat–milk-tea-brown palette: bottled milk tea and lattes in clear or white cups, cookies and tiramisu on ceramic plates, linen bedding by sunlit windows, rattan baskets, oatmeal knits, study desks with laptops and washi-taped prints. Natural window light, clean blog-style compositions and slow-living minimalism give it a cozy-yet-mature tone, with cuteness admitted only as tiny character accents (Rilakkuma, Line Friends, Sanrio). Recognize or generate it through neutral palette dominance, orderly negative space, faceless candid presence, and cafe-study-home subject matter.

name: Krocha
description: Krocha is the flash-lit, neon-on-black youth subculture look of Viennese malls, fairgrounds and Netlog profiles circa 2005–2008: gelled bleached Vokuhila mullets, solarium-orange tans, keffiyeh scarves, neon Ed Hardy caps, V-neck tees and oversized belt buckles over tight jeans and white sneakers. It survives visually as harsh compact-flash party snapshots and motion-blurred phone-camera video stills, plus a Vectordelia-style graphic arm of black dancing silhouettes on pink/yellow/fluorescent-green splatter with distorted-capitalization slang ("BAM OIDA", "kRocHa traxx"). Recognize it by teenage group poses with peace signs and pointing fingers, argyle diamonds, brand-logo maximalism, and consumer-leisure settings (mall atriums, funfair ride platforms, contest stages).

name: Krushclub
description: Krushclub is the strictly monochrome cover-art and edit aesthetic of the early-2020s bitcrushed Jersey Club microgenre — black, white and dithered grey only, soaked in CRT scanlines, pixel crush and radiant bloom glow. Its signature stock is stars, hearts and butterflies in repeating scatters, anime angels and goth girls with blown-out glowing eyes, low-poly and PlayStation-era packaging relics, barcodes, vertical Japanese text and illegible metal-style logotypes. Recognize it by greyscale digital decay (scanlines, dither, photocopy contrast) fused with Y2K gaming nostalgia and rave-cute iconography.

name: LOLcore
description: LOLcore is a short-lived mid-2010s fashion aesthetic (peak autumn 2014) that turns Pop Art and mass consumerism into couture — clashing high-chroma primaries and secondaries, cartoon/manga and fast-food logo prints, oversized childlike accessories such as giant lollipops, mascot-head backpacks and cartoon gloves, staged in candy shops, supermarket aisles and runway sets. Recognize it by its deliberate silliness and self-mockery: bodycon dresses, colorful faux fur and patent vinyl loaded with branded kitsch, shot as flash-bright editorials, runway looks or flat magazine illustrations, in open revolt against Normcore minimalism.

name: Lad_Culture
description: Lad Culture (Laddism) is the visual language of 1990s British working-class male youth crews — groups of lads in Adidas tracksuits, football shirts, striped rugby polos, parkas and bucket hats, caught in boisterous snapshot realism on terraces, pub benches, high streets and playing fields. Its palette is sportswear block color: kit red, royal and sky blue, navy, optic white and black, lit by overcast UK daylight or harsh on-camera flash. Recognize it by the crew rather than the individual: arms over shoulders, mock-wrestling, deadpan banter, beer cans, football iconography and lads'-mag cheek, never solo glamour.

name: Larme_Kei
description: Larme Kei is the mid-2010s Tokyo "sweet girly artbook" aesthetic of LARME magazine — hyper-feminine coordinates that pair girlish pastel frill (pink puff-sleeve blouses, tulle, ribbons, pearls) with mature or sexy anchors (black pencil skirts, leather, chokers, garter details), shot in soft hazy light or assembled as collage-edited magazine spreads with transparent bows, hearts and dreamy English script. Signature cues: blunt or wispy bangs, cry-eye pink eyeshadow with circle lenses, unsmiling pouty faces, Mary Janes or pumps with sheer lace socks, and texture mixing of lace, sheer, fur and leather over a pink-black-red-white palette.

name: Laser_Grid
description: Laser Grid is the 1980s technosphere aesthetic of glowing perspective or flat grids, hand-drawn wireframe vector lines and airbrushed chrome on black grounds, extending into sleek right-angled interiors clad in mirror panels, glass blocks and chrome slats. Signature elements are luminous neon grid planes, laser beams with airbrushed halos, pinstriped logotypes, and metallic airbrush gradients; typical subjects are consumer-electronics ads, computing magazine covers, cartridge and package design, striped corporate logos, and monochrome reflective rooms. Recognize it by light-on-dark vector glow plus period airbrush grain, or by pale plaster rooms structured by chrome wire grids and mirrored walls.

name: Light_Academia
description: Light Academia is the 2010s Tumblr-born, sunlit counterpart of Dark Academia: a desaturated cream–beige–camel palette lit by natural golden light, populated by old books, white marble and plaster sculpture, Beaux-Arts colonnades and Haussmannian moldings, cursive letters, wool knits and plaid, porcelain tea sets and cozy domestic study scenes. Recognize it by its optimistic, tender scholarship — hope, friendship and happy endings rendered in ivory, tan and pale gold — never by gothic gloom, blackness or tragedy.

name: Liminal_Space
description: Internet-born aesthetic (crystallized in the late 2010s around The Backrooms legend) of transitional spaces devoid of people — school hallways, mall concourses, waiting rooms, stairwells, parking lots, vacant playgrounds, pool halls — dressed in late-20th-century institutional fabric: linoleum, drop-ceiling tiles, beige ceramic tile, cool fluorescent troffers. Palette runs cream yellow and building-neutral beige through black-and-grey shadow, frequently degraded by grain, compression noise and camera date stamps. Mood is uncanny familiarity: nostalgia and comfort fused with quiet dread, a place waiting for people who never arrive.

name: Live_Laugh_Love
description: Live Laugh Love is the 2000s-born US feel-good slogan aesthetic: brushy, thick-thin script and tall narrow Rae Dunn-style block caps carrying saccharine or winking-ironic affirmations across wooden signs, chalkboards, glazed pottery, wall decals and social-media shareables. Its palette is cream, greige beige, wood brown, chalkboard black and blush-pink pastels, lit soft and high-key, with terracotta or gold-foil script as the accent. Recognize it by word art as the compositional hero over domestic subjects — coffee, home, family, self-love, wine-mom irony — never mascots, pastoral narrative or western iconography.

name: Living_Doll
description: Living Doll is an early-2010s internet beauty aesthetic in which a human face and body are styled — circle lenses, doll makeup, poreless airbrushed skin, waist-length saturated hair, hyperfeminine frilled fashion — into a manufactured toy doll, uncanny and serene. Its palette is pink and pastels over porcelain matte skin, with platinum-blonde or crimson hair as the saturated accent; images are soft, evenly lit portraits, selfies, paired doll portraits and thumbnail-framed video stills. Recognize it by lens-enlarged wide eyes with heavy liner and lashes, tiny glossy lips, stiff posed stillness and a heavy digital-retouch sheen that sits between photograph and illustration.

name: Lo-fi_Art
description: Lo-fi Art is the 2010s stream-culture aesthetic of quiet, anime-styled slice-of-life scenes — a solitary figure studying or listening with headphones in a cluttered cozy room, or an empty rain-slick city street at night — rendered in muted analogous cool colors (blues, purples, pinks) punctuated by small pockets of warm lamp or screen glow. Signature elements include rainy windows, houseplants, sleeping pets, Japanese signage, and deliberate analog degradation (film grain, soft focus, VHS static, pixel dithering). Recognize it by its "chill-cozy" stillness: low-energy mundane moments, environment-first composition, and a nostalgic pre-digital finish.

name: Lobotomy_Chic
description: Lobotomy Chic (aka the dissociative pout / selfie nihilism) is a 2020s Instagram-born aesthetic of feminine detachment: lo-fi point-and-shoot flash snapshots of young women holding a vacant, parted-lip pout or an eye-roll inside mundane, liminal interiors. Its palette is flash-bleached white, grey, brown, beige-yellow and light blue, with messy hair, smudged or absent makeup, ironic Catholic iconography (wall crucifixes, cross necklaces, nun habits) and plain-text parody tees. It reads as an amateur film scan or early digicam frame — grain, dust, awkward crops, deadpan mood — never as polished editorial photography.

name: Logomania
description: Logomania (Brandmania) is a maximalist fashion aesthetic built on the saturated, all-over repetition of luxury-house monograms and wordmarks across jackets, suits, tights, bags and hardware. Born in 1980s Harlem through Dapper Dan's sampled luxury streetwear, peaking again in Y2K pop culture and the 2010s streetwear-luxury merger, it favors brown monogram canvas, black-and-white jacquard, navy, red and green, oversized silhouettes, bucket hats, sunglasses and oversized branded hardware. Recognize it by logo-as-fabric density: the brand mark is the textile itself, covering whole garments rather than appearing as a single small chest hit.

name: Lolicore
description: Lolicore is the deliberately trashy visual language of the mid-2000s 4chan breakcore/speedcore scene: moe and slice-of-life anime cutouts defaced with black censorship bars, blood and firearm gurokawa overlays, Windows-UI debris, and maximalist deep-fried collages of stolen fan art, pixel fonts and graffiti tags over pastel-neon-black-red palettes. Recognize it by amateur cut-and-paste execution, censor-barred anime eyes, deadpan real-person photo inserts, and satirical shock juxtaposition; its 2020s register trades shock imagery for muted blue-purple databent glitch while keeping an anime anchor.

name: Lolita
description: Japanese fashion subculture (Harajuku, late 1990s–2000s) built on a petticoat-held bell or A-line skirt at knee length, dense lace, bow and ruffle trim, and headwear such as bonnets and head bows. Palette is keyed to substyle — Sweet pastels (baby pink, sax blue, butter yellow, ivory), Classic muted earth tones (brown, wine, sage, cornflower), Gothic blacks and dark reds — with prints of sweets, animals, florals, tartan or crosses. Recognize by the poofy skirt volume, opaque tights, round-toe strap shoes, shaped bags and parasols, photographed as everyday wear in soft-daylight street snaps.

name: Lovecore
description: Lovecore (also Heartcore, Crushcore, Cupidcore, Valentinecore) is a 2010s Tumblr-born internet aesthetic built on the commercial iconography of Valentine's Day — hearts on nearly every surface, love letters, roses, heart-shaped chocolates, lipstick kisses, cherubs — rendered in a strictly pink, red and white palette ranging from powdered blush to oxblood. Its surfaces are satin, pearl, matte paper, glossy plastic, yarn and neon glass; its lighting swings between diffused high-key blush and dark rooms lit by heart-shaped light. The mood is sweet, nostalgic and unapologetically sentimental, celebrating love itself — crushes, courtship rituals, queer joy — and never heartbreak.

name: Low_Poly
description: 3D aesthetic of deliberately sparse polygon meshes — blocky, triangular faceted models rendered with flat or per-vertex shading, in either textureless vibrant simple colors or low-resolution pixelated textures. Born from 1990s PlayStation, Nintendo 64 and Dreamcast hardware and revived in the 2010s as an intentional, Modernist anti-realism. Signature cues: hard visible facets, saturated azure skies with cumulus clouds and turquoise water (the Sega Blue Sky lineage), liminal empty spaces, and — in its PSX branch — texel-gritty textures and dim vertex-lit interiors used for uncanny horror.

name: Lowbrow
description: Lowbrow (Pop Surrealism) is the underground Los Angeles painting movement born in the late 1960s from underground comix, hot-rod and tiki culture, punk and pulp kitsch. Recognize it by its glossy airbrush-or-glaze finish, big-eyed doll-children and anthropomorphic animal characters, candy-saturated sunset palettes or porcelain-antique pastels, and creepy-cute humor built on retro pop-culture citation. Typical subjects include tiki idols, rat-fink monsters, pinups, animated objects, meat-and-sweet still lifes, and parodies of old-master tableaux.

name: Lulicore
description: Lulicore (可露丽风 / "Canelé Style") is a 2025 Chinese fashion aesthetic born on Rednote that dresses the body like a French canelé: a dominant base of crust browns and mocha mousse punctuated by discrete creamy pastel accents (pistachio, strawberry cream, butter yellow, lavender) standing in for the dessert's filling. Signature elements include canelé and dessert props, brown-outer-over-pastel-inner layering, slouch socks, berets and pearls, art-toy plush staging, and color-blocked poster layouts with retro cursive wordmarks. Mood is sweet, gentle and playful; typical subjects are full-body fit checks, café and street snapshots, and dessert-styled still lifes.

name: Lumberjack
description: Late-2000s "lumbersexual" workwear aesthetic built on red-and-black buffalo plaid flannel, raw selvedge denim, duck-canvas overalls, heritage work boots, watch-cap beanies and full beards. Its palette pins one loud brick-red plaid against earth-muted neutrals — brown, khaki, olive, indigo, weathered-wood grey — in posed outdoor portraits with axes at rest, split firewood, vintage pickups and conifer forest. Reads as romanticized manual labor: rugged, earnest, texture-forward, anti-gloss.

name: Lunarpunk
description: Lunarpunk is the nocturnal twin of Solarpunk — a late-2010s speculative aesthetic imagining a sustainable, hopeful future that lives by night, lit only by moonlight, starlight and bioluminescence. Its visual DNA is a deep indigo-violet-black palette pierced by soft teal, foxfire-green and orchid glows emanating from living things (glowing mushrooms, radiant flora, moths, fireflies), over dark reflective water, moon-dominated skies, organic living-wood architecture and solitary cloaked or hooded figures. Recognize it by night-as-setting plus living light plus occult-natural motifs; distinguish it from Solarpunk's daylight greens, Cyberdelia's chemical neon, Dreampunk's hazy liminality, Goth's mourning black, and Naturecore's sunlit coziness.

name: MDLR
description: MDLR ("Mec de la Rue") is the late-2010s Spanish street-rap subculture of working-class barrio youth: glossy puffer jackets and hooded tracksuits in black, gray and navy, a fanny pack (riñonera) slung diagonally across the chest, air-unit sneakers, hoods up or balaclavas, posed in duos on tiled sidewalks beside parked cars or under harsh phone-flash at night. Signature cues include acronym hand gestures, electric scooters, snapshot-real lighting, and a saturated poster-graphic variant, all tied to Morad's drill scene and an ethos of neighborhood pride. Use this skill for images of Spanish/Mediterranean street youth in sportswear, flash-lit corner poses, or flat-color graphic portraits carrying the same codes.

name: MLG
description: MLG (Major League Gaming / montage parodies) is a 2010s YouTube-born parody aesthetic (peak 2014–2017) that mocks competitive Call of Duty and Halo frag movies through maximalist collage: over-saturated rainbow gradients, neon green and gold, hitmarkers stamped onto non-gaming objects, 8-bit "Deal With It" sunglasses, Doritos and Mountain Dew logos, sniper scopes, air horns, Illuminati triangles and meme faces layered with zero negative space. Recognize it by ironic "epic" gaming-HUD grammar applied to mundane subjects, glossy sponsor-logo parody, and compressed JPEG clip-art clutter; separate it from plain meme maximalism by its FPS montage vocabulary and from deep-fried memes by the fact that degradation is incidental, not the point.

name: Mad_Scientist
description: Mad Scientist is a camp-gothic laboratory aesthetic in which neon green and ultraviolet purple glow against steel, glassware and dark haze — cluttered labs of imposing, deliberately confusing machinery, specimen tanks, bubbling flasks and manic white-coated experimenters. It runs from Frankenstein's gothic origins through 1930s horror-film labs to 1990s cartoon labs and synth-pop irony, always balancing ominous dread with knowing camp. Recognize it by self-luminous toxic liquids, tesla arcs, biohazard marks, brass-and-rubber gadgetry, and figures lit from below by their own experiments.

name: Madchester
description: Madchester (aka Baggy or the Second Summer of Love) is the visual culture of Manchester's indie-dance scene, 1987–1992: saturated rainbow psychedelia, hand-painted bubble-letter logotypes, 1960s pop-art portraits and paper collage, and baggy streetwear — bucket hats, oversized T-shirts, wide-legged jeans, trainers — captured in grainy snapshot or duotone-wash photography. Recognise it in band group shots, club and warehouse rave imagery, type-hero psychedelic posters and sleeves, and Manchester civic-pride signage; it fuses indie-guitar iconography with acid-house colour euphoria, which is what separates it from pure Acid House, Casuals, or grey anorak indie.

name: Mafia_Aesthetic
description: Mafia Aesthetic (Mafiacore, Mobster Chic) is the romanticized visual language of the fictional Italian-American mob — pinstriped suits, fedoras, overcoats, Tommy guns, cigars, crystal tumblers and red velvet, rendered in high-contrast black-and-white or near-monochrome muted color pierced by a single oxblood-red or amber accent. Low-key chiaroscuro, cigarette smoke, film grain and fragmentary close-ups of hands, weapons and luxury props convey poised threat, ceremonial loyalty and imminent betrayal. Load this skill for Prohibition-through-Sopranos-era gangster tableaux, mob-wife glamour, smoky back-room still lifes, and greyscale editorial collages in this register.

name: Magical_Girl
description: Magical Girl (mahou shoujo) is the Japanese heroine aesthetic born of 1960s shoujo media and codified by 1990s Sailor Moon-era cel anime: young girls caught mid-transformation in color-coded frilled costumes, wreathed in ribbon light-trails, stars, hearts and glitter, anchored in pink and gold. Recognition hinges on metamorphosis signifiers — wands, lockets, compact brooches, floods of white light, sailor-collar frills, brightly colored hair, animal mascots — plus team color-coding where each girl owns one hue, weapon and power. Load this skill for anime heroine transformation scenes, mahou kei fashion and prop still-lifes, sparkle-laden team lineups and ensemble poster collages; not for generic cuteness (Kawaii, Moe), retro anime mundanity (Animecore) or pastel street fashion without hero props (Fairy Kei).

name: Magician
description: Magician (Magiciancore / Stage-Magician Core) is the theatrical aesthetic of the stage illusionist, from 18th-century magic shows to vaudeville poster art and modern street-magic drama: tailcoats, top hats, white gloves, playing cards, crystal balls, rabbits, wands, velvet curtains and spotlight chiaroscuro. Its palette is jewel-dark — burgundy, deep blue, emerald, purple, black — pierced by gold, silver, cyan or lime accents, or faded cream-and-rose paper tones in lighthearted vintage takes. Recognize it by showman poster typography, levitation and trick tableau, ornate proscenium framing, and the declared tension of staged deception ("it's all an act") rather than lived sorcery.

name: Maid
description: Japanese pop-culture service-uniform aesthetic born in 2000s Akihabara maid cafés, built on the ruffled apron-dress: fitted bodice, flared skirt, contrasting lace-trimmed apron, frilled headdress, thigh-high socks. Palette splits between classic black-and-white servant contrast and kawaii pastels (pink, baby blue, lavender) cut by white lace; signature props are feather dusters, tea trays, parfaits and ketchup-doodled omurice, set in rococo pastel café interiors or promo-poster graphics. Recognize by the apron-plus-headdress uniform grammar and performed cuteness, whether in café promo photography, cosplay snaps, anime cel illustration, or menu/poster design.

name: Maidcore
description: Maidcore is the mid-2010s Russian VK music-scene aesthetic of anonymous "X the Maid" personas (Nijiura Maids borrowed from 2chan), rendered as lo-fi "Oekaki Punk" anime cover art: jagged non-anti-aliased lines, sketchy flat fills, muted monochrome or fog-grey palettes pierced by neon magenta/cyan glitch accents, post-Soviet doomer settings, drug paraphernalia and bitmap pixel typography. Recognize it by the deliberate dissonance between a cute frilled maid costume and a bleak, noisy, depressive-aggressive treatment.

name: Maillard_Style
description: Maillard Style (Maillard Feng) is a Chinese fashion microtrend of autumn 2023–24 that builds monochrome, head-to-toe outfits on a seared-steak gradient of browns — tan, caramel, rust, chocolate, burgundy — mixed through leather, shearling fur, chunky knits and satin brocade, with khaki or off-white accents. Recognize it by tonal brown layering, deliberate plush-versus-smooth texture clashes, quiet-luxury silhouettes (oversized coats, wide corset belts, slouchy boots, structured leather bags) and smoky matte brown makeup; it reads warm, autumnal, heritage-minded and faintly "appetizing," the deliberate opposite of Dopamine brightness.

name: Mall_Ninja
description: Mall Ninja is the early-2000s internet stereotype of unearned "badass" weapon posturing, captured in low-resolution flash photographs, meme macros and forum screenshots of people in cheap black coats, fedoras and sunglasses brandishing tacky katanas, nunchaku and oversized or iridescent rainbow blades in basements, suburban yards and mall corridors. Its palette yokes camouflage olive/tan and polyester black to oil-slick rainbow blade accents, dragon embroidery and boastful overlaid first-person quotes, all rendered with sincere, unselfaware grandeur. Recognize it by the gap between lethal self-image and mundane, cheap, domestic reality.

name: Mallgoth
description: Mallgoth is the North American teen subculture look of the late 1990s to mid-2000s: a mall-bought, commercialized goth fused with nu-metal bagginess — black band tees, wide-leg Tripp-style bondage pants hung with chains and straps, fishnet, platform boots, studded belts, spiked chokers and ankh or inverted-cross silver, over pale skin with "raccoon" black eyeliner and dark lips. It photographs like a consumer snapshot: direct on-camera flash in bedrooms, basements, parking lots and shopping-mall interiors, black-dominant palette accented with red, purple and silver, mood of performative teenage angst undercut by dark humor.

name: Mallsoft
description: Mallsoft (Mallwave) is a 2010s vaporwave-offshoot aesthetic built on 1980s–90s shopping-mall architecture: skylit atriums, multi-level concourses, indoor fountains, potted palms, and neon storefront signage in pink, teal, mint, lavender, white, and gold. Its images split between bright "golden era" mercantile spaces and shuttered "dead mall" decay, typically softened by VHS grain, haze, or pastel CGI dreaminess to stage empty, nostalgic liminality. Recognize it by people-free tile-floored concourses, fluorescent coffered ceilings, skylight trusses, and consumerist architecture treated as memory rather than documentation.

name: Manba
description: Manba is the extreme late-1990s/early-2000s Shibuya gyaru substyle: a deep, uniform artificial chocolate-brown tan armored with stark white "panda" concealer bands around the eyes and lips, voluminous bleached-platinum or neon-dyed hair extensions, face stickers and glitter, and loud neon or Hawaiian-hibiscus clubwear with leis and platform boots. Recognize it in flash-lit maximalist portraits, purikura booth prints and egg/Ranzuki magazine scans where saturated pink, mint, yellow and orange collide against dark tan skin, always with a deliberate, gleeful anti-elegance.

name: Mandrake
description: Mandrake is the funk carioca street identity of Brazilian favela youth (Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo; music roots in the 1980s–90s, style cohering in the 2000s), built on logo-loud football club jerseys and brand tracksuits, gold or silver chains and watches, large mirrored sunglasses, snapback caps, visible tattoos and customized motorcycles, captured in harsh-daylight phone selfies, crew snapshots and glossy KondZilla-style video stills. Its palette is high-contrast club color — red-black, orange-black, white, saturated cyan and royal blue — punctured by metallic gold and mirror-lens glints. Recognize it by ostentatious "chave" posing, tropa crew groupings, baile funk and bare concrete street settings, and an attitude of defiant pride.

name: Manguebeat
description: Manguebeat (Manguebit) is the visual language of the 1990s Recife counterculture — maracatu-bright primaries (white, blue, yellow, red, green) on sun-bleached grounds, crabs and parabolic dishes grafted into mangrove mud, rope-laced alfaia drums, straw hats and dark sunglasses over thrifted rainbow stripes. Recognize it by flat print-like color, sunburst poster logic, mud-anchored fusion of folk percussion with analog tech, and a defiant, groove-carried mood of social and ecological critique.

name: Manueline
description: Manueline (Portuguese Late Gothic, c. 1490–1521) is the maritime ornament style of Manuel I's Portugal: honey-gold and cream limestone in which portals, windows, columns and arcades erupt into carved ship's rope, armillary spheres, shells, coral, oak and laurel sprigs and the Cross of the Order of Christ, all laid over a rigorous Late-Gothic skeleton of pointed arches, rib vaults and tracery. Recognize it by stone that behaves like rope and growing plants, by Age-of-Discoveries nautical emblems, and by sunlit pale-gold masonry against Atlantic sky or water; typical subjects are monastery cloisters and portals, water-edge fortified towers, great traceried chapter-house windows, pillories, fonts and tombs.

name: Marshmallow_Girl
description: Marshmallow Girl (Mashumaro Joshi) is a 2010s Japanese body-positive fashion aesthetic coined by La Farfa magazine, built on yurufuwa (loose-fluffy) dressing: rounded, uncinched silhouettes in bright candy pastels (mint, bubblegum pink, lemon, sky blue) over white and cream, with sweets-and-fruit prints, lace and bow trim, opaque tights and Mary Janes. Recognition hinges on joyful plus-size or soft-rounded subjects giving cute open expressions (waves, peace signs, smiles), high-key catalog or idol-group photography, and rounded coral-pink Japanese magazine typography. It differs from Gyaru (tanned, glam-sexy), general Kawaii (structured Lolita silhouettes, any body type), and Western Soft Girl (muted, dreamy pastels).

name: Martial_Industrial
description: Martial Industrial is the album-sleeve and poster language of the 1980s European post-industrial scene: sepia or monochrome archival photography, grainy halftone and blind-stamped leather, centred heraldic or esoteric sigils, and letterspaced blackletter or roman capitals on black, olive drab, oxblood or parchment grounds. Signature subjects are massed shields and parade formations, classical and baroque sculpture, eagles and ossuaries, and hooded or turned-away uniformed figures, all arranged with funereal symmetry and propaganda-poster discipline. Recognize it by the combination of archival degradation, monumental statuary or military mass, and austere typographic framing.

name: Maximalism
description: Maximalism is the aesthetic of deliberate excess, descended from Baroque and Rococo horror vacui, Victorian eclecticism, and the post-2010s anti-minimalist resurgence, recognisable by bold clashing colours, layered prints, wallpaper, rugs and collections that fill every inch of the frame. Signature elements include gilded ornament (rococo cartouches, c-scrolls, cresting), pattern-on-pattern surfaces, cabinets of curiosities and crowded shelves, trompe-l'œil ceilings, carved lacquer, and sentimental clutter; typical subjects run from ornament-saturated interiors and portrait-like gilded objects to baroque façades, dense figurative panoramas and candy-bright contemporary rooms. If a surface is empty, it is not maximalism.

name: McBling
description: McBling (Trashy Y2K, Glam Y2K, 2000s Glam) is the maximalist "trashy glamour" aesthetic of US celebrity culture c. 2000–2008: hot-pink velour tracksuits, rhinestones and glitter, logo-mania (Juicy Couture, Von Dutch, Playboy), low-rise jeans, bedazzled flip phones, shot in harsh paparazzi flash or saturated music-video pink. Recognize it by a pink-dominant palette punctured by metallics and black/white graphics, animal prints, curvy 1970s script and tabloid typography, and candid fame-culture framing. It is not sleek chrome Y2K Futurism, nor the cleaner modern Barbiecore/Baddie revivals.

name: Meatcore
description: Meatcore (also Fleshcore) is an obscure web-native aesthetic of raw meat, organs, blood and body horror treated with cuteness or artistic tenderness — styrofoam trays under cling film, marbled steak closeups, flesh-assemblage creatures and kawaii characters, in arterial red, reddish white and tray pink. It holds discord, discomfort and disgust in tension with body-positive and feminist readings of "we are all just meat," and circulates as supermarket flash snapshots, dithered digital edits and flat cute illustration. Recognize it by uncooked flesh as the hero subject, commodity packaging print, and sweet-or-deadpan framing of abject material.

name: Mecha
description: Mecha is the Japanese postwar aesthetic of giant piloted humanoid machines and sleek androids: stark white and metallic-gray armor plate split by black panel lines, accented with primary reds and blues or military olive, cool blue sensor glow, samurai-crest silhouettes and exposed hydraulic joints. Subjects range from skyscraper-scale combat robots framed against smoke and explosion light, to catalog-clean gynoid renders, split-face mechanical portraits, and wearable headgear props on ordinary people — all unified by engineered panel-line logic and the man-machine union. It emerges from 1950s manga (Astro Boy, Tetsujin 28-go), matures through Gundam's military realism, and darkens with Evangelion's psychological turn.

name: Med-Tech_Visions
description: Med-Tech Visions is the slick pseudo-CGI stock imagery of medical and science communication from the mid-1990s onward: glossy 3D renders of organs, cells, neurons, DNA helices and microchips suspended in deep blue or black voids, lit from within by cyan glow with a single warm red-orange-yellow highlight element.
